questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 3-year-old child is brought to the OPD with complaints of persistent delayed developmental milestones, and hyperpigmented macular lesions on the body which are more pronounced on exposure to sunlight. What is the error in DNA multiplication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nucleotide excision repair

The history points to a diagnosis of xeroderma pigmentosum. It is characterized by defective nucleotide excision repair.

UV radiation leads to pyrimidine dimerization in DNA strands, preventing further replication by DNA polymerase. The nucleotide excision repair mechanism corrects the dimer formation in DNA. Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by an inability to repair DNA pyrimidine dimers caused by UV exposure. This leads to clinical and cellular hypersensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

In XP the skin is normal at birth and has a three-stage progression:

• Diffuse erythema, scaling, and freckle-like areas over the sun-exposed regions of the body at around 6 months of age.
• The second stage is characterized by poikiloderma. This results in skin atrophy, telangiectasias with mottled hyperpigmentation, and hyperpigmentation.
• In the third stage appearance of cutaneous malignancies like squamous cell carcinomas, malignant melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and fibrosarcoma.

Most of the cases with XP have ocular manifestations. Initially, it appears as photophobia, conjunctivitis, ectropion, and symblepharon with ulceration. Accumulation of pyrimidine dimer causes corneal opacification and neovascularization. Ocular malignancies are common in the lids, conjunctiva, and cornea as they are exposed to as much as facial skin. XP is ultimately fatal, and early detection of the skin lesions and their management with prevention of UV ray exposures prolong life.
questions.learning: Nucleotide excision repair — The history points to a diagnosis of xeroderma pigmentosum. It is characterized by defective nucleotide excision repair.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 20-year-old male came with complaints of pain over the left flank associated with fever and chills. On examination, the patient had pain on the passive extension of the hip over the left side. Lab investigations reveal leucocytosis. CT scan shows findings as shown. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Psoas Abscess

The clinical vignette of a patient with flank pain, fever, leucocytosis, positive psoas sign, and the CT scan showing a mass in the psoas muscle lateral to the vertebral column is diagnostic of a psoas abscess.

Psoas Abscess -

Commonly presents in males > females. In developed countries, the age of presentation is between 44 - 58 years and in developing countries <20 years of age.

Clinical features include fever, pain in the back or flank region, mass in the inguinal region, anorexia, and unintentional weight reduction. "Psoas sign" is pain brought on by extension of the hip.

Lab investigation - Leucocytosis, increased ESR, and mild anemia may be seen.

Diagnosis - Commonly confirmed using a CT scan. Blood culture and abscess material should be obtained in all cases to guide therapy.

Treatment - Percutaneous or surgical drainage plus Antibiotics
questions.learning: Psoas Abscess — The clinical vignette of a patient with flank pain, fever, leucocytosis, positive psoas sign, and the CT scan showing a mass in the psoas muscle lateral to the vertebral column is diagnostic of a psoas abscess.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young man presented with severe muscle weakness and ptosis. Chest X-ray revealed an anterior mediastinal mass. Further investigation reveals the presence of AchR antibodies. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis? AchR -Acetylcholine receptor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

The given clinical scenario of weakness, ptosis, anterior mediastinal mass( thymoma), and the presence of AchR antibodies are suggestive of myasthenia gravis.

Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorder due to autoimmune damage to the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the NMJ. It is characterized by weakness and muscle fatigue. Weakness increases with usage and muscle movement is difficult at the end of the day. It affects proximal muscles leading to weakness of the limbs. Ocular features like ptosis and diplopia can also be seen. Myasthenia gravis is often related to thymomas. Symptoms of myasthenia gravis improve after excision of the thymus gland even in the absence of a thymoma.  Treatment includes Anticholinesterase drugs like Pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, and even Thymectomy if the condition is associated with a Thymoma. Recently Rozanolixizumab has been approved for treating cases of generalized Myasthenia gravis.

Other options:

Option B: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder affecting the presynaptic membrane at the NMJ. Patients present with proximal muscle weakness of the lower limbs, ptosis, and diplopia.  Treatment involves plasmapheresis, immunotherapy, and drugs such as 3,4-diaminopyridine (3,4-DAP) and pyridostigmine.

Option C: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked muscular dystrophy due to mutations in the dystrophin gene. It most commonly affects boys in their childhood. Patients initially present with proximal muscle weakness predominantly in the lower limbs. Calf muscle hypertrophy is a cardinal feature. Other features include mental retardation, cardiac failure, and myoglobinuria. Treatment includes corticosteroids, Eteplirsen, and Casimersen.

Option D: Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disorder affecting multiple systems. It is associated with skeletal muscle weakness, cataracts, endocrinopathy, and cardiomyopathy. The treatment is mainly symptomatic however, mexiletine is indicated for reducing myotonia.
questions.learning: Myasthenia gravis — The given clinical scenario of weakness, ptosis, anterior mediastinal mass( thymoma), and the presence of AchR antibodies are suggestive of myasthenia gravis.

1. Female population is at greater risk of developing blindness.
2. People dwelling in rural areas are at increased risk of developing blindness.
3. Risk of developing blindness increases with age.
4. Illiteracy leads to increased risk of developing blindness.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3 and 4

The correct statements drawn from the values given in the table are 3 and 4.

An odds ratio is a measure of the association between an exposure and an outcome. It represents the odds that an outcome will occur given a particular exposure in comparison to the odds of the outcome occurring in the absence of that exposure.

An odds ratio of 1 indicates that the risk factor is not related to the disease.

An odds ratio of less than 1 indicates that a person with the disease is less likely to have been exposed to the factor, implying that the factor may be a protective factor against the disease.

An odds ratio greater than 1 indicates that the odds ratio is significant, and the factor can be ascertained as a risk factor.

The p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one that was actually observed in the biological or clinical experiment. A p-value of less than 0.05 indicates that the test result is statistically significant.

Other options:

Statement 1: Female population is at greater risk of developing blindness is a false statement; since the odds ratio is <1, the female population will be at lesser risk of developing blindness than the male population.

Statement 2: People dwelling in rural areas are at increased risk of developing blindness is also false; a p-value of >0.05 means that this association is not statistically significant.
questions.learning: 3 and 4 The correct statements drawn from the values given in the table are 3 and 4. An odds ratio is a measure of the association between an exposure and an outcome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis was taking Indomethacin for pain. He was started on an ACE inhibitor for hypertension. What is the potential adverse effect that is likely to occur with this combination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperkalemia

A patient taking Indomethacin who is started on an ACE Inhibitor is at risk for hyperkalemia.

ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers cause hyperkalemia in the background of renal failure or diabetes. The following drugs, when taken along with ACE inhibitors and ARBs, can cause significant hyperkalemia:

* NSAIDs like Indomethacin

* Potassium-sparing aldosterone antagonists like Spironolactone, Eplerenone

* Direct renin inhibitors like Aliskiren

* Potassium supplements

* β receptor blockers like Metoprolol

Beta-blockers and NSAIDs both inhibit renin release. Additionally, beta-blockers also cause a cellular shift of potassium from the cell to the bloodstream. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reducing blood flow to the kidneys and causing renal impairment.

Hyperkalemia commonly presents as cardiac arrhythmias like sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, slow idioventricular rhythms, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and asystole. It can also present with ascending paralysis, which may lead to diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory failure.
questions.learning: Hyperkalemia — A patient taking Indomethacin who is started on an ACE Inhibitor is at risk for hyperkalemia. ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers cause hyperkalemia in the background of renal failure or diabetes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A bodybuilder starts eating raw eggs for protein. He starts to develop fatigue on moderate exercise. The doctor prescribes a vitamin. Which enzyme is deficient in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyruvate Carboxylase

The patient developed pyruvate carboxylase enzyme deficiency.

• Biotin serves as co-enzyme for the synthesis of several carboxylase enzymes such as:

• Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
• Pyruvate carboxylase
• Propionyl CoA carboxylase
• Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase

• Individuals who eat an excess of uncooked egg-white, develops biotin deficiency and as a result deficiency of the carboxylase enzymes. This is because, a protein called, avidin present in the egg-white bind to biotin in the diet, and makes biotin unavailable for intestinal absorption.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During the assessment of drinking water from a village tank. Which of the following parameters is not within the acceptable limits for safe drinking water?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cadmium- 0.3 mg/L

The guideline value for cadmium in drinking water is established at 0.3 µg/L. Therefore cadmium level of 0.3 mg/L is higher than the permissible limit.

Cadmium is released into the environment through wastewater, fertilizers, and air pollution, and contamination in drinking water may also occur from galvanized pipes and metal fittings. Since cadmium accumulates in the kidneys and has a very long biological half-life in humans (10–35 years), exceeding the safe limit poses significant health risks. Absorption of the cadmium compound is dependent on the solubility of the compound.

Other options:

Option A: Fluoride content of 1.5mg/L or above in water leads to dental fluorosis. Levels lower than that value is within the acceptable limits for safe drinking water.

Option B: The Maximum permissible limit of nitrate is 50 mg/L.

Option C: Water with concentrations of Total Dissolved Solids(TDS) below 1000 mg/L is generally acceptable to the consumers.
questions.learning: Cadmium- 0.3 mg/L The guideline value for cadmium in drinking water is established at 0.3 µg/L. Therefore cadmium level of 0.3 mg/L is higher than the permissible limit.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: After an initial serum β-hCG test in a patient with suspected pregnancy, when should the repeat β-hCG level ideally be checked to assess viability or progression?
questions.explanation: In early pregnancy, the doubling time of serum β-hCG is a critical marker of trophoblastic health and pregnancy viability. The standard clinical practice is to repeat the test after 48 hours. In a viable intrauterine pregnancy, the β-hCG level is expected to rise by at least 66% over this 48-hour window. A slower rise or a plateau in levels is highly suspicious of an ectopic pregnancy, while falling levels typically indicate an ongoing miscarriage. Checking after 24 hours (Option A) is often too early to see a meaningful trend, while 72 or 96 hours (Options C and D) may delay a critical diagnosis if the patient is unstable. Additionally, the "discriminatory zone" (usually ≥1,500 IU/L) is used alongside these trends to confirm the presence of a gestational sac on ultrasound
questions.learning: In early pregnancy, the doubling time of serum β-hCG is a critical marker of trophoblastic health and pregnancy viability. The standard clinical practice is to repeat the test after 48 hours.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In the preparation for a standard VATS (Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery), which of the following is considered the first essential step before port insertion?
options: Collapse of the lung using double-lumen endotracheal intubation
Positioning of the patient in lateral decubitus position
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Collapse of the lung using double-lumen endotracheal intubation

Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) requires a clear operative field within the pleural cavity, which is only possible if the ipsilateral lung is collapsed. Therefore, the first essential step in standard VATS preparation is establishing one-lung ventilation (OLV), most commonly achieved with a double-lumen endotracheal tube (DLT) (or bronchial blocker when DLT is not feasible).

Collapsing the operative lung:

• Creates adequate intrathoracic working space
• Improves visualization of pleura, lung, mediastinum
• Reduces risk of lung injury during port placement
• Facilitates safe manipulation and dissection

Only after confirming effective lung isolation and collapse should the team proceed with lateral decubitus positioning and subsequent port/camera insertion. Thus, lung collapse using double-lumen intubation is the first essential step before port insertion in VATS.
questions.learning: Collapse of the lung using double-lumen endotracheal intubation Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) requires a clear operative field within the pleural cavity, which is only possible if the ipsilateral lung is collapsed.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 65-year-old man is brought in urgently with a sudden change in speech, characterized by rapid, fluent output that lacks meaningful grammar and is nonsensical. Which specific type of speech disorder is most likely present in this patient?
questions.explanation: The symptoms described—rapid, fluent speech that is meaningless and lacks grammar (often called "word salad")—are the hallmark of Fluent (or Wernicke's) aphasia. This condition results from a lesion in Wernicke's area (superior temporal gyrus) of the dominant hemisphere. Patients are typically unaware of their deficit and have severely impaired comprehension. Motor (or Broca's) aphasia (Option A) is "non-fluent"; patients speak with great effort, using short, meaningful phrases but with poor grammar. Anomic aphasia (Option B) primarily involves difficulty in finding the correct names for objects, though fluency is preserved. Conduction aphasia (Option D) involves a specific inability to repeat phrases, though fluency and comprehension are relatively intact. Fluent aphasia is often seen following a stroke in the posterior division of the middle cerebral artery. Management involves speech-language therapy, though recovery of comprehension is often limited in older patients. Recognizing this "fluent but senseless" pattern is critical for localizing brain lesions during a neurological examination
questions.learning: The symptoms described—rapid, fluent speech that is meaningless and lacks grammar (often called "word salad")—are the hallmark of Fluent (or Wernicke's) aphasia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
Which of the following is NOT part of AMTSL?

AMTSL : Active Management of Third Stage of Labour
options: Delivery of placenta by controlled cord traction
Administration of oxytocin after shoulder delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bimanual compression

Bimanual compression is not part of AMTSL.

AMTSL is recommended by the WHO to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). Uterotonics are the most important components in AMTSL to do so.

1.
Injecting uterotonics within 1 minute of delivery of the baby or immediately after delivery of the anterior shoulder (Option D)
Most important step
Oxytocin 10 IU im/iv infusion is the preferred uterotonic.
(Not recommended by WHO- carboprost)

2.
Delayed cord clamping

• Done within 1-3 mins of delivery
• 80 ml of additional blood goes to the fetus
• Prevents fetal anemia

3.
Delivery of placenta by controlled cord traction: Modified Brandt Andrews technique (Option B)

• The uterus is pushed upwards and backward
• The traction of cord is downwards and forwards

4.
Intermittent assessment of uterine tone
Done every 15 mins for 2 hours

Note: Uterine massage or fundal massage is not recommended as an intervention to prevent PPH in women who have already received prophylactic uterotonics such as oxytocin (core component of AMTSL). Hence, it is now an optional component of AMTSL that is done in patients with uterine atony as a part of the management of PPH.  (Option A)
questions.learning: Bimanual compression Bimanual compression is not part of AMTSL. AMTSL is recommended by the WHO to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not an advantage of USG over Mammography?
options: Can be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically non palpable breast mass
Useful in young females with dense breast
Differentiates between solid and Cystic lesions in the Breast
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Can be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically non palpable breast mass

USG cannot be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically nonpalpable breast mass. Although ultrasound has its advantages in certain scenarios, mammography remains the primary screening tool for breast tumor detection.

Mammography is complementary to physical examination and can detect clinically non-palpable breast mass. The primary purpose of mammography is to detect small breast tumors. While mammography is typically the initial screening tool for breast cancer detection, there are specific scenarios where ultrasound may be preferred or used in conjunction with mammography. Advantages of USG over mammography include:

• USG is preferred in pregnant women, lactating women, and young women since breast tissue is dense (Option B) in these populations.
• USG can differentiate between solid and cystic lesions (Option C) of the breast and is able to detect abnormal axillary lymph nodes.
• Ultrasound can assist in guided breast biopsy (Option D) procedures.
questions.learning: Can be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically non palpable breast mass USG cannot be used for screening mammographically undetectable clinically nonpalpable breast mass.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: At which of the following centers are the records of eligible couples maintained?
questions.explanation: The Sub-centre is the peripheral-most unit of the Indian healthcare system, serving a population of 3,000 to 5,000. It is the designated primary site where the records of all "eligible couples" (those where the wife is in the reproductive age of 15–49) are meticulously maintained in the Eligible Couple Register. This task is primarily performed by the Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) or Female Health Worker. While the Primary Health Centre (PHC, Option A) supervises the sub-centres and maintains aggregate data, the primary source and repository of individual couple data is at the sub-centre level. Community Health Centres (CHC, Option B) and District Hospitals (Option D) are higher-level referral facilities that do not maintain these localized community family records. The maintenance of this register is critical for planning family welfare services, tracking contraceptive use, and ensuring the delivery of maternal and child health interventions. It serves as the foundation for the "eligible couple" surveillance system in the national family planning program

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During which gestational period is it legally required to obtain the approval of two registered medical practitioners for performing a medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)?
questions.explanation: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 in India, the legal requirements for abortion change based on gestational age. For pregnancies up to 12 weeks (Option C), the opinion of only one registered medical practitioner is required. For pregnancies between 20 and 24 weeks (Option B), the opinion and approval of two registered medical practitioners are mandatory. Option A is partially correct but includes the week period where rules differ. Option D (greater than 24 weeks) generally requires the approval of a State-level Medical Board for specific cases of substantial fetal abnormalities. Therefore, the 20-24 week window is the specific legal threshold where a "second opinion" is required for termination. This ensures additional oversight for later-term procedures
questions.learning: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 in India, the legal requirements for abortion change based on gestational age.

questions.text: Which of the following structures develops from the structure marked A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Median umbilical ligament

The structure marked A is the allantois. Its distal portion forms the urachus, which in turn gives rise to the median umbilical ligament.

The given image shows an embryo at the end of the third week.

Meckel's diverticulum is a congenital diverticulum arising from anti-mesenteric border of ileum. It is a remnant of the proximal part of the vitelline duct, which is made up of pluripotent cell lining. Meckel's diverticulum may harbor abnormal tissues, containing embryonic remnants of other tissue types, mostly gastric mucosa.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to subcutaneous contraceptive implant?
questions.explanation: Undiagnosed genital bleeding is an absolute contraindication (WHO Category 4) for all hormonal contraceptive methods, including subcutaneous implants. The primary concern is that the bleeding might be caused by an underlying malignancy (like cervical or endometrial cancer) that could be masked or its diagnosis delayed by hormonal use. Hypertension (Option A) and Diabetes (Option B) are not contraindications for progestin-only implants unless they are severe or accompanied by major vascular disease. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) (Option C) is a contraindication for intrauterine devices but not for subcutaneous implants, which do not interact with the pelvic organs directly. Therefore, the etiology of bleeding must be clarified before the implant can be safely used
questions.learning: Undiagnosed genital bleeding is an absolute contraindication (WHO Category 4) for all hormonal contraceptive methods, including subcutaneous implants.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient with post partum hemorrhage has been given ergometrine and oxytocin. The bleeding still continues. Which prostaglandin derivative can be given in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carboprost

Carboprost, 15-methyl PGF2α can be used in a setting where both ergometrine and oxytocin have not been able to control the bleeding.

Oxytocin is used as the first-line agent in preventing postpartum hemorrhage. When oxytocin fails or is not available, ergot derivatives can be used for second-line treatment.

Carboprost, 15-methyl PGF2α is the drug of choice for PPH and can be used for uterine atony in a dose of 0.25 mg IM. This dose can be repeated if necessary at 15-90 min intervals, up to a maximum of eight doses.

Misoprostol: PGE1

* In settings where injectable uterotonics are not feasible or recommended, PGE1 is a useful option.

* Misoprostol-induced fever can be distressing and may result in unnecessary sepsis workups and antibiotic use.

* No evidence shows that misoprostol is better than other uterotonics for treating PPH.

Postpartum hemorrhage:

It is defined as a loss of more than 500 ml of blood after completion of the third stage of labor (in vaginal delivery).

PPH is blood loss of more than 1000 mL from the genital tract following cesarean section.

Depending upon the amount of blood loss, PPH can be, minor (<1L) or major (>1L). Major is further subdivided into moderate (1L-2L) and severe (>2L).

Types of PPH:

Primary/early PPH: Hemorrhage occurring within 24 hours of childbirth. Causes include

* Atony: Primi, grand multipara, over-distended uterus, hydramnios, precipitate labor, prolonged labor, uterine malformations, fibroid uterus

* Trauma: Instrumental deliveries, episiotomy, precipitate labor, macrosomia

* Retained tissues: retained placenta, blood clots

* Bleeding disorders: Sepsis, Intrauterine death, HELLP syndrome.

Secondary/ late PPH: Hemorrhage after 24 hours - 12 weeks postpartum. Causes include

* Placental polyp forms when retained placental tissue undergoes necrosis and fibrin deposition; detachment from the myometrium can then result in sudden, heavy bleeding

* Abnormal involution of the placental site.

* Retention of placental cotyledon or products of conception.

* Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm.

* Endometritis

* Coagulopathy

Resuscitative measures include

* Airway, breathing, circulation assessment

* A high concentration of oxygen (10–15 l/min) via a facemask

* Blood transfusion if clinically required

* Fluid resuscitation with warmed fluids up to 3.5 liters, starting with up to 2 liters of crystalloids such as normal saline and ringer's lactate. Colloids can be used when there is a need for packed RBCs transfusion, until blood is arranged.
questions.learning: Carboprost Carboprost, 15-methyl PGF2α can be used in a setting where both ergometrine and oxytocin have not been able to control the bleeding. Oxytocin is used as the first-line agent in preventing postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the treatment option with the image given below:
questions.explanation: The surgical diagram illustrates Type 3 tympanoplasty, also known as myringostapediopexy. This procedure is performed when the malleus and incus are absent or diseased, but the stapes is intact and mobile. The tympanic membrane graft is placed directly onto the head of the stapes to restore the sound conduction mechanism. Regarding the distractors, Type 1 (Option A) is a simple repair of a perforated ear drum (myringoplasty) where the ossicular chain is intact. Type 2 (Option B) involves placing the graft onto the incus when the malleus is eroded. Type 4 (Option D) is used when only the stapes footplate remains; the graft is placed between the oval and round windows to protect the round window while allowing sound to hit the footplate directly. Therefore, the direct connection to the stapes head as shown in the image is diagnostic of Type 3
questions.learning: The surgical diagram illustrates Type 3 tympanoplasty, also known as myringostapediopexy. This procedure is performed when the malleus and incus are absent or diseased, but the stapes is intact and mobile.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following marked areas in the histopathological specimen shows calcification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given specimen is that of an epiphyseal cartilage, where zone 3 corresponds to the zone of calcification.

Epiphyseal cartilage is divided into five zones :

• The resting zone consists of hyaline cartilage without morphological changes in the cells (option 1)
• In the proliferative zone, chondrocytes divide rapidly and form columns of stacked cells parallel to the long axis of the bone (option 2)
• The hypertrophic cartilage zone contains large chondrocytes whose cytoplasm has accumulated glycogen. The resorbed matrix is reduced to thin septa between the chondrocytes.
• Simultaneous with the death of chondrocytes in the calcified cartilage zone, the thin septa of cartilage matrix become calcified by the deposit of hydroxyapatite.
• In the ossification zone, endochondral bone tissue appears (option 4). Blood capillaries and osteoprogenitor cells formed by mitosis of cells originating from the periosteum invade the cavities left by the chondrocytes. The osteoprogenitor cells form osteoblasts, which are distributed in a discontinuous layer over the septa of the calcified cartilage matrix. Ultimately, the osteoblasts deposit bone matrix over the three-dimensional calcified cartilage matrix.

The epiphyseal cartilage is responsible for the growth in the length of bone and it disappears in adults, which is why bone growth ceases in adulthood.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A firefighter presents with fever, cough, and lung consolidation. Microbiological testing reveals a gram-negative, oxidase-positive organism. The culture shows colonies that show a property of transillumination when light is passed. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

The gram-negative, oxidase-positive organism that forms greenish-yellow colonies exhibiting transillumination is indicative of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative, catalase-positive, oxidase-positive, non-lactose fermenting bacteria that shows swarming motility. They produce a characteristic blue-green pigment called pyocyanin and a greenish-yellow pigment called fluorescein/pyoverdin. Other pigments produced by these organisms include pyorubin (Red), pyomelanin (Brown).

Diseases caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa include-

* Malignant otitis externa in diabetics

* Pneumonia and sepsis in cystic fibrosis

* Wound infection and sepsis in burns

* Hot tub folliculitis/Pseudomonas aeruginosa folliculitis/ Jacuzzi syndrome is a type of folliculitis, occurring after hot tub exposure

* Shanghai fever is a febrile illness that manifests as severe enteric disease, sepsis with invasive disease.

* Ecthyma gangrenosum

Pathogenesis - It is an obligate aerobe that exerts its pathogenicity by the production of diphtheria-like exotoxin A and a slime layer. Breach in primary body defenses as in burns predisposes to Pseudomonas infection.

Clinical features - It is characterized by blue-green pus. It is notorious for being resistant to antimicrobials and antiseptics and hence is a frequent contaminant in hospital samples. Repeated isolation and associated clinical features should prompt the diagnosis of Pseudomonas.

Diagnosis - It grows well on most media and pigment production makes its identification easy. Species identification is made possible by biochemical tests - arginine hydrolysis and oxidase reaction.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa growth in a nutrient agar showing green coloured colonies are shown in the image below.

Other Options:

Option A: Klebsiella is cultured on MacConkey or blood agar, forming large, mucoid colonies. MacConkey agar differentiates Klebsiella by lactose fermentation, producing pink colonies as shown in the image given below.

Option B: Staphylococcus aureus produces golden-yellow colonies on blood agar.

Option D: Streptococcus pneumoniae produces alpha-hemolytic, small, grey colonies on blood agar with no pigmentation or fluorescence.
questions.learning: Pseudomonas aeruginosa — The gram-negative, oxidase-positive organism that forms greenish-yellow colonies exhibiting transillumination is indicative of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the nerve supply of the structure marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Median nerve

The marked structure is second lumbrical which is supplied by the median nerve.

The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve and the medial two are supplied by the ulnar nerve. Function of these muscles is flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at both the interphalangeal joints.
questions.learning: Median nerve — The marked structure is second lumbrical which is supplied by the median nerve. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve and the medial two are supplied by the ulnar nerve.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn admitted to the NICU is diagnosed with a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). To promote pharmacological closure of the ductus arteriosus, which drug is most commonly used?
questions.explanation: In the neonatal period, the closure of the ductus arteriosus is triggered by a rise in oxygen and a fall in circulating prostaglandins. If the ductus remains patent (PDA), causing significant hemodynamic shifts, pharmacological closure is attempted using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Indomethacin is the most commonly used agent for this purpose as it is a potent inhibitor of prostaglandin synthesis. Ibuprofen is also frequently used. Magnesium sulfate (Option A) is used for neuroprotection or seizure prophylaxis, not PDA closure. Alprostadil (Option B), a synthetic prostaglandin , is used for the opposite purpose: to keep the ductus arteriosus open in infants with ductal-dependent congenital heart defects. Aspirin (Option D), while an NSAID, is not used in neonates due to the risk of Reye's syndrome and lower efficacy for this specific indication. Indomethacin therapy requires careful monitoring of renal function and platelet counts, as it can decrease renal perfusion and impair platelet aggregation
questions.learning: In the neonatal period, the closure of the ductus arteriosus is triggered by a rise in oxygen and a fall in circulating prostaglandins. If the ductus remains patent (PDA), causing significant hemodynamic shifts, pharmacological closure is attempted using…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which anatomical structure is primarily responsible for preventing lateral displacement of the patella during knee flexion?
questions.explanation: The patella has a natural tendency to dislocate laterally due to the "Q-angle" formed by the pull of the quadriceps muscles. The vastus medialis, particularly its distal horizontal fibers known as the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO), is the primary dynamic stabilizer that prevents this lateral displacement. It exerts a medial pull that keeps the patella centered within the trochlear groove of the femur during knee flexion and extension. The patellar ligament (Option B) connects the patella to the tibial tuberosity but does not provide specific medial-lateral stabilization. The gracilis (Option C) is an adductor muscle of the thigh and does not act directly on the patella. The rectus femoris (Option D) is a central quadriceps muscle that actually contributes to the lateral-pulling force on the patella. Therefore, strengthening the vastus medialis is a standard therapeutic goal for patients with patellofemoral pain syndrome or recurrent dislocations

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding viscoelastic substances used in cataract surgery?
options: It can be left in the eye at the end of surgery.
It damages the corneal epithelium or the endothelium.
SF6 and perfluorocarbon are commonly used viscoelastics.
It is used to maintain the anterior chamber during capsulorhexis and IOL insertion.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is used to maintain the anterior chamber during capsulorhexis and IOL insertion.

Ophthalmic viscoelastic devices (OVDs) are essential in cataract surgery to maintain anterior chamber depth and protect intraocular structures.

Primary function:

• Maintain anterior chamber during critical steps:

• Capsulorhexis
• Phacoemulsification
• Intraocular lens (IOL) implantation

• Provide space and stability inside the eye
• Protect corneal endothelium from surgical trauma

Why other options are incorrect:

• A) Can be left in the eye:

• Incorrect → must be removed at the end
• Retained OVD can cause postoperative rise in IOP

• B) Damages cornea:

• Incorrect → actually protects endothelium

• C) SF6 & perfluorocarbon:

• These are intraocular gases/liquids used in vitreoretinal surgery, not viscoelastics
questions.learning: It is used to maintain the anterior chamber during capsulorhexis and IOL insertion. Ophthalmic viscoelastic devices (OVDs) are essential in cataract surgery to maintain anterior chamber depth and protect intraocular structures.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: How much illumination is recommended by the Illuminating Engineering Society for the general office work?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 400 lux

Illumination is the amount of light falling on a surface and is measured in lux (lx). Adequate illumination improves visual performance, reduces eye strain, and enhances work efficiency. According to the Illuminating Engineering Society (IES), the recommended illumination for general office work is 400 lux.

• General office work: 400 lux
• Corridors and staircases: 100 lux
• Classrooms: 150–300 lux
• Drawing/design work: 700–1000 lux
• Operation theatre: 1000–10,000 lux (shadow-free lighting)
• Direct sunlight: Approximately 100,000 lux

Units of Light

• Luminous flux: Lumen (lm)
• Illumination: Lux (lx) = Lumen/m²
• Luminous intensity: Candela (cd)
questions.learning: 400 lux Illumination is the amount of light falling on a surface and is measured in lux (lx). Adequate illumination improves visual performance, reduces eye strain, and enhances work efficiency.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presents to the outpatient department with a swelling over the palm that developed several months after sustaining a thorn prick injury. Based on the clinical presentation shown in the image, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An implantation dermoid (or epidermal inclusion cyst) is a common clinical entity that occurs when surface epithelium is traumatically driven into the deeper tissues. The patient’s history as a "farmer" who sustained a "thorn injury" is classic, as these cysts frequently occur on the palms or fingers of manual laborers. Over months, the trapped epithelial cells proliferate and produce keratin, forming a firm, non-tender, slow-growing subcutaneous cyst. Embryogenic or sequestration dermoids (Options B and C) occur along embryonic fusion lines (like the midline or outer canthus) and are present from birth rather than resulting from trauma. Ameloblastoma (Option A) is an aggressive odontogenic tumor of the jaw, unrelated to palmar skin lesions. Treatment for an implantation dermoid involves complete surgical excision to prevent recurrence or secondary infection. The diagnosis is usually straightforward based on the history of penetrating trauma followed by a localized swelling in a high-contact area like the palm
questions.learning: An implantation dermoid (or epidermal inclusion cyst) is a common clinical entity that occurs when surface epithelium is traumatically driven into the deeper tissues.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy who is a football player comes to the casualty with complaints of epistaxis while playing football on the ground. There is no history of trauma or falls. He gives a history of recurrent spontaneous nasal bleeding, unilateral nasal obstruction and denasal speech. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head is shown below. What is this sign known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Holman Miller sign

The given CT scan showing the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus is called the Holman Miller sign or Antral sign.

The given clinical picture along with a CT scan showing the Holman Miller sign is suggestive of the diagnosis of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. It most commonly arises from the sphenopalatine foramen. From here the tumour grows into the:

* Nasal cavity

* Nasopharynx

* Pterygopalatine fossa

* Pterygomaxillary fossa

* Infratemporal fossa

Other options:

Aquino sign is the blanching of the tumour mass in a glomus tumour when the ipsilateral carotid artery is compressed manually.

Hanging drop/tear-drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum.

Given below is CT showing the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus - Antral sign or Holman Miller sign
questions.learning: Holman Miller sign — The given CT scan showing the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus is called the Holman Miller sign or Antral sign.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient sustained a crush injury on their right arm as depicted in the given image. He was brought to the hospital and on examination, his arm is pulseless, swollen and dark red. What would be the best way to manage this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fasciotomy

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a crush syndrome with compartment syndrome. If compartment syndrome is confirmed (by measuring intra-compartmental pressure), then fasciotomy is performed.

Crush syndrome can result when a limb is compressed for a prolonged period (e.g. getting crushed or entrapped in a vehicle or rubble) and after extended use of a pneumatic antishock garment. This results in hypoperfusion and myonecrosis in the crushed limb. When the limb is released from the compression, toxic metabolites get released to cause reperfusion injury.

Management of crush syndrome involves aggressive management of the open wound and radical excision of necrosed muscle to avoid sepsis. Encouraging high urine flow, along with alkalization of urine with sodium bicarbonate to prevent precipitation of myoglobin in the renal tubules. Renal hemofiltration is recommended if there is oliguria or renal failure. If compartment syndrome is confirmed (by measuring intra-compartmental pressure), then fasciotomy is performed.

The diagnosis can be confirmed by measuring the intra-compartmental pressure using a split catheter introduced into the compartment. The difference between diastolic pressure and compartment pressure is known as differential pressure (ΔP). If the differential pressure (ΔP) is less than 30 mm Hg (4.00 kilopascals), immediate compartment decompression is indicated.

Treatment:

* Prompt decompression of the affected compartment is done.

* All the dressings, bandages, and cast on the affected limb are removed and the limb is nursed flat.

* Fasciotomy is done if the differential pressure is less than 30 mm Hg

* Fasciotomy wounds are left open and after 2 days if there is necrosis debridement is done. If the wounds are healthy it can be sutured without tension or skin grafting can be done.
questions.learning: Fasciotomy — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a crush syndrome with compartment syndrome. If compartment syndrome is confirmed (by measuring intra-compartmental pressure), then fasciotomy is performed.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct in the diagnosis of Giardiasis?
options: Stool sample at 2–3 days interval should be examined for cysts
String test is done to find out cysts of Giardia lamblia
Jejunal biopsy samples can show presence of larvae of Giardia lamblia
Cystic form of Giardia lamblia remains viable in water upto 1 week only
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stool sample at 2–3 days interval should be examined for cysts

Giardiasis is an intestinal protozoal infection caused by Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis or G. duodenalis). Since cyst excretion in stool is intermittent, multiple stool examinations (usually three samples collected at 2–3 day intervals) significantly increase the diagnostic yield.

Why not the other options?

• B. String test is done to find out cysts of Giardia lamblia: The string test (Entero-Test) is used to obtain duodenal contents containing trophozoites, not cysts.
• C. Jejunal biopsy samples can show presence of larvae of Giardia lamblia: Giardia is a protozoan, not a helminth; it has trophozoite and cyst forms, not larvae.
• D. Cystic form of Giardia lamblia remains viable in water up to 1 week only: Giardia cysts remain viable for several weeks to months in cold water, making waterborne outbreaks common.
questions.learning: Stool sample at 2–3 days interval should be examined for cysts Giardiasis is an intestinal protozoal infection caused by Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis or G. duodenalis).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 167.An 8-year-old boy is brought by his parents due to progressively worsening difficulty in walking and increasing muscle weakness. On examination, there is apparent enlargement of the calf muscles due to pseudohypertrophy. With respect to this condition, which of the following statements is true?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of progressive muscle weakness in an 8-year-old boy, specifically with calf "pseudohypertrophy" (where muscle is replaced by fat and fibrous tissue), is the classic description of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). DMD is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the DMD gene, leading to a complete absence of the protein dystrophin. Dystrophin is essential for maintaining the structural integrity of the muscle fiber's sarcolemma; without it, muscle fibers undergo repeated damage and necrosis during contraction. Abnormal collagen (Option A) is seen in conditions like Osteogenesis Imperfecta or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Expansions of CTG repeats (Option C) cause Myotonic Dystrophy, which typically presents later with myotonia and distal weakness. Defective fibrillin (Option D) is the cause of Marfan syndrome. In DMD, the weakness typically starts proximally in the pelvic girdle, leading to the characteristic Gowers' sign. Since the question asks for the true statement regarding the underlying pathology of DMD, the absence of dystrophin is the correct answer
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of progressive muscle weakness in an 8-year-old boy, specifically with calf "pseudohypertrophy" (where muscle is replaced by fat and fibrous tissue), is the classic description of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which type of learning is demonstrated when a medical intern is guided step by step on how to correctly elicit the knee reflex?
questions.explanation: In medical education, learning objectives are categorized into three domains. Psychomotor learning (Option B) involves the acquisition of physical skills and manual dexterity, such as the correct technique for using a reflex hammer to elicit a knee jerk. This type of learning requires the coordination of cognitive understanding with physical performance. Cognitive learning (Option A) focuses on the acquisition of knowledge, facts, and theoretical concepts. Affective learning (Option C) pertains to the development of attitudes, professional values, and empathy. Repeated learning (Option D) is a method of study but not a recognized educational domain. Because the intern is being taught a specific procedural skill that requires physical action and precision, it is the classic example of psychomotor development. Clinical rotations are designed to bridge the gap between classroom cognitive knowledge and hands-on psychomotor proficiency. Therefore, mastering clinical examination techniques is a core psychomotor task
questions.learning: In medical education, learning objectives are categorized into three domains. Psychomotor learning (Option B) involves the acquisition of physical skills and manual dexterity, such as the correct technique for using a reflex hammer to elicit a knee jerk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which type of aphasia is seen in the lesions of the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluent

Lesions of the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus cause Wernicke’s or Fluent aphasia due to the involvement of the Wernicke's area. The speech is full of jargon and neologisms that make little sense (area no 22).

Broca's (Option B) or motor/non-fluent aphasia is seen in lesions of the inferior frontal gyrus which contains the motor speech area. Speech is non-fluent and interrupted, with a paucity of functional words.

Comprehension of written language and the ability to name objects are compromised in anomic aphasia (Option C). This aphasia is caused by damage to the angular gyrus that disrupts visual information processing and transmission to the Wernicke area.

Conduction aphasia (Option D) is seen in lesions of the arcuate fasciculus, the bundle of nerve fibers connecting the Wernicke and Broca's areas. Repetition of words is impaired and paraphasias are observed, though not as much as in Wernicke aphasia.
questions.learning: Fluent Lesions of the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus cause Wernicke’s or Fluent aphasia due to the involvement of the Wernicke's area. The speech is full of jargon and neologisms that make little sense (area no 22).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The most common triggering factor of the given condition is ________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Infection

The given image shows characteristic target lesions of erythema multiforme. This most commonly occurs following a herpes simplex virus infection.

The common triggers are:

• Herpes simplex infection
• Mycoplasma infection
• Bacterial infections
• Fungal infections
• Vaccinations
• Malignancy- carcinoma, lymphoma, leukemia
• Drugs- sulfonamides, rifampicin, penicillins, hydantoin derivatives
• Miscellaneous- lupus erythematosus (Rowell Syndrome), sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa

Erythema multiforme is best regarded as a self‐limiting cytotoxic dermatitis resulting from cell‐mediated hypersensitivity.

It presents clinically with a spectrum of macular, papular, or urticarial lesions, as well as the classic acral iris or ‘target lesions’.

Target lesions are less than 3 cm in diameter, rounded, and have three zones:

1. Central area of dusky erythema or purpura
2. Middle paler zone of edema
3. Outer ring of erythema with a well‐defined edge

Lesions may involve the palms and the trunk. Oral and genital mucosal membranes lesions are associated with erosions

The image below shows target lesions.
questions.learning: Infection — The given image shows characteristic target lesions of erythema multiforme. This most commonly occurs following a herpes simplex virus infection.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During a forensic autopsy of a gunshot victim, the firearm wound is noted to have a stellate (star-shaped) appearance. What does this finding indicate about the range of the gunshot?
questions.explanation: A stellate or star-shaped entrance wound is a pathognomonic feature of a "hard contact" gunshot wound, particularly when the weapon is pressed against skin overlying a flat bone, such as the skull. When the muzzle is in tight contact with the skin, the rapidly expanding gases produced by the gunpowder combustion are forced into the subcutaneous space between the skin and the bone. This gas pressure causes the skin to bulge outward and eventually burst or tear in a radiating, irregular pattern, creating the classic stellate appearance. In a close shot (Option A) or near shot (Option C), usually within a few centimeters to a meter, one would expect to see singeing, smudging, or tattooing (stippling) around a more circular hole rather than a stellate tear. A distant shot (Option D) typically produces a neat, circular or oval hole with an abrasion collar but lacks the gas-expansion effects required to create a stellate-shaped entrance wound
questions.learning: A stellate or star-shaped entrance wound is a pathognomonic feature of a "hard contact" gunshot wound, particularly when the weapon is pressed against skin overlying a flat bone, such as the skull.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a nodule of the neck presents to the surgery OPD. A junior resident performs the following method to palpate it. Identify the procedure shown in the video below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lahey's method

The video depicts Lahey’s method of palpation of the left lobe of the thyroid gland.

In Lahey's method, for palpating the left lobe, the examiner initially pushes the right lobe medially with the left hand, and then using the right hand, the border and consistency of the left lobe is palpated.

Other options:

Option B: In Crile's method the patient is asked to swallow, while the examiner palpates the gland with the thumb. This gives a clear indication regarding the slight enlargement of the thyroid gland or small nodules.

Option C: Kocher's method is done to demonstrate the pressure effect of the thyroid gland on the trachea or larynx. Lateral compression will result in stridor.

Option D: Pemberton's sign (not method), is engorgement of neck veins when the patient is asked to raise their hands above the head and the arms should touch the ears. It is seen in patients with retrosternal goiter.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In 18th century British East India company used to transport which substance of abuse to China:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Opium

In the 18th–19th century, the British East India Company extensively traded opium from India to China, leading to widespread addiction and major historical consequences.

• Opium was cultivated in British-controlled India and exported to China
• Resulted in large-scale substance dependence in China
• Led to the Opium Wars between Britain and China

Forensic and public health relevance:

• Opium is a natural opioid derived from Papaver somniferum
• Acts as a CNS depressant causing:

• Analgesia
• Euphoria
• Respiratory depression (in overdose)

Why not other options:

• Marijuana: Cannabis use, not historically traded in this context
• Cocaine: Derived from coca plant (South America)
• Magic mushrooms: Hallucinogens, not part of this trade

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the recommended first-line management approach for urinary symptoms in a patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?
questions.explanation: The recommended initial medical management for symptomatic Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) centers on alpha-1 blockers, with Tamsulosin being the most common first-line agent. Alpha-blockers provide rapid symptomatic relief by relaxing the smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, thereby decreasing urethral resistance and improving urinary flow. While Finasteride (Option C), a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, is effective for long-term reduction of prostate volume, its onset of action is slow (taking 6–12 months) and it is usually reserved for patients with larger prostates or as part of combination therapy. TURP (Option A) is a surgical intervention reserved for patients who fail medical therapy or develop complications like refractory retention or renal failure. Observation (Option D) is appropriate only for patients with very mild, non-bothersome symptoms. Given the need for effective and immediate symptom control in most clinical presentations, initiation of tamsulosin is the standard pharmacological starting point for BPH
questions.learning: The recommended initial medical management for symptomatic Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) centers on alpha-1 blockers, with Tamsulosin being the most common first-line agent.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following can reduce the risk of endometrial cancer in a post-menopausal woman on hormone replacement therapy (HRT)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Adding progesterone to oestrogen

Adding progesterone to estrogen in HRT can reduce the risk of potential endometrial cancer.

For women with a uterus, it is recommended to add micronized progesterone to prevent endometrial hyperplasia which can occur after 6 months of oestrogen therapy. For women without a uterus, just estrogen therapy is sufficient.

Hormone therapy is only indicated for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms,genitourinary syndrome of menopause like vaginal and vulvar atrophy and for the prevention of osteoporosis.

The daily estrogen content in most oral contraceptive pills is 35µg or less and levonorgestrel is 100-150 mg. But the HRT commonly used have a different concentration of estrogen and progesterone. Hence the regular combined oral contraceptive pills are not used.

Clonidine reduces hot flashes during menopause but does not have any action on endometrium. Vitamin E has no role in endometriual proliferation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The type of hypoxia based on the graph is_____ (Consider the plot in red as normal)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anemic hypoxia

The graph represents the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve that would be seen in anemic hypoxia and normal. The X-axis represents the partial pressure of oxygen(PO2). The Y-axis represents the percentage saturation between the hemoglobin and the oxygen.

The graph indicates two lines: a red line representing normal hemoglobin and a purple line representing reduced hemoglobin levels. The red line corresponds to an arterial blood oxygen content of approximately 19 mL/dL, and venous blood oxygen content of 14 mL/dL. On the other hand, the purple line represents an arterial blood oxygen content of 9 mL/dL and venous blood oxygen content of 4 mL/dL.

This scenario demonstrates a 50% decrease in oxygen saturation of hemoglobin, while the partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) remains within the normal range. This condition is characterized as anemic hypoxia.

In anemic hypoxia, the blood oxygen content is decreased. The patients might not experience any difficulty during rest because 2,3-DPG increases in the red blood cells. However, they may have difficulty during exercise because of a limited ability to increase O2 delivery to the active tissues.

Conditions that cause a right shift in the oxygen hemoglobin curve are: (Conditions with the increased requirement of O2 - metabolically active tissues)

• Hypoxia
• Hypercarbia
• Decreased pH
• Increased temperature
• Increased 2,3-biphosphoglycerate

Conditions that cause a left shift in the oxygen hemoglobin curve

• Increased oxygen
• Decreased carbon dioxide
• Increased pH
• Decreased temperature
• Decreased 2,3-biphosphoglycerate
• Fetal hemoglobin.
questions.learning: Anemic hypoxia — The graph represents the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve that would be seen in anemic hypoxia and normal. The X-axis represents the partial pressure of oxygen(PO2).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A child after eating an unknown fruit ,has been brought to your emergency department with the following signs and symptoms - Dry mouth, irrelevant slurred speech, dry and hot skin, dilated pupils. On examination there was tachycardia and hyperthermia.What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Datura poisoning

The clinical syndrome in the question is that of Datura poisoning.

Dhatura:

Active principle:

* Scopolamine

* Hyoscyamine

* Trace amount of atropine

* The active principle called “Dhaturine” on heating would yield atropine

* Seeds or other parts of the plant can be ingested or smoked and produce delirium, hallucinations, and seizures along with other classic anticholinergic effects, such as mydriasis, tachycardia, dry mouth and skin, blurred vision, urinary retention, and hyperthermia.

Mode of Action:

* Anticholinergic

Toxic manifestations of Datura:

* Mnemonic: "hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, and mad as a hatter"

* Also, remember the D's of Datura

* Dry hot skin (Temp rises upto 42 C, a scarlet rash may also be appreciated).

* Dilatation of pupils along with loss of accommodation

* Diplopia

* Dryness of the mouth and throat, unquenchable thirst

* Dysphagia

* Dilatation of cutaneous blood vessels

* Dysarthria (Difficulty in talking)

* Drunken gait

* Delirium

* Drowsiness

* Death due to respiratory or cardiac failure

Treatment

* Gastric emptying is often delayed, and the small, plentiful seeds can become trapped among the gastrointestinal folds after ingestion; thus gastric decontamination can be an important therapy.

* Physostigmine in severe toxicity given 1-2 mg IM/IV after every half hour as required. It is a physiological antidote. Pilocarpine may also be given.

Note:

In India, datura is employed mainly as a stupefying poison prior to robbery, kidnapping and rape. It is sometimes known as rail-road poison, as it is commonly encountered during a journey. Many a time, robbers disguised as saints offer ‘prasad’ mixed with dhatura seeds and rob the passengers.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Universal health coverage (UHC) means that all people and communities receive the quality health services they need, without financial hardship. Which of the following are the challenges to implementing UHC?
options: Inequalities in the distribution, adequate support, and access to quality-assured products only in low-income settings
The purpose of UHC is to find a balance between countries' income, health provision, and financial burden
To provide healthcare to everyone regardless of the country's income
UHC only deals with the financial aspect of health and cannot cover health provisions for all
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. To provide healthcare to everyone regardless of the country's income

Providing healthcare to everyone, regardless of the country's income, is one of the challenges to implementing Universal Health Coverage. A challenge related to this is mobilising sufficient resources in low-income countries to provide equitable care.

UHC aims at ensuring that all people have access to quality health services without suffering financial hardship.

Components:

• Equity in access: Everyone receives the healthcare they need.
• Quality of services: Delivered in a manner that improves health outcomes.
• Financial protection: Avoiding financial hardship for those accessing services.

Challenges:

• Health inequities.
• Resource constraints in low- and middle-income countries.
• Balancing financial protection and service delivery.

Strategies to Achieve UHC:

• Strengthening health systems.
• Universal health insurance.
• Public-private partnerships.

Other options

Option A: Inequalities in the distribution, adequate support, and access to quality-assured products are a challenge, but they occur across income settings, not only in low-income ones.

Option B: The purpose of UHC to find a balance between countries’ income, health provision, and financial burden describes a goal of UHC and not a challenge.

Option D: UHC encompasses both financial protection and access to quality health services.
questions.learning: To provide healthcare to everyone regardless of the country's income Providing healthcare to everyone, regardless of the country's income, is one of the challenges to implementing Universal Health Coverage.

questions.text: Identify the finding seen in this hysterosalpingogram:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bilateral hydrosalpinx

Bilateral hydrosalpinx is observed in the given image of hysterosalpingogram.

The interstitial end of the tube is open whereas the fimbrial end is indrawn and closed. This permits the dye to enter but not exit the tube during hysterosalpingography.

questions.learning: Bilateral hydrosalpinx Bilateral hydrosalpinx is observed in the given image of hysterosalpingogram. Hydrosalpinx is often bilateral and occurs following acute salpingitis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During an explosion, a patient sustains a crushed injury to the lower limb due to collapse of a building. Which type of blast injury does this represent?
questions.explanation: Blast injuries are classified by their physical mechanism. Quaternary injuries are miscellaneous trauma resulting from the blast, including crush injuries from building collapses, burns, and traumatic asphyxia. Primary blast injuries (Option A) result directly from the air compression wave (overpressure) and typically damage hollow organs like the ears (tympanic membrane), lungs, and GIT. Secondary blast injuries (Option B) are caused by flying missiles or projectiles propelled by the blast hitting the body. Tertiary blast injuries (Option C) occur when the individual is physically lifted and thrown against the ground or walls, often leading to fractures or dislocations. A quinary injury category (Option E) also exists for injuries from environmental contaminants like radiation or chemicals. Since this specific patient suffered a crush injury from a structural collapse, it is definitively classified as a quaternary injury
questions.learning: Blast injuries are classified by their physical mechanism. Quaternary injuries are miscellaneous trauma resulting from the blast, including crush injuries from building collapses, burns, and traumatic asphyxia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A city has a total population of 70,00,000, of which 30% resides in slum areas. According to the existing Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS), how many Urban Primary Health Centers (Urban PHCs) should be established to cater to the slum population?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 42

As per IPHS norms, one Urban PHC caters to \~50,000 slum population.

Slum population = 30% of 70,00,000 = 21,00,000.

According to IPHS / NUHM guidelines:

Required Urban PHCs = 21,00,000 ÷ 50,000 = 42. Thus, 42 Urban PHCs are needed to adequately serve the slum population.

Urban PHCs were strengthened under the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM). Urban poor populations often face:

• Overcrowding
• Poor sanitation
• Limited healthcare access
• Higher communicable disease burden

Thus, more densely distributed health centres are required.

Urban Health Facility Structure (NUHM)
questions.learning: 42 As per IPHS norms, one Urban PHC caters to \~50,000 slum population. Slum population = 30% of 70,00,000 = 21,00,000.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient who underwent right limb amputation 2 years back, now presents with severe pain in the limb (Phantom limb pain). On radiological investigations, What is the finding seen?
options: Projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the right somatosensory cortex
Projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex

In the given scenario of phantom limb pain, on the radiological investigation of the brain projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex can be seen. This pain is based on cortical plasticity.

Cortical structures are capable of reorganization after the loss of a body part. The cortical representation of the neighbouring parts spreads into the cortical area that was formerly occupied by the representation of the amputated part. This is called cortical plasticity leads to the phenomenon of phantom limb pain. The sensory cortical area occupied by the right limb is the left somatosensory cortex.

Cortical plasticity / Phantom limb: It is the sensation that an amputated or missing limb is still attached. Plasticity is the ability of the brain to adapt to such a condition by reorganization of thalamic and cortical structures.

The converse also holds true: if the cortical area representing a limb is removed, the somatosensory map of the limb moves to the surrounding cortex.

Diagnosis and Management :

• PET scan is used to document these plastic changes in cortex.
• Use of epidural analgesia during amputation surgery decreases incidence of phantom pain.
• Spinal cord stimulation also helps in reducing phantom pain. (interferes with ascending impulses to brain)
questions.learning: Projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex In the given scenario of phantom limb pain, on the radiological investigation of the brain projection of adjacent fibres to overlap the left somatosensory cortex can be seen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the function of the proteasome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Protein degradation

The proteasome takes part in protein degradation.

The proteasome is a cylindrical structure in the cytosol that degrades polyubiquitinated proteins. It has a central core with proteolytic enzymes. Proteins that are tagged by ubiquitin to be degraded enter the core through regulatory rings on either side of the cylinder.

Clinical relevance: It plays an important role in antigen presentation to T lymphocytes as it degrades viruses and other molecules to small peptides.
questions.learning: Protein degradation — The proteasome takes part in protein degradation. The proteasome is a cylindrical structure in the cytosol that degrades polyubiquitinated proteins.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in a case of otitis media?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Battle sign

Battle sign refers to retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from a fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma. It is prominent when there is a fracture of the temporal bone. Battle sign is not seen in the case of otitis media.

Option A: Bezold abscess is a complication of acute otomastoiditis where the infection/pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck.

Option B: Griesinger sign refers to edema of the postauricular soft tissues overlying the mastoid process as a result of thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein seen in sigmoid sinus thrombosis. It is a complication of acute otomastoiditis.

Option D: Delta sign is a contrast-enhanced CT finding seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis, which can occur as a complication of acute mastoiditis or chronic suppurative otitis media. It is a triangular area with rim enhancement and the central low-density area is seen in the posterior cranial fossa on axial cuts. MR venography is useful to assess the progression or resolution of a thrombus.

The image below depicts a filling defect (thrombus) outlined by contrast medium in the sagittal sinus.
questions.learning: Battle sign Battle sign refers to retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from a fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman is diagnosed to be positive for HIV in her first trimester. What is the appropriate management?
options: Start ART immediately and continue till 6 weeks after delivery
Start ART after 1st trimester and continue life-long
Start ART immediately and continue life-long
Start ART after 1st trimester and continue till 6 weeks after delivery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start ART immediately and continue life-long

ART should be initiated immediately and continued lifelong in all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV. This is regardless of their WHO clinical stage and CD4 cell count.

*Note: Pearl attached below has been updated according to the NACO ART guidelines 2021. Efavirenz has been replaced by Dolutegravir as per the new guidelines.
questions.learning: Start ART immediately and continue life-long ART should be initiated immediately and continued lifelong in all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe unilateral eye pain, headache, and blurred vision after watching a movie in a dark theatre. On examination, the eye is red, cornea is hazy, and pupil is mid-dilated and non-reactive. What is the first line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mannitol + Pilocarpine

Sudden eye pain and decreased vision after being in a dark environment (movie theater) suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG).

• Darkness → pupillary dilation (mid-dilated pupil)
• Leads to pupillary block → iris bows forward → angle closure
• Rapid rise in IOP

First-line management:

• Mannitol (IV): Rapidly lowers IOP by osmotic dehydration
• Pilocarpine: Causes miosis → opens angle by pulling iris away from trabecular meshwork

Why not others:

• Moxifloxacin: Antibiotic, no role
• Atropine: Causes mydriasis → worsens angle closure
• Lubricants: No role in IOP reduction
