questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient was received in the casualty following a road traffic accident. His BP was 90/60 mmHg and his pulse rate was 120/min. The emergency room physician asked you to replace the fluid loss in this patient. What is the maximum flow rate of fluid with the IV canula given in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 103 ml/ min

The green IV cannula used in this hemodynamically unstable patient is an 18G cannula, which has a maximum flow rate of 103 ml/ min.
questions.learning: 103 ml/ min The green IV cannula used in this hemodynamically unstable patient is an 18G cannula, which has a maximum flow rate of 103 ml/ min.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A student got his jaw locked while yawning. Identify the muscle attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lateral pterygoid

The lateral pterygoid muscle inserts into the neck of mandible and the articular disc of the TMJ, controlling disc movement during mouth opening.

Excessive contraction during yawning can displace the disc, leading to jaw locking.

Temporalis, medial pterygoid, and masseter attach to the mandible but do not insert into the articular disc.
questions.learning: Lateral pterygoid — The lateral pterygoid muscle inserts into the neck of mandible and the articular disc of the TMJ, controlling disc movement during mouth opening.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient with a negative urine pregnancy test presents to you with galactorrhea. An MRI was done which revealed a large pituitary tumor. If the patient is not willing for surgery, which of the following is the best drug for treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bromocriptine

The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of prolactinoma and the best drug for the treatment of the condition is bromocriptine.

Prolactinomas are pituitary tumors that can present as microadenomas or macroadenomas. Tumors <1cm in diameter and no regional invasion are known as microadenomas. It is more commonly seen in women. Tumors >1cm in size are known as macroadenomas. It can be locally invasive. Prolactin levels >200μg/L are suggestive of prolactinomas.

Women present with features such as amenorrhea, infertility, and galactorrhea. Visual field defects can also be seen. Symptoms in males include impotence, infertility, and loss of libido. An MRI is recommended in all patients who present with hyperprolactinemia.

Microadenomas can be managed with regular monitoring of prolactin levels and MRI scans, if fertility is not a requisite. Oral dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine and cabergoline are used for medical management. They are agonists at D2 receptors. Side effects include constipation, nasal stuffiness, and dry mouth. Resistance or intolerance to these drugs requires surgical debulking. Cases that do not respond to medical or surgical management can be treated with radiotherapy.

Other options:

Option B: Promethazine is an antihistamine used to treat motion sickness, pruritus, and oculogyric crisis.

Option C: Octreotide is a somatostatin analog that is used in acromegaly, variceal bleeding, and hepatorenal syndrome.

Option D: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic used in refractory schizophrenia and mania.
questions.learning: Bromocriptine — The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of prolactinoma and the best drug for the treatment of the condition is bromocriptine. Prolactinomas are pituitary tumors that can present as microadenomas or macroadenomas.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under which of the following data sets can information be found on monitoring fertility, family planning, maternal and child health, nutrition, and infectious diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. National family health survey

The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) provides comprehensive data on fertility, family planning, maternal and child health, nutrition, and infectious diseases in India.

It is a large-scale, periodic household survey that supports policy formulation, program monitoring, and evaluation.

In contrast, the Census focuses on population counts, SRS on fertility and mortality rates, and CRS on registration of births and deaths, not detailed health indicators.
questions.learning: National family health survey — The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) provides comprehensive data on fertility, family planning, maternal and child health, nutrition, and infectious diseases in India.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The image given below is from a chronic smoker's oral examination. Identify the lesion given.
questions.explanation: The image shows a thick, white, well-demarcated patch on the oral mucosa that cannot be scraped off, which is the clinical definition of "Leukoplakia". Chronic tobacco use (smoking or chewing) is the most significant risk factor. Leukoplakia is considered a potentially malignant disorder, as it can progress to squamous cell carcinoma. Erythroplakia (Option A) is a red patch that has a much higher risk of malignancy. Fordyce's granules (Option C) are benign, ectopic sebaceous glands that appear as small yellow-white spots. Koplik's spots (Option D) are small, blue-white spots on an erythematous base seen on the buccal mucosa in the prodromal phase of measles. Because leukoplakia is a diagnosis of exclusion, a biopsy is mandatory to check for dysplasia or carcinoma. Management involves smoking cessation and, in cases of high-grade dysplasia, surgical excision or laser ablation
questions.learning: The image shows a thick, white, well-demarcated patch on the oral mucosa that cannot be scraped off, which is the clinical definition of "Leukoplakia".

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about GFR? GFR- Glomerular filtration rate RPF- Renal Plasma Flow
options: Increase in sympathetic function increases GFR
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase in RPF increases GFR

The true statement about GFR is that the increase in RPF increases GFR.

With a constant glomerular hydrostatic pressure, an increase in blood flow into the glomerulus tends to increase the GFR and a lower rate of blood flow into the glomerulus tends to decrease the GFR.

GFR decreases with sympathetic stimulation as there is afferent arteriolar constriction. Strong activation of the renal sympathetic nerves can constrict the renal arterioles and decrease renal blood flow and GFR.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: When yellow, needle-shaped rhombic crystals are seen under microscopic examination in Barberio’s test, what substance is being detected?
questions.explanation: Barberio’s test is a forensic screening test used for the presumptive identification of semen on clothing or skin. The test involves adding a saturated solution of picric acid to the suspected stain. If semen is present, the picric acid reacts with spermine (a polyamine found in high concentrations in seminal fluid) to form spermine picrate. These appear under the microscope as characteristic yellow, needle-shaped, or rhombic-shaped crystals. Option B is incorrect; blood is detected using the Kastle-Meyer test or crystal tests like Teichmann and Takayama. Options C and D are not related to Barberio’s test. While useful, Barberio’s test is not as specific as the Florence test (which detects choline) or the definitive identification of spermatozoa under a microscope. Modern forensic labs now rely on more specific tests like the Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA/p30) test to confirm the presence of seminal fluid in medicolegal cases
questions.learning: Barberio’s test is a forensic screening test used for the presumptive identification of semen on clothing or skin. The test involves adding a saturated solution of picric acid to the suspected stain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 62-year-old woman with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with a two-day history of worsening breathlessness, cough, and increased sputum production. She appears distressed, with a respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute and an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. What is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
options: Initiate high-flow oxygen therapy to maintain oxygen saturation above 95%
Start nebulised bronchodilator therapy with salbutamol and ipratropium
Order a chest X-ray before any treatment is provided
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of COPD, evidenced by increased breathlessness and sputum production. Nebulized bronchodilators are the first-line immediate therapy to relieve bronchospasm and improve air movement. Initiating high-flow oxygen to (Option A) is dangerous in COPD, as it can suppress the hypoxic respiratory drive, leading to life-threatening retention; oxygen should be controlled to a target of 88–92%. Glucocorticoids (Option C) are important but typically given orally and take hours to act, making them secondary to bronchodilators. While a chest X-ray (Option D) is necessary to rule out complications like pneumonia, it should not delay the initiation of life-saving bronchodilator therapy in a distressed patient. Immediate management focuses on airway relief and stabilized gas exchange
questions.learning: The patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of COPD, evidenced by increased breathlessness and sputum production. Nebulized bronchodilators are the first-line immediate therapy to relieve bronchospasm and improve air movement.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 15-day-old infant had conjunctivitis, which later developed into respiratory distress and pneumonia. Chest Xray examination revealed bilateral lung infiltrates. Peripheral smear count showed 14,300/µL (N 43, L 54, E3). Which of the following is the most likely pathogenic organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlamydia trachomatis

The organism most likely to cause conjunctivitis, progressing to respiratory distress, and then pneumonia is Chlamydia trachomatis.

It is not possible to differentiate between chlamydial pneumonia and other causes of atypical pneumonia, like Mycoplasma (option D) based solely on the clinical presentation. Here, the history of conjunctivitis makes it more likely to be a chlamydial infection.

Pneumonia caused by C. trachomatis can develop in infants born to women with an untreated chlamydial infection in 10-20% of cases. It has a very characteristic presentation in infancy, disease onset usually occurs around 1 and 3 months of age and is insidious, with a persistent cough, tachypnea, and absence of fever (atypical pneumonia). Auscultation reveals rales; wheezing is uncommon.

The absence of fever and wheezing helps to distinguish C. trachomatis pneumonia from respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia.

A distinctive laboratory finding is the presence of peripheral eosinophilia (>400 cells/µL). The most consistent finding on chest radiographs is hyperinflation accompanied by minimal interstitial or alveolar infiltrates.

Other options:

Option B: Pneumococcal pneumonia generally presents with features of lobar pneumonia. Fever, dyspnea, and productive cough are the primary symptoms.

Option C: Although Neisseria gonorrhoeae is an important cause of ophthalmia neonatorum, it does not cause pneumonia-like features.

Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular organisms that produce basophilic inclusion bodies. They are called energy parasites as they lack enzymes for ATP synthesis. They cannot grow on artificial media but can grow on cell lines (McCoy, HeLa, or the yolk sac of the chick embryo)

Chlamydiae occur in two forms, the elementary body (extracellular, infective form)  and the reticulate body (intracellular, non-infective, and replicative form) which are found inside inclusion bodies.

Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of ophthalmia neonatorum in developed countries. Neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis is caused by serotypes D to K. Chlamydia trachomatis inclusion conjunctivitis manifests relatively late, usually over 1 week after birth.

It is usually a venereal infection derived from the cervix or urethra of the mother during delivery. On examination, the conjunctiva is swollen and edematous. The discharge is initially watery, but later becomes mucopurulent or bloody.

Newborns with suspected chlamydia infection should have samples drawn from both the conjunctivae and oropharynx. Since it is an obligate intracellular organism, swabs should also include conjunctival epithelial cells if possible. Giemsa staining shows characteristic intracellular inclusion bodies. Diagnosis is usually established by PCR.

The treatment includes oral erythromycin for two weeks. Topical erythromycin to tetracycline ointment may also be used.

If left untreated, associated systemic diseases such as chlamydial otitis and pneumonia may develop later. In all cases, both parents must receive appropriate treatment for genital infection.

questions.learning: Chlamydia trachomatis — The organism most likely to cause conjunctivitis, progressing to respiratory distress, and then pneumonia is Chlamydia trachomatis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A disease with mitochondrial inheritance is inherited from which family member?
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial inheritance follows a strict maternal pattern because mitochondria are inherited exclusively from the egg. During fertilization, the sperm contributes its nuclear DNA but its mitochondria are typically degraded or excluded, meaning only the mother passes mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) to her offspring. Consequently, an affected mother will pass the trait to all of her children, while an affected father (Option C) will not pass it to any of his offspring. Option B (paternal grandmother) is incorrect as paternal lineages do not transmit mtDNA. Option D is incorrect because inheritance is uniparental. Classic examples of mitochondrial disorders include Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) and MELAS syndrome. These diseases often exhibit variable expression due to heteroplasmy, where a cell contains a mix of both normal and mutated mtDNA. Therefore, the maternal line is the only source of transmission for these specific genetic conditions

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following substances does not usually show a reduction in concentration as the filtrate passes through the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)?
questions.explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) is responsible for the bulk reabsorption of filtered solutes. Substances like glucose (Option B) and amino acids (Option A) are almost 100% reabsorbed in the early PCT via sodium-linked cotransporters, causing their concentration in the tubular fluid to drop precipitously. Bicarbonate (Option D) is also preferentially reabsorbed in the early PCT, leading to a decrease in its concentration. In contrast, chloride (Option C) is not actively reabsorbed in the very first segment of the PCT; instead, as water and other solutes are removed, the concentration of chloride actually "increases" slightly in the tubular fluid. It is only later in the PCT that chloride is reabsorbed down its concentration gradient through paracellular and transcellular pathways. Therefore, on a "TF/P" (Tubular Fluid/Plasma concentration) graph, glucose and amino acids show the sharpest decline, while chloride is the only substance among the choices that remains above a ratio of 1.0 throughout the PCT

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis. Specimen revealed that she had gall bladder carcinoma infiltrating the muscularis layer. What is the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extended cholecystectomy

In the given clinical scenario, gallbladder carcinoma with T1b lesions is detected incidentally after cholecystectomy. Treatment guidelines for the same are as follows:

• Up to stage Ia and stage Ib with negative margins, a standard cholecystectomy would suffice.
• Stage Ib with perineural, lymphovascular invasion, positive cystic duct margins, or poor differentiation, and stage II, extended cholecystectomy should be performed. Extended cholecystectomy involves the removal of the gall bladder, segments IVB and V of the liver, and lymph nodes along the hepatoduodenal ligament, with or without removal of the common bile duct (CBD).

However, the likelihood of nodal disease increases significantly with T1b lesions and perineural, lymphatic, or vascular invasion, therefore, extended cholecystectomy is generally recommended for all patients who are medically fit with T1b or greater level of invasion.
If the initial procedure was performed laparoscopically, the surgeon should examine the laparoscopic port sites. The finding of disease at the port sites is a sign of generalized peritoneal disease and carries a very poor prognosis. However, resection of port sites is no longer recommended.

Chemotherapy is not required in early gallbladder cancer. Radiation has no role.

Treatment of gallbladder carcinoma:

TNM staging
Treatment

T1a
Simple cholecystectomy

T1b, T2, T3
Radical cholecystectomy

T4
Unresectable, chemotherapy and palliative nonsurgical therapy are provided

N1
Regional lymphadenectomy

N2
Radical cholecystectomy plus hepatopancreatic duodenectomy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman at 32 weeks of gestation presents with abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and uterine tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic clinical presentation of Abruptio Placenta (placental abruption) includes vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, and a tender, "woody-hard" uterus. This occurs when the placenta prematurely separates from the uterine wall before delivery. Placenta previa (Option D) classically presents with painless, bright red vaginal bleeding; the uterus is typically soft and non-tender. Uterine rupture (Option A) is a surgical emergency characterized by sudden, severe pain, loss of fetal station, and cessation of contractions, usually in a patient with a prior uterine scar. Vasa previa (Option C) presents with painless bleeding at the time of rupture of membranes, primarily affecting the fetus and causing rapid fetal distress. Abruptio placenta is a major cause of antepartum hemorrhage and can lead to maternal disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and fetal hypoxia. Given the tender uterus and painful bleeding, abruptio is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The classic clinical presentation of Abruptio Placenta (placental abruption) includes vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, and a tender, "woody-hard" uterus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Longitudinal growth of the bone is affected from fracture at:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Growth plate

Longitudinal growth of long bones occurs at the epiphyseal (growth) plate, where cartilage proliferation and ossification take place.

Fracture or damage to this plate in growing children can cause growth arrest or limb length discrepancy.

Epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis do not directly mediate longitudinal growth.
questions.learning: Growth plate Longitudinal growth of long bones occurs at the epiphyseal (growth) plate, where cartilage proliferation and ossification take place. Fracture or damage to this plate in growing children can cause growth arrest or limb length discrepancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A diabetic, hypertensive, and post-MI patient on atorvastatin, metoprolol, and aspirin has lipid profile results of total cholesterol: 238 mg/dL, triglycerides: 125 mg/dL, HDL: 50 mg/dL, and LDL: 160 mg/dL. Which additional medications should be considered to optimize lipid management in this patient? 1. Bemepedoic acid 2. Ezetimibe 3. Gemfibrozil 4. Evolocumab
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 4

This is a very high–risk ASCVD patient (diabetes, hypertension, post-MI) with persistently elevated LDL despite statin therapy. Target LDL according to major guidelines: <55 mg/dL

But his LDL is: 160 mg/dL

So intensification of lipid therapy is required.

Ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, and PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab) are appropriate add-on agents to further lower LDL.

| Drug | Target

| ---- | ------

| Statins | HMG-CoA reductase

| Bempedoic acid | ATP citrate lyase

| Ezetimibe | Intestinal cholesterol absorption

| PCSK9 inhibitors (Evolocumab) | LDL receptor degradation

Triglycerides are normal, so gemfibrozil is not indicated.

Thus, the correct combination is 1, 2, and 4.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of diabetes presents with cataract. Which of the following metabolic products is primarily responsible for cataract formation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sorbitol

A diabetic cataract occurs due to the accumulation of sorbitol within the lens.

In diabetic patients, increased levels of blood glucose lead to high levels of glucose in the aqueous humor. The excess glucose in the aqueous humor is metabolized into sorbitol through the polyol pathway by the enzyme aldose reductase. Sorbitol is then converted to fructose (option B) by sorbitol dehydrogenase but at a much slower rate. In addition, the polar nature of sorbitol prevents its intracellular removal through diffusion.

Sorbitol and fructose accumulate in the lens and the osmotic stress so produced results in overhydration, hydropic lens fibers, and apoptosis of the lens epithelial cells. Thus, the secondary osmotic overhydration is responsible for cortical opacities in a distinct pattern causing snowflake cataracts as shown below (Option B).

Other Options:

Option A: Mannitol is used to lower intracranial pressure. Features of raised of intracranial pressure are vomiting and papilledema.

Option C: In Classic Galactosemia, deficiency of galactose-1-uridyltransferase leads to the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol (dulcitol).

Pearl PF1394: Diseases and Associated Cataracts - Images

Wilson's Disease/Chalcosis: Sunflower Cataract

Diabetes mellitus:  Snowflake cataract

Blunt trauma: May present as rosette-shaped cataract

Myotonic dystrophy - Christmas tree cataract
questions.learning: Sorbitol — A diabetic cataract occurs due to the accumulation of sorbitol within the lens. In diabetic patients, increased levels of blood glucose lead to high levels of glucose in the aqueous humor.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly patient weighing about 70 kg is brought to the emergency department in a comatose state. Laboratory evaluation shows severe hyperglycemia (serum glucose 500 mg/ dL), arterial pH of 7.33, elevated plasma ketone levels, and normal serum potassium. While initiating treatment with intravenous saline, which additional substance should be included in the infusion for appropriate management?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with features of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): severe hyperglycemia (500 mg/dL), mild acidosis (pH 7.33), and elevated ketones. Initial management includes intravenous fluids (normal saline) followed by insulin therapy. However, an important principle in DKA management is potassium balance. Even though the serum potassium appears normal, total body potassium is actually depleted due to osmotic diuresis and insulin deficiency. Once insulin therapy is started, potassium shifts into cells, which can rapidly lead to dangerous hypokalemia, potentially causing arrhythmias. Therefore, potassium must be added to IV fluids early, provided serum potassium is not elevated. Why other options are wrong: (A) Insulin → necessary, but not added directly to saline infusion initially without addressing potassium (B) Bicarbonate → only in severe acidosis (pH < 6.9) (D) 14 units insulin IV → incorrect fixed dosing; insulin is given as infusion
questions.learning: The patient presents with features of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): severe hyperglycemia (500 mg/dL), mild acidosis (pH 7.33), and elevated ketones. Initial management includes intravenous fluids (normal saline) followed by insulin therapy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with a family history of breast and ovarian cancer seeks counseling about her risk and inquires about BRCA1/ BRCA2 genetic testing. In which of the following situations is BRCA1/BRCA2 testing not indicated?
options: Breast cancer diagnosed in a postmenopausal female >50 years of age
questions.explanation: Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations is prioritized for individuals with clinical features suggesting a high probability of a hereditary cancer syndrome. Testing is strongly recommended for male breast cancer (Option B), as a significant percentage of these cases are linked to BRCA2 mutations. Bilateral breast cancer (Option C) and the occurrence of both breast and ovarian cancer in the same individual (Option D) are classic hallmarks of the Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer (HBOC) syndrome and warrant testing. Breast cancer diagnosed in a postmenopausal woman over the age of 50 without a significant family history (Option A) is much more likely to be sporadic rather than hereditary. Guidelines typically recommend testing if breast cancer is diagnosed at age , or if older, only when specific family history criteria are met. Therefore, routine testing for an isolated case of postmenopausal breast cancer over 50 is not standard practice
questions.learning: Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations is prioritized for individuals with clinical features suggesting a high probability of a hereditary cancer syndrome.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: After consuming three cones of ice cream, a man notices that his ear feels colder than the central part of his body. Which area of the brain regulates body temperature?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypothalamus

The hypothalamus is responsible for regulating the body temperature.

The hypothalamus is the thermoregulatory centre of the body. It acts as a central command centre for thermoregulation, ensuring that the body maintains a relatively constant core temperature despite external temperature fluctuations.

* The reflex responses triggered by cold originate from the posterior hypothalamus,

* The reflex responses initiated by warmth primarily stem from the anterior hypothalamus.

Activation of the anterior hypothalamus leads to cutaneous vasodilation and sweating, while lesions in this area can result in hyperthermia, with rectal temperatures sometimes rising to 43°C (109.4°F).

Stimulation of the posterior hypothalamus induces shivering, and animals with lesions in this region experience a decrease in body temperature toward that of the surrounding environment.
questions.learning: Hypothalamus — The hypothalamus is responsible for regulating the body temperature. The hypothalamus is the thermoregulatory centre of the body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure shown originates from which pharyngeal arch during embryological development?
questions.explanation: The image displays the malleus and incus, which are two of the three middle ear ossicles. Embryologically, the malleus and incus are derived from the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch, known as Meckel's cartilage. Specifically, the dorsal end of Meckel's cartilage ossifies to form these structures. In contrast, the stapes (except for its footplate) is derived from the cartilage of the second pharyngeal arch, known as Reichert's cartilage (Option B). The third arch (Option C) gives rise to the greater horn of the hyoid and the stylopharyngeus muscle. The fourth arch (Option D) contributes to laryngeal cartilages like the thyroid and epiglottis. Understanding ossicular development is vital for diagnosing congenital hearing loss syndromes, such as Treacher Collins, where first arch derivatives are malformed. The malleus remains attached to the tympanic membrane, while the incus acts as a bridge to the stapes, facilitating sound conduction to the inner ear
questions.learning: The image displays the malleus and incus, which are two of the three middle ear ossicles. Embryologically, the malleus and incus are derived from the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch, known as Meckel's cartilage.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Bony septal perforation occurs in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Syphilis

Syphilis involves the perforation of the bony and cartilaginous parts.

Lupus, tuberculosis, and leprosy cause perforation only in the cartilaginous part.

Septal perforation can be caused by:

* Trauma

* Pathological:

* Septal abscess

* Nasal myiasis

* Rhinolith

* Chronic granulomatous disease

* Wegner's granulomatous disease

* Drug-related:

* Chronic use of steroid spray

* Cocaine abuse

* Arsenic/ chromium

* Idiopathic
questions.learning: Syphilis Syphilis involves the perforation of the bony and cartilaginous parts. Lupus, tuberculosis, and leprosy cause perforation only in the cartilaginous part.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Physiological dead space :
options: Is lesser than anatomical dead space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Represents inadequately perfused alveoli

Physiological dead space represents inadequately perfused alveoli.

Physiological dead space is the part of the respiratory system where no gas exchange occurs. It includes:

1. Anatomic dead space: Air in the conducting airways (nose, trachea, bronchi) that doesn't reach the alveoli.
2. Alveolar dead space: Air in alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused by blood.

Together, it represents the total volume of air that doesn't participate in oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.(Option B)

Anatomical dead space refers to the volume of all the space of the respiratory system other than the alveoli that do not participate in gas exchange. The anatomical dead space is not altered with a change in ventilation.

In healthy individuals:

• Anatomical dead space = 150 mL.
• Alveolar dead space is usually zero (increased in diseased conditions).

Alveolar Dead space represents inadequately perfused alveoli (wasted ventilation). (Option C)

In normal individuals, physiological dead space remains unaltered and is equal to the anatomical dead space (volume of all the space of the respiratory system other than the alveoli that do not participate in gas exchange).

Dead space cannot be measured using spirometry. (Option A)
questions.learning: Represents inadequately perfused alveoli Physiological dead space represents inadequately perfused alveoli. Physiological dead space is the part of the respiratory system where no gas exchange occurs.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the correct anatomies from the CT scan given below:
options: A- Kidney, B- Liver, C- Pancreas
A- Liver, B- Pancreas, C- Spleen
A- Spleen, B- Kidney, C- Liver
A- Pancreas, B- Liver, C- Spleen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A- Liver, B- Pancreas, C- Spleen

The correct identification of structures marked as A, B, and C in the CT image is: A-Liver, B-Pancreas, C-Spleen.

A - Liver: The liver is an organ located in the upper right portion of the abdomen. On a CT scan, the liver has a homogeneous appearance with well-defined borders. The liver's density is higher compared to surrounding organs due to its composition of hepatocytes and blood vessels. Additionally, blood vessels such as the hepatic artery and portal vein can be seen supplying blood to the liver.

B - Pancreas: The pancreas is a glandular organ situated behind the stomach and adjacent to the first part of the small intestine (duodenum). On a CT scan, the pancreas appears as a soft tissue structure with a slightly lower density compared to the liver. It typically has a lobulated appearance and is located in the retroperitoneal space. The pancreatic duct may also be visualized, extending from the pancreas to the duodenum.

C - Spleen: The spleen is an organ located in the upper left portion of the abdomen, beneath the diaphragm and behind the stomach. On a CT scan, the spleen appears as a well-defined structure with a homogeneous density similar to the liver. It typically has a slightly lower density compared to the liver.
questions.learning: A- Liver, B- Pancreas, C- Spleen — The correct identification of structures marked as A, B, and C in the CT image is: A-Liver, B-Pancreas, C-Spleen. A - Liver: The liver is an organ located in the upper right portion of the abdomen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents to OPD at 36 weeks of gestation and presents with complaints of breathlessness and excessive abdominal distension. On examination, fetal movements are normal, fetal parts not easily felt and muffled fetal heartbeat is heard. Symphysis fundal height came out to be 41weeks. Per abdomen examination reveals tense abdomen but not tender. What can be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Polyhydramnios

Polyhydramnios is diagnosed by ultrasound using:

| Parameter | Value

| --------- | -----

| Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) | > 24 cm

| Deepest vertical pocket | > 8 cm

Causes of Polyhydramnios

Maternal causes

• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

Fetal causes

• Anencephaly
• Esophageal Atresia

Idiopathic

• Most common (\~60%).

Complications

| Maternal | Fetal

| -------- | -----

| Breathlessness | Preterm birth

| Preterm labor | Cord prolapse

| Postpartum hemorrhage | Malpresentation

Excessive distension, SFH far ahead of dates, difficulty feeling fetal parts and muffled FHR are classic of polyhydramnios. Abdomen is tense but non-tender with no bleeding or pain suggestive of abruption. Hydrocephalus alone doesn’t explain this degree of maternal breathlessness and distension.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young boy presents to the outpatient department with severe nighttime itching. On examination, burrows are seen in the intertriginous areas, axillae, umbilicus, and between the fingers. Which organism is responsible for transmitting this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of nocturnal pruritus (severe itching at night), specific distribution (web spaces of fingers, axillae, and umbilicus), and the presence of burrows is diagnostic for Scabies. Scabies is a contagious skin infestation caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite. The female mite tunnels into the stratum corneum to lay eggs, creating the characteristic linear or S-shaped burrows. Lice (Option A) transmit pediculosis and certain fevers. Ticks (Option B) and fleas (Option D) are vectors for diseases like Lyme disease or plague but do not cause this specific burrowing skin infestation. Scabies is transmitted through direct, prolonged skin-to-skin contact. Management requires the application of a topical scabicide, such as 5% permethrin cream, to the entire body from the neck down. Crucially, all household members and close contacts must be treated simultaneously, regardless of symptoms, to prevent reinfection
questions.learning: The clinical triad of nocturnal pruritus (severe itching at night), specific distribution (web spaces of fingers, axillae, and umbilicus), and the presence of burrows is diagnostic for Scabies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following organs has the highest incidence of graft rejection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lungs

The lungs have one of the highest occurrences of graft rejection among solid organ transplants.

Graft rejection is the process by which T lymphocytes and antibodies destroy tissue grafts. It can be classified into:

Graft rejection
Time taken for rejection

Mechanism

Morphology

T-cell-mediated

Seen within the initial months after transplantation;

Clinical and biochemical signs of organ failure;

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: If division occurs on the 7th day during twin gestation, the result would be: (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diamnionic, monochorionic

The timing of division of a monozygotic twin pregnancy determines chorionicity and amnionicity.

Timing of division:

• 0–3 days → Diamniotic, dichorionic
• 4–8 days → Diamniotic, monochorionic
• 8–13 days → Monoamniotic, monochorionic
• 13 days → Conjoined twins

Division on the 7th day occurs after formation of the chorion but before formation of the amnion, resulting in:

• One chorion
• Two amniotic sacs

Thus, the twins are diamniotic and monochorionic.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the reason that hemoglobin cannot pass through the glomerulus in a normal physiological state?
options: It is a large molecule bounded with another protein.
It gets attracted to the positive charge of the glomerular filtration barrier.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a large molecule bounded with another protein.

The haemoglobin (Hb) cannot pass through the glomerulus in a normal physiological state because it is a large molecule bound with another protein.

The Hb molecule released into the blood from RBCs is immediately bound by a protein called haptoglobin (size: 12.4 nm). It forms the haemoglobin-haptoglobin complex which is large enough to be prevented from crossing the glomerular filtration barrier.

Free haemoglobin undergoes extensive glomerular filtration, which is blocked by Haptoglobin. The filtration of Hb leads to renal tubule iron deposition (brown) and hemoglobinuria. This is prevented by the sequestration of Hb by haptoglobin.

Another reason is because of the negative charge of Hb. Both the Hb and glomerular filtration barrier are negatively charged. Hence Hb is repelled away from the filtration barrier.

The glomerular filtration barrier consists of:

* The endothelium of the capillary

* A basement membrane - contains type IV collagen, glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge.

* A layer of epithelial cells (podocytes) surrounding the outer surface of the capillary basement membrane.

The capillary endothelium is perforated by thousands of small holes called fenestrae, which measure from 4 nm up to 8nm. Therefore, neutral substances with molecular diameters of less than 4 nm are freely filtered, and filtration of those with diameters of more than 8 nm approaches zero.

In addition to the size of the particles, the filtration also depends mainly on the charge of the particle being filtered. The glomerular capillary wall consists of highly negatively charged proteins called sialoproteins, which repel the negatively charged substances (anions). The glomerular filtration barrier is negatively charged, which will repel most of the negative charges (anionic substances). Whereas, the cationic substances are easily filtered.
questions.learning: It is a large molecule bounded with another protein. The haemoglobin (Hb) cannot pass through the glomerulus in a normal physiological state because it is a large molecule bound with another protein.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency leads to Laryngismus stridulus?
questions.explanation: Laryngismus stridulus (or spasmodic croup) is a clinical condition involving a sudden, involuntary spasm of the larynx that causes difficulty breathing and a high-pitched crowing sound. This is most often a manifestation of tetany caused by hypocalcemia. Since Vitamin D is the primary regulator of calcium absorption, its deficiency leads to low calcium levels, which in turn causes the neuromuscular irritability seen in tetany. Vitamin K (Option A) is essential for blood clotting. Vitamin E (Option B) acts as an antioxidant and is rarely deficient. Vitamin A deficiency (Option D) affects vision and immunity. This "spasm of the throat" is a classic, though now less common, sign of severe, infantile rickets. Management focuses on immediate correction of the hypocalcemia, often with intravenous calcium gluconate, followed by long-term Vitamin D and calcium supplementation to address the underlying nutritional deficiency
questions.learning: Laryngismus stridulus (or spasmodic croup) is a clinical condition involving a sudden, involuntary spasm of the larynx that causes difficulty breathing and a high-pitched crowing sound.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The full form of the Urban HEART programme is __.
options: Urban Health Equity Assessment and Response Tool
Urban Health Evaluation Assessment and Response Tool
Urban Health Equity Assessment and Response Technique
Urban Health Evaluation Assessment and Response Technique
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urban Health Equity Assessment and Response Tool

Urban HEART stands for Urban Health Equity Assessment and Response Tool and facilitates the process of addressing health inequities across the world.

Urban HEART guides local policymakers and communities through a standardized procedure of gathering relevant evidence and planning efficiently for appropriate actions to tackle health inequities.

Three main approaches applied to measure and tackle inequities in health are:

* targeting disadvantaged population groups or social classes

* narrowing the health gap

* reducing inequities throughout the whole population.

Core elements of Urban HEART:

* sound evidence

* intersectoral action for health

* community participation

Urban HEART is expected to achieve the following:

* local and national authorities equipped with relevant evidence to inform important decisions related to prioritization and resource allocation

* communities mobilized and empowered to promote health equity

* multiple sectors engaged in addressing common goals, including the promotion of health equity

* people living in cities with better health and social status, and reduced inequities in health between population groups.
questions.learning: Urban Health Equity Assessment and Response Tool Urban HEART stands for Urban Health Equity Assessment and Response Tool and facilitates the process of addressing health inequities across the world.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is called leukocyte common antigen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CD45

CD45, also known as the Leukocyte Common Antigen (LCA), is a transmembrane protein tyrosine phosphatase expressed on virtually all nucleated hematopoietic cells. It plays a crucial role in leukocyte activation and signal transduction, particularly in T- and B-cell receptor signaling.

• CD45 is expressed on most leukocytes, including:

• T lymphocytes
• B lymphocytes
• NK cells
• Monocytes
• Granulocytes

• It is absent on mature erythrocytes and platelets.
questions.learning: CD45 CD45, also known as the Leukocyte Common Antigen (LCA), is a transmembrane protein tyrosine phosphatase expressed on virtually all nucleated hematopoietic cells.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 24-year-old male with a previous history of psychiatric disorder has become aggressive with neighbours. He is cheerful, speaking rapidly and also sleeping little. He exhibits hyperactive behaviour after discontinuing his prescribed medication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bipolar disorder (Manic episode)

The given clinical vignette showing increased activity, energy, and euphoria with a decreased need for sleep is indicative of an acute manic episode in the setting of bipolar disorder.

Lithium is used in the management of bipolar disorder, and mania, and has anti-suicidal properties. It has a narrow therapeutic index, and blood levels in excess of this may cause symptoms of toxicity. Therapeutic drug monitoring is done by measuring lithium levels 12 hours after the last dose.

Lithium therapy for acute mania:

* Three individual 10-mg/kg doses of a sustained-release preparation administered at 2-h intervals.

* The sustained-release form is used to minimize GI adverse effects (e.g., nausea, diarrhea)

* Subsequent treatment may then be continued with Li+ carbonate.

Steady state-concentrations for therapy :

* For maintainance therapy in bipolar disorder - 0.5-0.8 mEq/L

* For episodes of acute mania - 0.8-1.2 mEq/L

* Toxic levels - >1.5 mEq/L

The blood sample for serum lithium estimation is to be collected after a time interval of 10-12 hours from the previous dose of lithium which is used to estimate the steady-state concentration.

Other Options:

Option A: Depression is consistent with feelings of hopelessness, hollowness, and low self-esteem lasting less than two-week intervals during which depressive episodes occur.

Option C: Diagnosis of Schizophrenia requires:

A 6-month period with at least 1-month overt psychotic symptoms where 2 or more of the following have to be present. And at least one must be delusion, hallucination or disorganised speech.

* Delusion

* Hallucination

* Disorganized speech (or formal thought disorder)

* Disorganized behaviour

* Affective flattening or other negative symptoms

Option D: The patient's history does not make mention of the use of any substances.
questions.learning: Bipolar disorder (Manic episode) — The given clinical vignette showing increased activity, energy, and euphoria with a decreased need for sleep is indicative of an acute manic episode in the setting of bipolar disorder.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with a respiratory rate of 66 breaths per minute, along with chest indrawing and nasal flaring. There are no other significant findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pneumonia

According to IMNCI guidelines, a 2–12 month old infant with fast breathing (respiratory rate ≥50/min) is classified as pneumonia. In this case, a respiratory rate of 66/min indicates fast breathing for age.

• Age-specific fast breathing:
• <2 months: ≥60/min
• 2–12 months: ≥50/min
• 1–5 years: ≥40/min
• Chest indrawing in infants may be present due to compliant chest wall and does not always indicate severe disease
• Severe pneumonia is diagnosed when there are danger signs such as inability to feed, lethargy, convulsions, or central cyanosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive woman in her third trimester presents to the hospital with a viral load of 1,200 copies/mL and is started on antiretroviral therapy. She delivers a healthy infant at 38 weeks via normal vaginal delivery. The baby is exclusively breastfed. Which of the following is the most appropriate prophylactic therapy for the newborn?
options: Nevirapine single dose and continue breast feeding
Zidovudine plus Nevirapine for 6 weeks and continue breast feeding
Nevirapine for 12 weeks and stop breast feeding
Zidovudine plus Nevirapine for 12 weeks and continue breast feeding
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Zidovudine plus Nevirapine for 12 weeks and continue breast feeding

In HIV-exposed infants, the choice and duration of prophylaxis depend on maternal viral load and transmission risk.

High-risk exposure (e.g., maternal viral load >1000 copies/mL, late ART initiation) → dual prophylaxis is required.

Recommended management:

• Zidovudine + Nevirapine for 12 weeks
• Continue exclusive breastfeeding (with maternal ART)

Why not others:

• Single-dose nevirapine → inadequate prophylaxis
• 6 weeks regimen → for low-risk infants only
• Stopping breastfeeding → not recommended in resource-limited settings (benefits outweigh risks with ART)
questions.learning: Zidovudine plus Nevirapine for 12 weeks and continue breast feeding In HIV-exposed infants, the choice and duration of prophylaxis depend on maternal viral load and transmission risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not correct regarding Behçet's disease?
options: Pathergy test is a criterion as per the ISG diagnostic criteria
Ulcers are common on the dorsum of the penis
Aphthous ulcers occur similar to Crohn’s disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ulcers are common on the dorsum of the penis

Behçet’s disease is like a restless storm that targets vessels of all sizes, leaving behind a trail of ulcers, eye inflammation, and systemic mischief.

• Immune-mediated vasculitis (both arteries & veins)
• Strong association with HLA-B51
• Neutrophil hyperactivity → endothelial damage

| System | Manifestation

| ------ | -------------

| Oral | Recurrent aphthous ulcers (most common)

| Genital | Painful ulcers (scrotum in males)

| Eye | Bilateral uveitis, hypopyon

| Skin | Erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions

| Vessels | Thrombosis, aneurysms

| Test | Pathergy test positive

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In a patient with sarcoidosis undergoing ophthalmic examination, Koeppe’s nodules are observed. On which ocular structure are these nodules typically located?
questions.explanation: Koeppe's nodules are a hallmark clinical finding in granulomatous uveitis, such as that seen in sarcoidosis or tuberculosis. These nodules are specifically located on the iris (Option C). More precisely, Koeppe's nodules are found at the pupillary border. They are small, white-to-gray cellular aggregates that may lead to the formation of posterior synechiae. Busacca nodules are similar granulomatous inflammatory deposits found on the anterior iris stroma away from the pupil. The cornea (Option A), conjunctiva (Option B), and retina (Option D) do not house these specific iris nodules. Clinically, identifying these nodules on slit-lamp examination helps the ophthalmologist confirm a granulomatous etiology for the patient's intraocular inflammation. Therefore, based on anatomical classification in uveitis, the iris is the correct and only location for Koeppe's nodules
questions.learning: Koeppe's nodules are a hallmark clinical finding in granulomatous uveitis, such as that seen in sarcoidosis or tuberculosis. These nodules are specifically located on the iris (Option C).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate was brought with complaints of poor feeding, vomiting, acidosis, and cataract. Urine Benedict’s test was positive, while urine glucose was negative. The enzyme defective in this case is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

A neonate with poor feeding, vomiting, acidosis, cataracts, and positive Benedict’s test (reducing sugar present) but negative glucose is classic for galactosemia.

Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT)

• Inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate → UDP-galactose
• Accumulation of:

o    Galactose-1-phosphate (toxic to liver)

o    Galactitol (via aldose reductase → causes cataracts)

Clinical features explained:

• Vomiting, poor feeding: After milk intake (lactose → glucose + galactose)
• Hepatic dysfunction → acidosis
• Cataracts: Due to galactitol accumulation
• Benedict’s positive, glucose negative: Indicates non-glucose reducing sugar (galactose)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Fructokinase: Essential fructosuria (benign)
• Sucrase: Causes sucrose intolerance (no cataracts)
• Lactase: Causes lactose intolerance (diarrhea, no systemic toxicity)
questions.learning: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase — A neonate with poor feeding, vomiting, acidosis, cataracts, and positive Benedict’s test (reducing sugar present) but negative glucose is classic for galactosemia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Causes of non-immune hydrops fetalis are all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ABO incompatibility

Hydrops fetalis is defined as abnormal accumulation of fluid in two or more fetal compartments and is classified into immune and non-immune causes.

• Immune hydrops is caused by red cell alloimmunization (e.g., Rh incompatibility; ABO incompatibility is also immune-mediated, though usually milder)
•

Non-immune hydrops (more common) includes:

•

Cardiac causes (congestive cardiac failure)

• Infections (e.g., parvovirus B19 causing fetal anemia)
• Chromosomal anomalies (e.g., Turner syndrome, trisomies)

Why option A is correct:

• ABO incompatibility is an immune cause, not a non-immune cause

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 26-year-old male patient, an accident victim started developing difficulty in breathing. On examination, his BP was 80/40mmHg, pulses were feeble. JVP was found to be elevated with an absent 'y descent', and heart sounds were muffled. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiac tamponade

The given clinical scenario with Beck's triad including hypotension, muffled heart sounds and elevated JVP suggests a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade.

Symptoms of cardiac tamponade include dyspnea, chest discomfort or fullness, peripheral edema, and fatigue. Examination findings are:

* Tachycardia and hypotension

* Jugular venous distention with a prominent x (early systolic) descent but an absent y (early diastolic) descent

* Pericardial rub

* Pulsus paradoxus refers to the fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg with inspiration

* Beck's triad: Distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and hypotension.

An eFAST is reliable and will show fluid in the pericardial space. A chest X-ray will show an enlarged heart shadow. ECG shows reduced voltage and electrical alternans. Electric alternans is a specific finding caused by the anteroposterior swinging of the heart with each contraction.

Management of cardiac tamponade:

* Emergency management - ultrasound-guided needle pericardiocentesis via subxiphoid route

* Definitive management - emergency thoracotomy or sternotomy

Pearl PF0262: JVP waveform and the abnormalities

1) The a-wave corresponds to atrial contraction.

Abnormality
Conditions

Pulmonary hypertension, right atrial thrombus/ mass, and tricuspid stenosis

2) The c-wave corresponds to the bulging of tricuspid valve into right atrium during ventricular contraction.

3) The x-descent corresponds to atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 51-year-old man complains of abdominal pain and blood stained stools. The barium enema study of his intestines shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intussusception

The given clinical scenario and the radiological image of the claw sign/pincer sign in barium enema is suggestive of intussusception.

Intussusception occurs when a portion of the alimentary tract is telescoped into an adjacent segment. It is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction between 5 months and 3 years of age. The most common location of intussusception is ileocolic.

The combination of paroxysmal abdominal pain, vomiting, and a palpable abdominal mass is a highly characteristic clinical presentation; the presence of associated rectal bleeding invariably confirms the diagnosis. Palpation of the abdomen usually reveals a slightly tender, "sausage-shaped" mass, sometimes ill-defined, which might increase in size during an episode of pain and is most often in the right upper abdomen, with its longitudinal axis cephalocaudal. However, approximately 30% of patients do not have a palpable mass.

Barium contrast enemas demonstrate a filling defect or cupping in the head of the contrast media where its advance is obstructed by the intussusceptum. This is known as the claw sign (shown below). A central linear column of contrast media may be visible in the compressed lumen of the intussusceptum, and a thin rim of contrast may be seen trapped around the invaginating intestine in the folds of mucosa within the intussuscipiens (coiled-spring sign). The intussusception appears as a sausage-shaped mass in a longitudinal plane or a target mass in the transverse plane on CT and USG.

Ultrasound signs include:

* Target sign -also known as the doughnut sign

* Pseudokidney sign: this is seen in the longitudinal section of the bowel:

* The edematous bowel resembles renal parenchyma and

* the mesentery, which is dragged into the intussusception, resembles the renal hilum.

* Crescent in a doughnut sign.

Other options:

Option B: Volvulus presents with constipation, abdominal bloating, nausea and/or vomiting. It shows a coffee bean sign.

Option C: Barium enema radiograph in colonic diverticulitis shows multiple barium-coated outpouchings from the colonic wall and gives the appearance of a saw-tooth. In cases of severe abdominal pain, a CT scan is preferred to avoid the risk of intestinal perforation.

Option D: Ulcerative colitis causes lead pipe appearance.

Pearl PF1800: Barium Studies

Barium swallow: Used to assess the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach. (Barium paste is used)

The image below is a barium swallow showing eosinophilic esophagitis and associated stricture:

Barium meal: Used to assess stomach and duodenum. (95% BaSO4 is used)

Barium meal followthrough: Used to assess the small intestine (50% BaSO4 is used)

Barium enema: Used to assess the large intestine (25% BaSO4 is used)

Pearl PF1850: Radiological findings in various GI disorders

Duodenal atresia: Double bubble sign

Jejunal and ileal atresia: Multiple air-fluid levels (plain erect X-ray abdomen) presenting as triple bubble sign.

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: Single enlarged gastric gas bubble - single bubble sign

Sigmoid volvulus: Coffee bean sign

Achalasia cardia: Bird-beak sign

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which fertility measure is affected by differences in age-specific mortality rates?
questions.explanation: The Net Reproductive Rate (NRR) is a vital fertility indicator defined as the average number of daughters a newborn female will bear during her lifetime, assuming she is subject to current age-specific fertility and mortality rates. Unlike the Gross Reproduction Rate (GRR), which only considers fertility, the NRR incorporates the probability of the mother surviving to and through her reproductive years. The General Fertility Rate (Option A) and Total Fertility Rate (Option B) are pure measures of births per women without considering maternal survival probabilities. Variations in age-specific mortality directly impact whether a daughter can "replace" her mother in the next generation, making the NRR a more realistic measure of population growth. An NRR of 1.0 represents replacement-level fertility. Therefore, because NRR is the only listed indicator that accounts for the risk of death before completing childbearing years, it is uniquely influenced by mortality fluctuations
questions.learning: The Net Reproductive Rate (NRR) is a vital fertility indicator defined as the average number of daughters a newborn female will bear during her lifetime, assuming she is subject to current age-specific fertility and mortality rates.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with a firm, painless lump on the upper eyelid that has been gradually increasing in size over several months. The swelling is situated away from the eyelid margin. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A chalazion is a chronic, non-infectious granulomatous inflammation of a Meibomian gland. Its classic clinical features match this scenario perfectly: it is a firm, painless nodule that develops slowly over weeks or months. Crucially, it is typically located within the tarsal plate, away from the lid margin (Option C). In contrast, a Stye or hordeolum (Option A) is an acute bacterial infection of the hair follicle or gland, which is intensely painful and located directly on the eyelid edge. Entropion (Option B) is the inward turning of the eyelid margin, not a discrete lump. Blepharitis (Option D) is a diffuse, chronic inflammation of the entire lid margin characterized by crusting and redness rather than a localized firm nodule. Therefore, based on the chronic, painless, and localized nature of the eyelid mass, chalazion is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: A chalazion is a chronic, non-infectious granulomatous inflammation of a Meibomian gland. Its classic clinical features match this scenario perfectly: it is a firm, painless nodule that develops slowly over weeks or months.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman complains of fatigue, dry skin and cold intolerance since 2 weeks. She was started on amiodarone 1 month ago for persistent atrial fibrillation. Tests show high TSH (15 mU/l) and low free T4 levels. How would you manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Supplement levothyroxine

Thyroxine supplementation is indicated for amiodarone induced hypothyroidism which is characterized by symptoms of hypothyroidism (fatigue, dry skin, cold intolerance) and lab findings (elevated TSH, reduced free T4) following amiodarone use.

Amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism (AIH) can occur shortly after (as early as 2 weeks) amiodarone use due to iodine induced thyroid suppression (Wolff Chaikoff effect). It is characterized by clinical features of hypothyroidism and lab findings of elevated TSH and reduced free T4. It occurs more frequently in women and those with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies. It is managed by thyroxine supplementation, without the need to discontinue amiodarone (Option A).

Amiodarone is an iodine-containing compound that is structurally related to thyroid hormone. It is a class III antiarrhythmic drug, which increases the duration of an action potential by blocking potassium channels, thereby increasing the time taken for repolarization. It is used to maintain normal sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation.

Amiodarone can cause hypothyroidism due to the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, where excessive iodine leads to transient inhibition of organification and synthesis of thyroid hormones. Patients with underlying autoimmune thyroid disease are at increased risk of amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism.

Other adverse effects of amiodarone include hypotension, bradycardia, myocardial depression, photosensitization, corneal microdeposits (corneal verticillata), pulmonary fibrosis, and peripheral neuropathy.

Other options:

Option C: Corticosteroids would be indicated in amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis and not amiodarone induced hypothyroidism.

Option D: Patients who are asymptomatic, with subclinical hypothyroidism following amiodarone use can be managed by observation and regular monitoring with thyroid function tests. Subclinical hypothyroidism is characterized by TSH level > 4.5 and ≤ 10 mU/l, normal FT4 and absence of clinical features of hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: As per the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, until when can an MTP be performed on grounds of contraceptive failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 20 weeks

As per the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act of 2021, the upper limit for termination of pregnancy on grounds of contraceptive failure is 20 weeks.

The MTP Act of 2021 specifies special circumstances for termination of pregnancy beyond 20 weeks till 24 weeks of gestation. These include:

* Survivor of sexual assault, rape or incest.

* Minors

* Mentally ill women including mental retardation

* Change of marital status during the ongoing pregnancy (widowhood and divorce)

* Women with physical disabilities (Major disability criteria - Rights of persons with disabilities act - 2016)

* Women with pregnancy in humanitarian settings or disaster or emergency situations as declared by the government.

* Fetal malformations that have a substantial risk of being incompatible with life or if the child is born, may suffer from serious physical or mental abnormalities to be seriously handicapped. (Option A)

Termination of pregnancy can be done only up to 20 weeks based on grounds of contraception failure.

* Until 20 weeks of gestation - Opinion of one doctor

* 20-24 weeks of gestation - Opinion of two doctors

* The name and particulars of the woman whose pregnancy has been terminated cannot be disclosed. It can only be revealed to a person in force authorised by law. The ground for failure of contraception is extended to women and their partners.

Pearl PF1638: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971

MTP Act with 2021 amendments

Indications:

* Therapeutic - to save the life of the mother

* Eugenic - to prevent the risk of the child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality i.e. first-trimester viral infections, teratogenic drug intake, radiation exposure

* Humanitarian - pregnancy resulted from rape or incest

* Social - pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives

Rules:

* Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in the performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy.

* MTP should be carried out in a government or government-recognized hospital. Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district.

* The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years.

Consent:

The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband or partner is not necessary.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police.

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state

Upper limit of MTP:

* Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations

* Up to 20 weeks in case of contraception failure (any female with her partner)

* At any gestational age for substantial fetal anomalies decided by the medical board

Confidentiality:

A register for recording the details of MTP must be kept for at least 5 years. The patient's name must not be entered, only the reference number is used. Unlawful disclosure of patient's details is punishable with 1-year imprisonment ± fine.
questions.learning: 20 weeks As per the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act of 2021, the upper limit for termination of pregnancy on grounds of contraceptive failure is 20 weeks.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During the court proceedings, the defense lawyer asks a leading question, which the prosecutor appeals against. The judge grants the appeal. Such questions are permitted during which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cross examination

Leading questions are not allowed in all of the given options except cross-examination, i.e leading questions are allowed during cross-examination.

As per section 141 of the Indian Evidence Act, a leading question is one which is suggestive of the answer that is desired or one which includes a fact and leads to the admitting of a conclusive answer, such as yes or no.

Cross-examination is one wherein the witness is questioned by the opposite party's lawyer, i.e the lawyer for the accused or the defense lawyer. It is undertaken with the objective to demonstrate favorable facts to their case, to test the accuracy of the witness statements, to unearth new or old facts, and to discredit the witness.

The sequence of examination while recording evidence is as follows:

* Examination-in-Chief/direct examination by the party that summoned the witness to elicit all the facts from the witness. Leading questions are not allowed (option C). The only exception is if the judge is satisfied that the witness is hostile.

* Cross-examination is done by the defence lawyer.

* Re-examination is done by the party that summoned the witness to correct or clarify or detail the statements made by the witness during cross-examination. Leading questions are not allowed (option A).

Other options:

Option D: A dying declaration is an oral or written statement made by a person who is dying. The doctor should certify that the person is conscious and with normal mental faculties before the declaration is recorded. It is recorded by the executive magistrate, or a doctor in the presence of two witnesses, if there is no time for the magistrate to come. Leading questions should not be asked.
questions.learning: Cross examination Leading questions are not allowed in all of the given options except cross-examination, i.e leading questions are allowed during cross-examination.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Following a surgical procedure, a patient develops a characteristic clinical sign. Injury to which specific nerve is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the classic “hand of benediction”, seen when a patient with median nerve injury attempts to make a fist. In this condition, the index and middle fingers fail to flex, while the ring and little fingers flex normally due to intact ulnar nerve function. This occurs because the median nerve supplies the flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus, which are responsible for flexion of the index and middle fingers. This deformity is typically observed in proximal median nerve injuries, such as those occurring at the elbow or during surgical procedures. Other options are incorrect: (A) Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop, not finger flexion defects. (C) Ulnar nerve injury leads to clawing of the ring and little fingers at rest, not inability to flex the index and middle fingers. (D) Long thoracic nerve injury causes winged scapula, unrelated to hand movements. Thus, the inability to flex the lateral two digits confirms a median nerve injury

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A mother of a 5 day old baby presents with the complaint that her baby is "unable to latch on " for breastfeeding. She also says there is some leakage of milk at times and on examination, there is bilateral tenderness and swelling. What is the most likely cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Breast engorgement

The most likely cause for this is due to breast engorgement.

Breast Engorgement :

* Common in women who do not breastfeed often, leakage of milk and breast pain is seen.

* Presents 24 to 72 hours post-partum, peaks 3 to 5 days after delivery and resolves spontaneously

* Characterized by bilateral breast tenderness and swelling typically

* Treatment is by cold compresses and analgesics.

* Breasts can be supported with a sports bra or binder.

* Antibiotics are not indicated.

* Pharmacological or hormonal agents are in general not recommended to suppress lactation.

Other options:

Lactational mastitis:

* Pathogenesis: Bacteria enters ducts through nipple and multiplies in stagnant milk.

* A firm, red, tender, swollen quadrant of unilateral breast, +/- myalgias, chills, malaise

* Treatment:analgesia,frequent breast feeding or pumping,antibiotic of choice: Dicloxacillin or Cephalexin

Bacterial mastitis

* Localized inflammationdue to ascending infection or infection due to milk stasis

* Dull pain

* Tenderness, erythema

* Antibiotics, analgesics

Breast abscess

* Occurs as a complication of mastitis, pus formation

* Throbbing pain

* Point tenderness, erythema

* Induration of skin(if chronic), lymphadenopathy

* Fluctuation test +ve

* Aspiration of Pus, antibiotics, analgesics

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A laborer's second child is brought to the OPD with a swollen belly and dull face. He has been fed rice water (rice milk) in his diet mostly. On investigations, the child is found to have low serum protein and low albumin. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kwashiorkor

The given clinical scenario of a child with a swollen belly, dull face with hypoproteinemia along with poor diet history suggests the diagnosis of kwashiorkor.

Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by edema and apathy. In edematous malnutrition, the initial appearance of edema is commonly observed in the feet and lower legs, progressing into generalized edema affecting the hands, arms, and face. The skin over the swollen areas may show dark, crackled, peeling patches (flaky paint dermatosis) with pale skin underneath, making it susceptible to infections.

There may be sparse and easily pluckable hair. Hepatomegaly with fatty infiltration is a common finding. Associated symptoms of misery, apathy, and loss of appetite are seen in children with edema.

Other options:

Option B: Marasmus is a severe form of wasting characterized by significant loss of fat and muscle tissue as the body utilizes these resources for energy. It is often triggered by acute starvation or illness in individuals with borderline nutritional status.

Option C: Indian childhood cirrhosis (ICC) is a chronic liver disease that affects infants and young children. Common symptoms include jaundice, pruritus, lethargy, and hepatosplenomegaly. The disease progresses rapidly, leading to the development of cirrhosis.

Option D: Kawasaki disease (KD) is a systemic inflammatory disorder with arteritis of medium to large-sized vessels. It presents with fever, rash, conjunctivitis,  and cervical lymph node enlargement.
questions.learning: Kwashiorkor — The given clinical scenario of a child with a swollen belly, dull face with hypoproteinemia along with poor diet history suggests the diagnosis of kwashiorkor.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are typical physical findings in pericardial effusion? 1. Raised JVP 2. Hypotension 3. Oliguria 4. Water hammer pulse Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Pericardial effusion is the accumulation of fluid within the pericardial sac. When the accumulation is large or rapid, it can cause cardiac tamponade, leading to impaired ventricular filling, reduced cardiac output, and hemodynamic compromise.

• Statement 1. Raised JVP: Correct. Raised JVP occurs due to impaired right atrial filling and elevated systemic venous pressure.
• Statement 2. Hypotension: Correct. Hypotension results from reduced ventricular filling and decreased cardiac output. It is one of Beck’s triad in cardiac tamponade.
• Statement 3. Oliguria: Correct. Oliguria develops due to reduced renal perfusion secondary to low cardiac output.
• Statement 4. Water hammer pulse: Incorrect. Water hammer pulse (collapsing pulse) is seen in aortic regurgitation, PDA, and other high stroke volume states—not in pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade.

questions.text: Chadwick’s sign describes:
options: The dusky hue of the vestibule and anterior vaginal wall visible at about 8th week of pregnancy
Softening of cervix at 6th week of pregnancy
The abdominal and vaginal fingers apposed below the body of the uterus during bimanual examination
Regular and rhythmic uterine contraction which can be elicited during bimanual examination at 4–8 weeks of pregnancy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The dusky hue of the vestibule and anterior vaginal wall visible at about 8th week of pregnancy

Chadwick’s sign is one of the probable signs of pregnancy and refers to the bluish or violaceous discoloration (dusky hue) of the vulva, vestibule, vagina, and cervix due to increased pelvic vascularity and venous congestion. It becomes apparent at approximately 6–8 weeks of gestation.

Why not the other options?

• B. Softening of cervix at 6th week of pregnancy: This is Goodell’s sign.
• C. The abdominal and vaginal fingers apposed below the body of the uterus during bimanual examination: This is Hegar’s sign, caused by softening of the uterine isthmus.
• D. Regular and rhythmic uterine contraction elicited during bimanual examination at 4–8 weeks: This is Palmer’s sign.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented with painless decrease in vision and metamorphopsia. Fundus examination revealed the lesion shown in the image. What is the expected finding on angiography?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Double circulation

The clinical vigenette is of a patient presenting with painless dimunition of vision and metamorphopsia with the right fundus showing choroidal melanoma superotemporal to the optic disc and involving the macula.

In this patient a “Double circulation” pattern consisting of an internal circulation within the lesion and the normal vascularity of the overlying retina will be seen on angiography.

Although collar stud(Option C) appearance is pathagnomic for choroidal melanoma, it can be seen on B-scan and not on angiography.

Choroidal melanoma is a primary intraocular malignancy in adults that peaks around 60 years of age.

Symptoms include a range of visual disturbances such as painless decrease in vision and metamorphosia when macula is involved.

Other features of Choroidal melanoma includes:

• A solitary elevated subretinal grey-brown dome shaped mass
• Clumps of orange pigment are common over the mass
• Collar stud appearance on B-scan (option C): It is pathagnomic of choridal melanoma. It is seen if the tumour breaks through the Bruch's membrane into the subretinal space .
• Associated haemorrhage

Smoke stack pattern (option A) and ink blot (option B) pattern is seen on FFA in central serous retinopathy (CSR).

CSR is the spontaneous serous detachment of the sensory neuroretina in the foveal region with or without retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) detachment.

This occurs due Choroidal vascular hyperpermeability.

On FFA it is initially seen as an ink-blot pattern or smoke stack pattern of hyperfluorescence which then spreads to take the configuration of mushroom or umbrella pattern.
