questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old male presented with a hard painless testicular swelling. There were no inguinal, intra-abdominal or mediastinal lymph nodes on CT Scan. The blood investigations showed AFP levels of > 3000. USG shows uniform echotexture and small areas of necrosis. The next line of management is _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. High inguinal orchidectomy

The given clinical features of painless testicular swelling with raised AFP levels without distant metastasis point towards the likely diagnosis of stage 1 non-seminomatous germ cell tumour (NSGCT) of the testis. The next step in management is a high inguinal orchidectomy.

Core needle trucut biopsy and FNAC should be never done when there is a suspicion of testicular neoplasm as it will result in the seeding of tumor cells into the skin and lymphatics, leading to upstaging of the tumor (Options B and C). Currently, there is no role for PET-CT in the routine evaluation of non-seminomatous germ cell tumor and seminoma at the time of diagnosis (Option D).

Testicular tumors are classified according to their predominant cell type:

• Germ cell tumors (90-95%): seminomatous (seminoma) or NSGCT (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, teratoma and choriocarcinoma).
• Sex cord-stromal tumors (1-2%): Leydig cell tumors, Sertoli cell tumors
• Lymphoma (3-7%)
• Other tumors (1-2%)

The most common presentation of testicular cancer is painless testicular mass. Pain is more commonly associated with NSGCT and two-thirds of patients present with metastatic disease at the time of diagnosis. The symptoms of metastatic disease include abdominal pain, dyspnea, chest pain, cough or hemoptysis.

Management of testicular tumours:

1. Ultrasound of the testis should be done in all suspected cases of a testicular tumour to confirm the diagnosis.
2. Tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH) are measured for the staging of cancer.
3. CT- chest, abdomen, and pelvis are done to detect metastasis.
4. Orchidectomy via an inguinal incision (high inguinal orchidectomy) is the best line of treatment in case of a suspected testicular tumour.
5. Further management is based on staging. The older staging is preferred over the TNM staging for treatment and is given below:

• Stage I: Tumour is confined to testis and epididymis
• Stage II: Nodal tissue is present but is confined to nodes below the diaphragm
• Stage III: Nodal involvement above the diaphragm
• Stage IV: Non-lymphatic metastatic spread (mostly in lungs)

6. Stage I tumours:

• Combination chemotherapy with bleomycin, etoposide, and cis-platinum (BEP chemotherapy) is given for NSGCTs, as they are radio-resistant.
• Chemotherapy with cisplatinum and radiotherapy to para-aortic lymph nodes can be given in seminomas as they are radiosensitive.

7. Stage II-IV tumours (seminomas and NSGCTs) are treated with BEP chemotherapy and retroperitoneal lymph node dissection if needed.
questions.learning: High inguinal orchidectomy — The given clinical features of painless testicular swelling with raised AFP levels without distant metastasis point towards the likely diagnosis of stage 1 non-seminomatous germ cell tumour (NSGCT) of the testis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pseudoexfoliation syndrome

The diagnosis based on the image given is pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is an age-related degenerative disorder, more commonly seen in women. It is marked by the deposition of exfoliative material on the iris, ciliary region, and lens capsule. They appear as flakes on the anterior lens capsule and edge of the iris.

The material can get collected in the anterior chamber angle and impede the aqueous humor drainage. Patients affected by this condition are at an increased risk of developing open-angle glaucoma. Rarely, angle-closure glaucoma can also be seen. Other ocular symptoms include iris sphincter atrophy, anisocoria, and heterochromia. Systemic manifestations due to abnormal fibrillary deposition may also be seen.

Other options:

Option A - Common intraocular foreign bodies include glass particles or metal chips. It can lodge in various sites like the anterior chamber, lens, posterior chamber, and vitreous. This can lead to cataract formation, retinal hemorrhages, and tears. Organic foreign bodies can cause infection. Iron foreign bodies can cause siderosis while copper ones can result in chalcosis. An entry wound can be identified with topical fluorescein.  In cases of metallic intraocular foreign bodies, MRI is contraindicated. CT scan can be done instead.

Option C - Ocular trauma can be a closed-globe or open-globe injury. Closed-globe injury can vary from simple corneal abrasions to widespread intraocular damage. Open-globe injuries include globe rupture or laceration.

A corneal abrasion highlighted with fluorescein staining is shown below.

Option D - Vossius ring is used to describe a ring-shaped pigment dispersal observed on the anterior surface of the lens due to the deposition of brown amorphous pigment granules. It is close to the miosed pupil in diameter. The force of the blow drives the cornea and iris backward, creating an impression of the iris on the lens.
questions.learning: Pseudoexfoliation syndrome — The diagnosis based on the image given is pseudoexfoliation syndrome. Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is an age-related degenerative disorder, more commonly seen in women.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true about interleukin-12?

1. Increases production of interferon-γ
2. Inhibits T cells
3. Inhibits B cells
4. Produced by macrophages
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 4

The true statements are that interleukin-12 (IL-12) is produced by macrophages and increases the production of interferon-γ (IFN-γ).

IL-12 is produced by dendritic cells and macrophages. Its principle actions are to promote the production of IFN-γ, which drives TH1-type responses and further stimulates macrophage activation. It also promotes the differentiation of CD4+ T-cells to Th1 cells.
questions.learning: 1 and 4 The true statements are that interleukin-12 (IL-12) is produced by macrophages and increases the production of interferon-γ (IFN-γ). IL-12 is produced by dendritic cells and macrophages.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: During a routine prenatal visit, a 25-year-old pregnant woman voices concern about traveling to a tropical area because of the risk of Zika virus infection. You counsel her on the importance of knowing the vectors involved in transmission. Which mosquito species is the primary vector responsible for spreading the Zika virus?
questions.explanation: Zika virus is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito from the Aedes genus. While Aedes aegypti is the world's most common primary vector, Aedes albopictus (the Asian tiger mosquito) is a significant and widespread secondary vector that is also capable of tr-ansmitting the virus (Option B). Aedes australis (Option A), Aedes mitchellae (Option C), and Aedes polynesiensis (Option D) are not the primary drivers of the global Zika epidemics. Zika infection during pregnancy is of major concern because it is neurotropic and can cause microcephaly and other severe fetal brain anomalies. Education for pregnant travelers focuses on using insect repellent, wearing long sleeves, and avoiding areas with known outbreaks. In many regions of the world where A. aegypti is absent, A. albopictus serves as the main threat. Therefore, among the choices provided, Aedes albopictus is the recognized vector for Zika virus transmission
questions.learning: Zika virus is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito from the Aedes genus. While Aedes aegypti is the world's most common primary vector, Aedes albopictus (the Asian tiger mosquito) is a significant and widespread…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man who recently underwent transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) presents three days later with drowsiness and altered sensorium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient is experiencing "TURP Syndrome," a recognized complication of prostatic surgery. This occurs when large volumes of non-conductive irrigating fluid (like glycine) are absorbed through opened prostatic venous sinuses during the procedure. This leads to dilutional hyponatremia (low serum sodium). Clinically, hyponatremia results in cerebral edema, manifesting as drowsiness, confusion, and altered consciousness. Hypernatremia (Option A) would be inconsistent with the rapid absorption of hypotonic irrigation fluids. While a stroke (Option C) could cause altered consciousness in an elderly patient, it would typically present with focal neurological deficits rather than generalized drowsiness following a specific surgical trigger. Meningitis (Option D) would present with high fever and neck stiffness, which are not described here. Standard management for symptomatic TURP-induced hyponatremia involves fluid restriction and, in severe cases, cautious administration of hypertonic saline. Therefore, dilutional hyponatremia is the most probable diagnosis following this specific urological intervention
questions.learning: The patient is experiencing "TURP Syndrome," a recognized complication of prostatic surgery. This occurs when large volumes of non-conductive irrigating fluid (like glycine) are absorbed through opened prostatic venous sinuses during the procedure.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which international agency supports the construction of sanitary latrines (toilets) in India?
questions.explanation: The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) has been actively involved in supporting water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programs in India. One of its key contributions includes promoting the construction of sanitary latrines, improving access to safe sanitation, and reducing open defecation. USAID collaborates with the Government of India and various NGOs under initiatives such as the Swachh Bharat Mission, aiming to improve public health by enhancing sanitation infrastructure and hygiene practices. These efforts help in preventing waterborne diseases and improving overall community health. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) CURE: Not a major international agency involved in sanitation programs in India (C) Red Cross: Focuses more on disaster relief and emergency health services (D) Ford Foundation: Works in development sectors but not specifically known for latrine construction programs
questions.learning: The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) has been actively involved in supporting water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programs in India.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which one of the following imaging modalities imparts the highest dose of ionizing radiation to the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT head and neck

The amount of ionizing radiation varies considerably among imaging modalities:

• (a) Ultrasound — Incorrect: Uses sound waves and therefore involves no ionizing radiation.
• (b) Chest X-ray — Incorrect: Uses ionizing radiation, but the dose is relatively low.
• (c) Screening mammography — Incorrect: Uses X-rays, but the radiation dose is generally lower than that of CT.
• (d) CT head and neck — Correct: CT uses multiple X-ray exposures and therefore delivers a substantially higher radiation dose than conventional X-rays or mammography.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient came to the casualty with acute bronchial asthma after treatment for glaucoma. Which of the following is most probable causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Timolol

Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that is used in glaucoma. Non-selective beta-blockers can cause precipitation of bronchial asthma in susceptible individuals (beta-2 block on bronchi).

Ocular beta-blockers reduce Intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous formation by blockade of β2 receptors. The most commonly prescribed non‐selective beta‐blocker eye drops is timolol and eye drops significantly affect lung function and increase asthma morbidity.

Betaxolol is a beta 1 selective blocker that is used in glaucoma and has a lower propensity to precipitate bronchial asthma. (option B)

Latanoprost and bimatoprost are prostaglandin (PGF2 alpha) analogs and does not precipitate bronchial asthma. (option C and D)
questions.learning: Timolol Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that is used in glaucoma. Non-selective beta-blockers can cause precipitation of bronchial asthma in susceptible individuals (beta-2 block on bronchi).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: According to Weigert Meyer's rule of duplication of the ureter, the lower pole ureter in the urinary bladder is:
options: Lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter
Lateral and caudal to the upper pole ureter
Medial and cephalad to the upper pole ureter
Medial and caudal to the upper pole ureter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter

The lower pole ureter is lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter.

According to Weigert Meyer's rule of congenital complete duplication of the ureter,

* The ureter draining the upper segment of the kidney inserts in the bladder inferior and medial to the ureter draining the lower segment of the kidney (Weigert–Meyer rule). The lower moiety of the completely duplicated system is generally normal.

* The upper ureter is considered ectopic and the lower ureter is considered orthotopic.

* Ectopic ureters are more prone to obstruction.

* Orthotopic ureters are more prone to reflux due to perpendicular entry into bladder musculature rather than oblique entry.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is most strongly associated with which type of head and neck cancer?
questions.explanation: High-risk HPV strains, particularly HPV-16, are most strongly associated with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, which includes sites like the tonsils and the base of the tongue. These tumors often present in younger, non-smoking individuals and generally carry a better prognosis than tobacco-related cancers. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Option A) is linked to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) rather than HPV. Hypopharyngeal carcinoma (Option B) is primarily driven by tobacco and alcohol abuse. While HPV may play a minor role in some laryngeal carcinomas (Option C), the association is significantly weaker than that seen in the oropharynx, and there is no proven prognostic benefit for HPV-positive laryngeal tumors. Because HPV oncoproteins E6 and E7 specifically target p53 and Rb pathways in the oropharyngeal mucosa, it remains the primary head and neck site for HPV-driven malignancy
questions.learning: High-risk HPV strains, particularly HPV-16, are most strongly associated with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, which includes sites like the tonsils and the base of the tongue.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During the first trimester of pregnancy, propylthiouracil (PTU) is considered the safer medication for managing hyperthyroidism, as it has a lower risk of teratogenic effects compared to methimazole.
questions.explanation: Managing hyperthyroidism during pregnancy requires a careful balance between maternal health and fetal safety. During the first trimester, Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the preferred and safer medication of choice (Option A). PTU is favored because it is more highly protein-bound and crosses the placenta less readily than other options, and it is less associated with major congenital malformations. In contrast, Methimazole (Option B) and its prodrug Carbimazole (Option C) are associated with a higher risk of "methimazole embryopathy," including defects like aplasia cutis and choanal or esophageal atresia when used in early pregnancy. Radioactive iodine (Option D) is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy as it can destroy the fetal thyroid gland and is potentially teratogenic. Many clinicians switch patients from Methimazole to PTU during the first trimester and then back to Methimazole for the remainder of the pregnancy to avoid PTU-induced maternal hepatotoxicity
questions.learning: Managing hyperthyroidism during pregnancy requires a careful balance between maternal health and fetal safety. During the first trimester, Propylthiouracil (PTU) is the preferred and safer medication of choice (Option A).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presents with a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) and undergoes enucleation of the affected eye. Histopathology reveals Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child is the most common sign of retinoblastoma, the most frequent primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. The definitive diagnostic hallmark provided is the microscopic finding of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. These rosettes are pathognomonic for retinoblastoma and consist of clusters of columnar or tall cuboidal cells arranged around a clear central lumen, representing an attempt at photoreceptor differentiation. Medulloblastoma (Option B) and Astrocytoma (Option D) are central nervous system tumors that do not primary involve the globe or show these specific rosettes. Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option C) is an orbital tumor that can cause protrusion but arises from soft tissue, not retinal tissue. Retinoblastoma is caused by mutations in the tumor suppressor gene. Therefore, given the age, the classic "cat's eye" reflex, and the pathognomonic histology shown in the image, retinoblastoma is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child is the most common sign of retinoblastoma, the most frequent primary intraocular malignancy of childhood.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a cyst on the neck anterior to the sternocleidomastoid at the junction of the upper and middle third of the muscle. This cyst is due to the persistence of which of the following embryological clefts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2nd cleft

A cyst presenting at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border is most likely a branchial cyst. It develops from the vestigial remnants of the second branchial cleft.

Branchial cyst is most commonly seen at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border. It is usually lined by squamous epithelium and contains thick, turbid fluid full of cholesterol crystals. It is fluctuant and may transilluminate to a lesser extent when it contains clear fluid.

A branchial fistula may be acquired or congenital. The congenital fistula is seen at the junction of the middle and lower third of the sternomastoid. An acquired fistula is usually seen in cases of incomplete surgery for the branchial cyst or spontaneous rupture, and it is seen at the same site as the cyst.

The below image shows a large right-sided branchial cyst.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a barking cough and noisy breathing. Anteroposterior neck X-ray reveals a steeple sign. What type of stridor is most commonly seen in this condition?
questions.explanation: In a child with croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis), the presence of a steeple sign on AP neck X-ray indicates subglottic narrowing. This region lies between the vocal cords and upper trachea, so obstruction here affects airflow during both inspiration and expiration, producing biphasic stridor. Although croup is commonly associated with inspiratory stridor in mild cases, classically and in exam context, subglottic involvement leads to biphasic stridor, especially when narrowing is significant. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Inspiratory: Seen in obstruction above the vocal cords (e.g., supraglottic), not typical for subglottic lesions. (B) Expiratory: Seen in lower airway obstruction (bronchi, bronchioles), such as asthma or bronchiolitis. (D) Uniphasic: Not a standard clinical classification of stridor and is not used diagnostically

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the recommended daily protein intake for a 30-year-old woman weighing 55 kg?
questions.explanation: The recommended daily protein intake for a healthy adult is commonly based on body weight. According to standard nutritional guidelines such as ICMR, the average requirement is approximately 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. For a 30-year-old woman weighing 55 kg: Protein requirement = 0.8 × 55 = 44 grams/day, which is rounded off to 45 grams/day This intake is adequate to maintain nitrogen balance, support tissue repair, enzyme and hormone production, and overall metabolic functions in a healthy adult with normal activity levels. Although some sources mention 1 g/kg/day, especially for easier calculation, the standard recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for adults remains closer to 0.8 g/kg/day, particularly in exam-based contexts like FMGE. Why Other Options Are Incorrect (B) 55 gm: Based on 1 g/kg, slightly higher than standard (C) 60 gm: More than required (D) 70 gm: Excess unless increased demand (pregnancy, illness)
questions.learning: The recommended daily protein intake for a healthy adult is commonly based on body weight. According to standard nutritional guidelines such as ICMR, the average requirement is approximately 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following dimorphic fungi causes subcutaneous mycosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sporothrix schenckii

The dimorphic fungus that causes subcutaneous mycosis is Sporothrix schenckii.

Sporotrichosis is caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a thermally dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation. The infection occurs following traumatic inoculation.

The lesion initially develops as a granulomatous nodule that may progress to form a necrotic or ulcerative lesion. The infection from the lesions in the skin and subcutaneous tissue can spread via the lymphatic channels to the lymph nodes. This condition is known as lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. This disease is commonly encountered among gardeners and forest workers.

The image below shows lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis.

Other options:

Option B: Histoplasmosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungi Histoplasma capsulatum. It is acquired by inhalation and causes a disease similar to tuberculosis and may present as fever, chills, headache, dry cough, dyspnea, and chest pain.

Option C: Blastomycosis is caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. It is contracted through the inhalation of contaminated soil. Primary infection usually presents as pneumonia.  Chest X-ray reveals consolidation. Disseminated disease may lead to multiple abscesses. Cutaneous lesions present as papules and nodules which progress into large ulcerative lesions.

Option D: T. marneffei is a dimorphic fungus that causes talaromycosis (penicilliosis). It is commonly seen in individuals with advanced AIDS. Clinical features include fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Umbilicated papules that resemble molluscum contagiosum may also be seen.
questions.learning: Sporothrix schenckii — The dimorphic fungus that causes subcutaneous mycosis is Sporothrix schenckii. Sporotrichosis is caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a thermally dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are the clinical features of septic abortion? 1. Persistent tachycardia ≥ 90 bpm 2. Impaired mental status 3. Hypothermia Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Septic abortion is an abortion complicated by infection of the uterus and surrounding tissues, which may progress to sepsis and septic shock. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt antibiotics, resuscitation, and uterine evacuation.

• 1. Persistent tachycardia ≥90 bpm: Correct. An early sign of systemic infection and sepsis.
• 2. Impaired mental status: Correct. Suggests severe sepsis or septic shock with organ dysfunction.
• 3. Hypothermia: Correct. Although fever is more common, hypothermia (<36°C) is a recognized feature of severe sepsis and is associated with a poorer prognosis.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Septic abortion is an abortion complicated by infection of the uterus and surrounding tissues, which may progress to sepsis and septic shock.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with SOB and fatigue. CXR was done. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Asbestosis is an occupational interstitial lung disease caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers. The hallmark radiologic finding is the presence of calcified pleural plaques, particularly along the parietal pleura and the diaphragm, often referred to as "peripheral pleural calcification". This is usually accompanied by interstitial fibrosis that predominantly affects the lower lobes. Symptoms include progressive shortness of breath (SOB) and restrictive patterns on pulmonary function tests. Tuberculosis (Option A) typically involves the lung apices and presents with cavitary lesions rather than pleural plaques. Silicosis (Option C) is characterized by upper lobe nodules and "eggshell" calcification of hilar lymph nodes. Byssinosis (Option D) is related to cotton dust exposure and generally does not show pleural calcifications on imaging. Given the specific visual findings of pleural plaques, asbestosis is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Hirschberg's test is being performed in this patient with squint. Which of the following is correct about the case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 90 Prism dioptre exotropia

From the given image of a Hirschberg test, it can be inferred that the patient has 90 prism dioptres (PD) of exotropia.

In the Hirschberg test, if the light reflection is on the nasal limbus, it means 45 degrees exotropia. One degree is equal to 2 PD (prism dioptre). Therefore, 45 degrees exotropia would mean 90 PD exotropia in the right eye.The Hirschberg test is used to detect squint.

The Hirschberg test gives a rough objective estimate of the angle of manifest strabismus. A pen torch is shone into the eyes from arm’s length, and the patient is asked to fixate on the light. The corneal reflection of the light will be centered in the pupil of the fixating eye but will be decentred in a squinting eye, in the direction opposite to that of the deviation. The distance of the corneal light reflection from the center of the pupil is noted; each millimeter of the deviation is approximately equal to 7°.

Other options:

Option A: 90 degrees exotropia is incorrect because ocular deviations are measured in prism dioptres, not in degrees.

Option B: 90 Prism dioptre esotropia is incorrect as the deviation is outward (exotropia), not inward (esotropia).

Option D: 90 degrees esotropia is incorrect due to wrong unit (degrees instead of prism dioptres) and wrong direction (exotropia, not esotropia).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the marked layer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sodium and water retention

The image shows a histological section of the adrenal gland and the layer marked is the outermost layer, ie, the zona glomerulosa, which secretes the mineralocorticoid - aldosterone, responsible for sodium and water retention.

Based on structure and function, the adrenal cortex has three zones, which from outer to inner, are:

• Zona glomerulosa: Secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) - which acts in response to the activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system (RAAS) and acts at the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting ducts favouring sodium and water retention and potassium excretion.
• Zona fasiculata: Secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol and corticosterone) - which has multiple functions that include metabolic effects which induce hyperglycemia inducing gluconeogenesis (Option A) and mediates anti-inflammatory and immunosuppresive effects by interacting with the cells of the immune system (Option D).
• Zona reticularis: Secretes sex steroids (dehydroepiandrosterone, androstenedione, estrogens, and glucocorticoids) (Option C)
questions.learning: Sodium and water retention — The image shows a histological section of the adrenal gland and the layer marked is the outermost layer, ie, the zona glomerulosa, which secretes the mineralocorticoid - aldosterone, responsible for sodium and water retention.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following agency provides seed and manure in applied nutrition programs in schools?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. UNICEF

UNICEF provides seed and manure in applied nutrition programs in schools.

Applied Nutrition Program is implemented with the aim of producing various types of productive food by the community for the community itself.

UNICEF assists the program by providing implements, seeds, manure, and water supply equipment. If free land is available in schools, the facilities provided by UNICEF should be used in developing school gardens.

The produce obtained from the gardens can be utilized for school feeding programs and for nutrition education.

Another strategy called GOBI was also implemented by UNICEF with the aim of a child health revolution.

Other options:

Option A- CARE- Cooperative for Assistance and Relief Everywhere aims at providing food for children in the age group of 6-11 years. It is also helping in projects like integrated nutrition and health project, better health and nutrition projects, anemia control projects, etc.

Option B- UNDP- The United Nations Development Program provides funds for technical assistance. Its main objective is to help poorer nations in developing their human and natural resources.

Option D- WHO- World Health Organization aims at the attainment of the highest level of health by all people, which helps them to lead a socially and economically productive life.
questions.learning: UNICEF UNICEF provides seed and manure in applied nutrition programs in schools. Applied Nutrition Program is implemented with the aim of producing various types of productive food by the community for the community itself.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with progressively blurred vision. Slit-lamp exam reveals superotemporal lens displacement with stretched zonules. He's tall, long-limbed, with arachnodactyly. Which best describes this ocular condition?
options: Lens dislocation due to inflammatory adhesions
Partial lens displacement due to zonular weakness
Posterior displacement of lens into the vitreous
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Partial lens displacement due to zonular weakness

Ectopia lentis refers to partial or complete displacement of the lens from its normal position, resulting from weak or defective zonular fibers (the suspensory ligaments anchoring the lens).

In this vignette, the combination of tall stature, long limbs, arachnodactyly, and superotemporal lens subluxation points strongly toward Marfan syndrome — where a fibrillin-1 defect leads to weakened zonules and characteristic upward-outward lens displacement.

Why the other options don't fit?

• A. Lens dislocation due to inflammatory adhesions: Inflammatory adhesions describe synechiae (iris adhering to lens or cornea), not ectopia lentis
• C. Lens opacification from protein aggregation: Protein aggregation causing lens opacity describes a cataract, a different pathology entirely
• D. Posterior displacement of lens into the vitreous: Posterior displacement into the vitreous describes true lens dislocation (complete separation), not the partial subluxation seen here

High-yield pearl:

Direction of lens displacement can help distinguish causes:

• Marfan syndrome → superotemporal
• Homocystinuria → inferonasal (also has zonular weakness, but opposite direction — a classic paired distractor in exams)
questions.learning: Partial lens displacement due to zonular weakness Ectopia lentis refers to partial or complete displacement of the lens from its normal position, resulting from weak or defective zonular fibers (the suspensory ligaments anchoring the lens).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most likely causative organism in a 45-year-old man, post–heart transplant and on immunosuppressive therapy, who presents with 48 hours of fever, headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness? Lumbar puncture shows neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis, and microscopy reveals an organism that is non- motile at 37°C but exhibits tumbling motility at 25°C.
questions.explanation: The patient presents with acute bacterial meningitis, indicated by the classic triad (fever, headache, neck stiffness) and neutrophilic pleocytosis in the CSF. In an immuno compromised patient (post-transplant on medications), Listeria monocytogenes is a major causative agent. The definitive diagnostic clue provided is the unique temperature-dependent motility: the organism is non-motile at 37°C but displays "tumbling motility" at 25°C (room temperature) . Streptococcus (Option B) and Staphylococcus (Option C) are common causes of meningitis but are always non-motile regardless of temperature. Giardia (Option D) is an intestinal parasite that does not cause meningitis. Listeria is a small gram-positive rod often contracted through contaminated food (like deli meats or soft cheeses). Therefore, the combination of the patient's immune status and the pathognomonic "tumbling motility" confirms Listeria as the causative pathogen
questions.learning: The patient presents with acute bacterial meningitis, indicated by the classic triad (fever, headache, neck stiffness) and neutrophilic pleocytosis in the CSF.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient has sustained an injury resulting in nerve damage. Based on the findings shown in the provided image, which nerve is affected?
questions.explanation: The provided image demonstrates a "wrist drop" deformity, which is the hallmark clinical presentation of a Radial nerve injury. The radial nerve provides motor innervation to the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers. When the nerve is damaged—classically at the spiral groove of the humerus due to a mid-shaft fracture or "Saturday night palsy"—the patient loses the ability to extend the hand against gravity. Ulnar nerve injury (Option A) typically results in a "claw hand" affecting the ring and little fingers. Median nerve damage (Option C) often leads to the "ape hand" deformity or "hand of benediction" during an attempt to make a fist. Axillary nerve injury (Option D) affects the deltoid muscle, causing impaired shoulder abduction rather than distal hand weakness. Physical examination for sensory loss in the first dorsal web space further confirms radial nerve involvement. Management involves splinting the wrist in extension to prevent contractures while the nerve recovers
questions.learning: The provided image demonstrates a "wrist drop" deformity, which is the hallmark clinical presentation of a Radial nerve injury. The radial nerve provides motor innervation to the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: During an anatomy teaching session, a spinal image is shown with a prominent blue line marked across the vertebral column. Based on the anatomical landmarks visible in the image, which vertebral level does this blue line correspond to?
questions.explanation: The "blue line" shown in the anatomical diagram represents Tuffier’s line (or the intercristal line). This is a horizontal line connecting the highest points of the iliac crests. In an adult, this clinically important landmark typically passes through the L4 vertebra or the L4-L5 intervertebral space. Options A (L2-L3), C (L5-S1), and D (L3-L4) are incorrect anatomical levels for this specific surface landmark. Tuffier's line is used as the primary guide for identifying the safe level for performing a lumbar puncture or administering spinal/epidural anesthesia. Since the spinal cord (conus medullaris) usually ends at the L1-L2 level in adults, inserting a needle into the spaces below Tuffier’s line (such as L4-L5 or L5-S1) minimizes the risk of direct spinal cord injury. Accuracy in identifying this landmark is essential for any clinician performing procedures involving the lumbar spinal canal
questions.learning: The "blue line" shown in the anatomical diagram represents Tuffier’s line (or the intercristal line). This is a horizontal line connecting the highest points of the iliac crests.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears. Which of the following is the most frequently associated with this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Down syndrome

A newborn with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears is most likely to have Down syndrome.

Down syndrome is a type of aneuploidy. It occurs due to the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21), leading to a total of 47 chromosomes instead of the normal 46.

There is a wide range of presentations. A few key features include characteristic facies such as a flat face, epicanthal folds, a small head, a flat nasal bridge, upward-slanting palpebral fissures, brushfield spots, a small nose, a protruding tongue, and small and low-set ears. Congenital heart defects can also be present.

Mechanism:

* Majority of cases – meiotic nondisjunction (95%) of chromosome 21 in the ovum

* Rarely – (4%) Robertsonian translocation of the long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (e.g., 22 or 14)

* Mosaic pattern: 1%

Clinical features of Down syndrome include (mnemonic: I C A PROBLEMS): Incurved or short fifth finger with clinodactyly, congenital heart disease, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia/ alzheimer's disease/ atlantoaxial instability/ atresia of the duodenum, protruding tongue, round face, occiput flat/open wide fontanelle/open mouth, brachycephalic/Brushfield's spots, low (depressed) nasal bridge, epicanthal fold, low-set and dysplastic ears, mongoloid slant (oblique palpebral fissure), simian palmar crease and wider gap between first and second toes.

A score based on eight signs in the diagnosis of Down's syndrome in the newborn (Hall's criteria)

* Abundant neck skin

* Mouth corners turned downwards

* General hypotonia

* Flat face

* Dysplastic ear

* Epicanthic fold

* The gap between first and second toes

* Protruding tongue

The presence of the last 3 points is considered clinically proven Down syndrome.

Combined first-trimester screening consists of serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A), and the measurement of the nuchal translucency (NT) on ultrasound. It is performed between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation.

The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in Down syndrome is duodenal atresia (double-bubble sign). Children with Down's syndrome have an increased risk of developing leukaemias, including acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). AML is more common during the first 3 years of life.

Other options:

Option A: Trisomy 18 results in Edward’s syndrome as a result of meiotic nondisjunction. The clinical features include micrognathia, low-set ears, prominent occiput, and rocker-bottom feet. Patients have significant hypertonia, including clenched hands with overlapping fingers. Cardiac anomalies (ventricular septal defects and patent ductus arteriosus) and gastrointestinal anomalies (Meckel’s diverticulum and malrotations) are common.

Option C: Turner syndrome (45, XO) results from the loss or structural abnormality of one X chromosome in females, leading to gonadal dysgenesis (non-functional ovaries). It is characterised by a short fourth metacarpal, a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and short stature.

Option D: Trisomy 13 causes Patau syndrome. It is characterised by forebrain and midline facial abnormalities, including cleft lip, cleft palate, nasal defects, and a single central eye (“cyclops”). Other defects include polydactyly, renal defects, and congenital heart disease.
questions.learning: Down syndrome — A newborn with a single palmar transverse crease and low-set ears is most likely to have Down syndrome. Down syndrome is a type of aneuploidy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ions is involved in peripheral oxygen sensing chemoreceptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Potassium

Potassium is involved in peripheral oxygen sensing chemoreceptors.

Type I glomus cells (carotid and aortic body) have O2-sensitive K+ channels, whose conductance is reduced in proportion to the degree of hypoxia.

This reduces the K+ efflux, depolarizing the cell and causing Ca2+ inﬂux.

The Ca2+ influx triggers action potentials and consequent excitation of the afferent nerve endings.
questions.learning: Potassium Potassium is involved in peripheral oxygen sensing chemoreceptors. Type I glomus cells (carotid and aortic body) have O2-sensitive K+ channels, whose conductance is reduced in proportion to the degree of hypoxia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following molecular analysis methods is used to detect RNA ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. RT-PCR

RT PCR(Reverse Transcriptase PCR) is a molecular analysis method used for the detection of RNA. It can be used to quantitate mRNA levels by generating complementary DNA (cDNA) copies of the mRNA using the reverse transcriptase enzyme.

The northern blot technique can also be used to detect RNAs. Here, the mixture of mRNA molecules is separated by electrophoresis and then transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane and hybridized with radiolabeled probes.

Sanger’s technique:

• This was the first technique used to determine the sequence of proteins.
• Sanger’s reagent is 1- Flouro 2,4 Dinitro benzene.
• The first protein to be sequenced by this method was insulin.
• Only dipeptides and tripeptides can be sequenced by this method.

G banding (Giemsa banding):

It is the most common technique used in cytogenetics to produce a visible karyotype by staining condensed chromosomes. It is useful for identifying genetic diseases through the photographic representation of the entire chromosome complement. The metaphase chromosomes are treated with trypsin (to partially digest the chromosome) and stained with Giemsa stain.

Heterochromatic regions, which tend to be rich with adenine and thymine (AT-rich) DNA and relatively gene-poor, stain darker and appear as dark bands in G-banding. In contrast, less condensed chromatin, which tends to be rich with guanine and cytosine (GC-rich) and more transcriptionally active incorporates less Giemsa stain, and these regions appear as light bands in G-banding. The image below shows a G-banding karyogram of a normal human male.

Western blot, also called immunoblots, is a technique used to study protein molecules. The proteins undergo electrophoresis and then are transferred to a membrane. These proteins are then tagged with the specific antibodies and visualized.
questions.learning: RT-PCR RT PCR(Reverse Transcriptase PCR) is a molecular analysis method used for the detection of RNA. It can be used to quantitate mRNA levels by generating complementary DNA (cDNA) copies of the mRNA using the reverse transcriptase enzyme.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 65-year-old man undergoing evaluation for suspected renal dysfunction has his creatinine clearance measured. Which statement best describes the significance and interpretation of creatinine clearance?
questions.explanation: Creatinine clearance is a widely used clinical measure to estimate the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR). It is considered comparable to inulin clearance, which is the "gold standard" for measuring GFR. Inulin is perfect because it is freely filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted. Creatinine is also freely filtered and not reabsorbed; however, a small amount is actively secreted by the renal tubules. This secretion causes creatinine clearance to slightly overestimate the true GFR (by about 10-20%). Despite this, it is far more practical for clinical use than inulin, which requires a continuous infusion. It is not "superior" (Option C) in accuracy, nor "inferior" (Option B) in clinical utility. It is not identical to renal plasma flow (Option D), which is much higher. For most clinical purposes, creatinine clearance provides a sufficiently accurate estimate of kidney function. Consequently, it remains the standard-of-care proxy for GFR in everyday medical practice
questions.learning: Creatinine clearance is a widely used clinical measure to estimate the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR). It is considered comparable to inulin clearance, which is the "gold standard" for measuring GFR.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient's relatives sent a message on social media to the consulting doctor, unaware about the other investigations. But he mentioned that urinary coproporphyrin is positive. What is the probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lead poisoning

Lead poisoning interferes with heme synthesis, leading to accumulation of porphyrin precursors such as coproporphyrin in urine. Lead inhibits key enzymes in the heme pathway:

• ALA dehydratase (ALAD)
• Ferrochelatase

Consequences:

• ↑ ALA and coproporphyrin in urine
• ↓ heme synthesis → anemia

Clinical features:

• Abdominal pain (lead colic)
• Neurological symptoms (irritability, neuropathy)
• Anemia with basophilic stippling
• Wrist/foot drop

Why other options are incorrect:

• Asbestosis: Lung fibrosis (no effect on heme synthesis)
• Silicosis: Occupational lung disease
• Mercury poisoning: Neurological and renal toxicity, not porphyrin metabolism

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the site which is responsible for relieving pain when pressure is applied to the painful area.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

It is a cross section of brain stem at pons.

• A is a periaqueductal gray matter which also consists of raphe nucleus.
• Descending pathways from the mesencephalic periaqueductal gray matter inhibit transmission in nociceptive pathways. This descending pathway includes a synapse in the ventromedial medulla (Raphe nucleus) and the release of endogenous opiates. So periaqueductal gray matter releases endogenous opiates.

Other marked structures are

B: Corticospinal tract

C: Medial lemniscus

D: Medial longitudinal fasciculus
questions.learning: A It is a cross section of brain stem at pons. • A is a periaqueductal gray matter which also consists of raphe nucleus. • Descending pathways from the mesencephalic periaqueductal gray matter inhibit transmission in nociceptive pathways.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A newly diagnosed HIV patient presented with fever, cough, and hemoptysis. What is the investigation of choice to test for TB in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CBNAAT

As per RNTCP guidelines, CBNAAT is the preferred diagnostic technique for testing TB in PLHIV (people living with HIV). Smear microscopy has poor sensitivity in detecting TB in PLHIV due to fewer organisms in sputum, and hence is not preferred.

Tuberculosis is the most common opportunistic infection in people living with HIV AIDS. The combined treatment of both TB and HIV has found to have profound impact on mortality. The main stay of treatment is to start ATT first and then start ART as soon as ATT is tolerated (between 2 weeks and 2 months) by the patient. This is done in order to avoid immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).

Patients with HIV-related TB may experience a temporary paradoxical exacerbation of symptoms and radiographic manifestations of TB after starting ATT. This occurs as a result of immune reconstitution due to simultaneous administration of ART and ATT.
questions.learning: CBNAAT As per RNTCP guidelines, CBNAAT is the preferred diagnostic technique for testing TB in PLHIV (people living with HIV). Smear microscopy has poor sensitivity in detecting TB in PLHIV due to fewer organisms in sputum, and hence is not preferred.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A lady from West Rajasthan presented with an ulcer surrounded by erythema on the right leg. Microscopy of the biopsy from the edge of the ulcer showed organisms with dark staining nuclei and kinetoplast. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leishmania tropica

The above clinical vignette is suggestive of cutaneous leishmaniasis.

Leishmaniasis is a slowly progressing indigenous disease caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Leishmania. It is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Phlebotomus sandfly which inoculates the flagellated promastigotes into the skin of the host in developing countries. In India, it is endemic to Bihar, West Bengal, Jharkhand, and Uttar Pradesh.

Causative organisms include:

• Old world leishmaniasis: Leishmania donovani, Leishmania major, and Leishmania tropica
• New world leishmaniasis: Leishmania mexicana complex and Leishmania braziliensis complex

The image given below shows a phlebotomus sandfly.

The image given below shows Chiclero ulcer/New World cutaneous leishmaniasis.

The image below shows Lutzomyia sandfly responsible for the New World cutaneous leishmanisis.

In human beings, the disease presents in four different forms with a broad range of clinical manifestations:

• Visceral leishmaniasis, or kala-azar,
• Cutaneous leishmaniasis,
• Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, and
• Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis.

The life cycle of Leishmania involves two forms:

• The promastigote which develops and lives extracellularly in the sandfly vector and
• The amastigote multiplies intracellularly in the reticuloendothelial cells of the host.

When the infected sandfly bites a person, infectious promastigotes are released into the host dermis along with the sandfly saliva, which potentiates parasite infectivity. Amastigote form (as shown in the image below) is also known as Leishman-Donovan (LD) body. It is an intracellular form found inside macrophages, monocytes, and reticuloendothelial cells. It contains a kinetoplast, which consists of a parabasal body and a blepharoplast. Flagellum is absent.

Promastigote form (as shown in the below image) is present in the midgut of the female sandfly. The kinetoplast lies transversely near the anterior end. A single flagellum is seen. It is the infective form of L. donovani for humans.

Given below is the lifecycle of L. donovanii.

This condition causes fever with rigor and chills associated with splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. It lowers immunity, causes persistent fever, anemia, and liver and spleen enlargement, and if left untreated, death may occur due to opportunistic infection.

Diagnosis of kala-azar is mainly by demonstration of amastigotes within macrophages in tissue aspirates such as blood smears, bone marrow, splenic, or lymph node aspirate. It is the gold standard for diagnosis.

The image below shows amastigotes located intracellularly within macrophages.

Tests to detect leishmaniasis include:

• Rapid diagnostic test: rK39 Rapid diagnostic test and Kala-azar dipstick test strip. This is recommended by National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) in India.
• Parasitological diagnosis: Demonstration of LD bodies in buffy coat smear - confirmatory.
• Aldehyde test of Napier: Widely used for surveillance.
• Serological tests for diagnosis: Rapid dipstick test, Direct agglutination test, ELISA, indirect fluorescent antibody test
• Leishmanin (Montenegro) test: Induration of 5mm or more is considered positive, usually positive 4-6 weeks (delayed-hypersensitivity) after onset in cutaneous leishmaniasis, valuable for distinguishing immune from nonimmune subjects and endemicity.

Drugs used in the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis are

• Sodium stibogluconate
• Miltefosine
• Amphotericin B

In Bihar, there is resistance to antimony so amphotericin-B-deoxycholate or miltefosine is preferred.

Other options:

Option B: Babesia is a protozoan parasite that causes babesiosis, a tick-borne disease. Babesiosis manifests as a malaria-like illness with fever, chills, and hemolytic anemia.

Option C: Trypanosoma is a genus of protozoan parasites responsible for diseases like African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) and American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease). These diseases present with different clinical features, such as fever, swollen lymph nodes, and neurological symptoms in African trypanosomiasis, and fever, swelling at the infection site, and cardiomyopathy in Chagas disease.

Option D: Histoplasma is a dimorphic fungus that causes histoplasmosis, a systemic mycosis. It primarily affects the lungs and can disseminate to other organs in immunocompromised individuals. The clinical presentation of histoplasmosis is variable, but it does not typically present as a skin ulcer with erythema as described in the clinical scenario.
questions.learning: Leishmania tropica — The above clinical vignette is suggestive of cutaneous leishmaniasis. Leishmaniasis is a slowly progressing indigenous disease caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Leishmania.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with ptosis, diplopia, and generalized muscle weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest. She also has difficulty chewing and swallowing, especially in the evening. A Tensilon test is positive. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of fluctuating weakness, ptosis, diplopia, and a positive Tensilon (edrophonium) test are classic for Myasthenia Gravis (MG). While the Tensilon test is a useful bedside screening tool, the Anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody test is the most specific laboratory investigation to confirm the diagnosis. Approximately 85% of patients with generalized MG will have detectable AChR antibodies. Single-fiber electromyography (SFEMG) (Option B) is the most sensitive test for MG, showing increased jitter, but it is not as specific as antibody testing. A CT scan of the chest (Option A) is performed after diagnosis to screen for an associated thymoma but is not a confirmatory test for MG itself. MRI of the brain (Option D) is done to rule out other causes of cranial nerve palsies but would be normal in MG. Early diagnosis is vital because MG is highly treatable with anticholinesterase inhibitors, immunosuppressants, and occasionally thymectomy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the transporter of iodine from follicular cells to follicular cavity within the thyroid gland:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pendrin

| Transporter | Location | Function

| ----------- | -------- | --------

| NIS (Na⁺/I⁻ symporter) | Basolateral membrane | Blood → cell

| Pendrin | Apical membrane | Cell → colloid

| TPO (enzyme) | Colloid | Organification

Pendrin transports iodide from thyroid follicular cells across the apical membrane into the follicular lumen for organification. The Na⁺/I⁻ symporter works on the basolateral membrane to bring iodide into the cell from blood. Defective pendrin impairs iodide efflux into colloid. This apical transport step is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A child is brought to the orthopedics OPD with a deformity in the lower limb and hyperpigmented skin lesions. The x-ray of her thigh is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fibrous dysplasia

The above X-ray shows the bending of the femur known as Shepherd's crook deformity. It is seen in fibrous dysplasia of proximal femur.

Fibrous dysplasia is a condition that affects bone development and is characterized by the replacement of the bone with fibrous tissue. The patient presents with a progressive limb deformity or a fracture through a previously asymptomatic lesion. The presentation often occurs in the second decade. Other symptoms include nonspecific bone pain, tenderness, and swelling in the affected area. The commonly involved sites are the proximal femur, tibia, pelvis, and foot. Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is associated with Albright-McCune syndrome.

Radiological findings include:

• Well-defined, expansile intramedullary lesions
• Hazy ground glass appearance is seen in the majority of cases
• Shepherd's crook deformity - Expansion with marked varus in the proximal femur

Other options:

Option A: Non-ossifying fibroma is the commonest variant of giant cell bone tumors. It is a benign, non-neoplastic lesion most commonly seen in the metaphyses of the long bones in children. Non-ossifying fibromas are usually asymptomatic, and often discovered incidentally on X-rays performed for other reasons. They commonly occur in the metaphyses of long bones and are characterized by well-defined, eccentric, cortically-based lytic lesions. The X-ray findings in the question do not match this description.

Option C: Paget's disease of the bone is a condition where there is an increased bone turnover followed by enlargement and thickening of the bone. In this condition, calcium levels are normal with raised ALP. Paget's disease typically presents in older adults and affects the axial skeleton, including the pelvis, spine, skull, and femur. It is characterized by increased bone turnover, leading to disorganized bone remodeling, resulting in enlarged and deformed bones. The X-ray findings and the patient's age do not match the characteristics of Paget's disease.

Option D: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic disorder characterized by increased bone fragility and susceptibility to fractures. It is associated with blue sclera, dental fragility, and hearing loss. It presents with the hallmark features of osteoporosis with increased fragility of bones along with blue sclera, dental fragility as well as hearing loss. The X-ray findings in the question do not show the characteristic features of osteogenesis imperfecta, such as thin cortices, multiple fractures, or wormian bones.
questions.learning: Fibrous dysplasia — The above X-ray shows the bending of the femur known as Shepherd's crook deformity. It is seen in fibrous dysplasia of proximal femur.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with developmental delay has absence of the developmental milestone of social smile by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 months

The social smile normally appears at 6–8 weeks (around 2 months). Failure to develop a social smile by 3 months is considered abnormal and is an early marker of developmental delay, warranting further evaluation for visual impairment, hearing impairment, autism spectrum disorder, or global developmental delay.

Why not the other options?

• A. 6 weeks ❌: Social smile is just beginning to appear; absence is still within normal limits.
• B. 10 weeks ❌: Many infants develop it by this age, but the upper limit of normal is 3 months.
• C. 3 months ✔️: Correct. Absence beyond this age is abnormal.
• D. 4 months ❌: Delay should be recognized earlier, by 3 months.
questions.learning: 3 months The social smile normally appears at 6–8 weeks (around 2 months). Failure to develop a social smile by 3 months is considered abnormal and is an early marker of developmental delay, warranting further evaluation for visual impairment, hearing…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following hormones is responsible for gallbladder contraction and release of bile into duodenum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cholecystokinin

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is a hormone secreted by the I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the intestinal lumen. It is the principal hormone responsible for gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, facilitating the release of bile into the duodenum for fat digestion.

• Secretin: Stimulates bicarbonate-rich secretion from the pancreas and bile ducts; does not cause gallbladder contraction.
• Gastrin: Stimulates gastric acid secretion and gastric mucosal growth.
• Cholecystokinin (CCK): Contracts the gallbladder, relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion, and slows gastric emptying.
• Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP): Relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle and increases intestinal water and electrolyte secretion.
questions.learning: Cholecystokinin Cholecystokinin (CCK) is a hormone secreted by the I cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to fatty acids and amino acids in the intestinal lumen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A chronic smoker comes with complaints of pain in his legs after walking 100 meters. On examination, he has an absent pulse in the bilateral dorsalis pedis, anterior tibial, and posterior tibial arteries, but no gangrene is present. Intermittent claudication is implicated. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?
options: Pain is more at night and sleep
Development of pain on the 1st step of walking
Pain aggravated by standing and relieved by bending forward
Pain develops after walking some distance and is relieved by rest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pain develops after walking some distance and is relieved by rest

In intermittent claudication, pain develops after walking some distance and is relieved by rest.

Intermittent(vascular) claudication is most commonly felt in the calf muscles because of the involvement of the superficial femoral artery in chronic vascular occlusive disease.

Intermittent claudication is the debilitating cramp-like pain felt in the leg muscles due to reduced blood flow and anaerobic metabolism brought on by peripheral arterial disease. It usually signifies mild to moderate chronic vascular occlusive disease. The pain is brought on by walking, not present on taking the first step. Relieved by rest in both the standing and sitting positions, usually within 5 minutes (option A). The distance that a patient can walk without stopping is known as claudication distance. It varies only slightly from day to day. The superficial femoral artery (70%) is the most commonly affected artery by claudication and manifests as pain in the calf muscles. Aorto-iliac occlusion may cause thigh or buttock claudication. Leriche's syndrome occurs due to aortoiliac occlusion and presents with a triad of claudication, impotence, and absent femoral pulses.

Boyd's classification of claudication:

• Grade I: Patient complains of pain after walking. If the patient continues to walk, due to increased blood flow in muscle and opening of collaterals metabolites causing pain are washed away and the pain subsides.
• Grade II: Pain persists on continuing to walk; but can walk with effort.
• Grade III: The patient has to take rest to relieve the pain.

Other options

Option A: Rest pain occurs when the occlusive disease progresses in severity. Though this pain is present during the day, it is exacerbated on lying down at night due to loss of gravity-dependent perfusion of the foot. This may be relieved by hanging the foot out of the bed to restore the gravitational effects.

Option B: The development of pain on taking the first step of walking is a classic sign of osteoarthritis.

Option C: Pain aggravated by standing and relieved by bending forward is seen in neurogenic claudication. It may be seen in cases of nerve compression from lumbar intervertebral disc prolapse or spinal stenosis.
questions.learning: Pain develops after walking some distance and is relieved by rest In intermittent claudication, pain develops after walking some distance and is relieved by rest.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Which of the following tests can be used if otoacoustic emissions is absent for screening?

1. Pure tone audiometry
2. Tympanometry
3. Free field audiometry
4. Speech audiometry
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 and 4

Among the given options, tympanometry (Test 2) and speech audiometry (Test 4) are used in cases where otoacoustic emission (OAE) is absent for screening.

Otoacoustic emissions are sounds produced by the outer hair cells of cochlea. These sounds then travel in the reverse direction from the outer hair — basilar membrane and perilymph of cochlea— oval window — ossicles and tympanic membrane (middle ear) — ear canal (external ear).

Hence in the absence of OAE, pathologies of the middle and external ear should be ruled out before making a definitive diagnosis of cochlear pathology.

Tympanometry is an objective test that can be performed in patients with absent OAE to rule out any middle ear pathologies. Speech audiometry is a subjective test that can be performed in these patients to confirm if the hearing loss is due to cochlear or retro cochlear pathology (neural hearing loss).

Impedance Audiometry also known as Tympanometry is an objective test that is based on the principle that when the sound strikes the tympanic membrane, certain amount of sound is absorbed, while the rest is reflected So a stiffer tympano-ossicular system would reflect greater sound than a compliant one. By marking the compliance of tympano-ossicular system against various pressure changes, different types of tympanograms are obtained which are diagnostic of various middle ear pathologies.

In speech audiometry, the patient’s ability to hear and understand speech is measured. The speech reception threshold (SRT) is the lowest intensity of sound at which 50% of the words are repeated correctly by the patient. Speech discrimination scores test the capacity of the patient to understand speech. Hence, speech audiometry is a subjective test.

The rollover phenomenon is diagnostic of retrochochlear pathologies. Here, the phonetically balanced word score falls with an increase in speech intensity above a particular level due to nerve fatigue. The graph in cochlear disorders will rather show a plateau after a certain level unlike the fall seen in the rollover phenomenon.

A better objective test that could be used to diagnose retro-cochlear pathologies is brainstem auditory evoked response audiometry (BERA). It is a noninvasive test that can find any pathologies of central auditory pathways through the VIIIth nerve to pons and midbrain.

Other options:

1. Pure tone audiometry (Test 1) is a test that measures the threshold of hearing by air and bone conduction and thus the degree and type of hearing loss. Pure tone audiometry is a subjective test for hearing and is not employed in cases where OAE is absent when better objective tests such as tympanometry are available.

3. Free field audiometry (Test 3), a part of behavior observational audiometry is used in the age group where children start localizing sounds when an auditory signal is presented. This test is not useful in this case as the possibility of hearing loss is already established with absent OAE.
questions.learning: 2 and 4 Among the given options, tympanometry (Test 2) and speech audiometry (Test 4) are used in cases where otoacoustic emission (OAE) is absent for screening.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of proptosis in a middle-aged person?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroid eye disease

The most common cause of proptosis in a middle-aged adult is thyroid eye disease (Graves’ orbitopathy).

• Autoimmune process associated with Graves disease
• Inflammation and deposition of glycosaminoglycans in:

• Extraocular muscles (muscle belly enlargement)
• Orbital fat

• Leads to increased orbital volume → proptosis

Key clinical features:

• Bilateral (often asymmetric) proptosis
• Lid retraction, lid lag
• Restrictive ophthalmoplegia (especially impaired upgaze)
• Exposure keratopathy

Why not others:

• Orbital varix: Intermittent proptosis (worse on Valsalva), rare
• Retinoblastoma: Pediatric tumor
• Cavernous hemangioma: Common benign orbital tumor in adults but not the most common cause overall

| Category | Adults – Most Common | Children – Most Common

| -------- | -------------------- | ----------------------

| Intraocular Tumors | Melanoma | Retinoblastoma

| Intraorbital Tumors | Hemangioma | Rhabdomyosarcoma

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man was brought in by the police, accused of sexual assault. The police claim that he is 19 years old, whereas his school certificate mentions 17 years, with signs of overwriting. Which of the following X-rays would be the best investigation for his age determination?
options: Medial end of clavicle, elbow, and sacrum
Medial end of clavicle, wrist, and pelvis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medial end of clavicle, wrist, and pelvis

When age is disputed (around 17–19 years), radiological age estimation using multiple ossification centers is the most reliable approach.

Use a combination of X-rays of different skeletal sites to assess epiphyseal fusion and narrow the age range.

Best combination (as in answer):

•

Medial end of clavicle + Wrist + Pelvis

Key fusion points

• Medial end of clavicle

• Appears: 18–19 yrs
• Fuses: 20–21 yrs
• Most important for ≥18 yrs

• Wrist (distal radius & ulna)

• Fusion: 16–19 yrs
• Helps confirm near 19 yrs

• Pelvis (iliac crest, ischial tuberosity)

• Fusion: 20–21 yrs
• If not fused → <20 yrs

Not useful for 18 yrs

• Elbow → fused by \~16 yrs
• Shoulder → fused by 17–18 yrs
• Skull sutures → fuse late (40+ yrs)
• Sternum → fuse 25–60 yrs

Final takeaway: ESHA ki Wrist (watch the FMT video if you dont what that means :)
questions.learning: Medial end of clavicle, wrist, and pelvis When age is disputed (around 17–19 years), radiological age estimation using multiple ossification centers is the most reliable approach.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient has a cardiac murmur that is best heard at the right second intercostal space. It increases with expiration. Also, the murmur reduces in intensity during sustained handgrip but increases in intensity on inhalation of amyl nitrite. The likely lesion is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aortic stenosis

Aortic stenosis (AS) produces an ejection systolic murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space, often radiating to the carotids. The murmur becomes louder during expiration (left-sided murmur), decreases with sustained handgrip (↑ afterload reduces the transvalvular gradient), and increases with amyl nitrite (↓ afterload increases the pressure gradient across the stenotic valve).

Why not the other options?

• A. Ventricular septal defect: Murmur is best heard at the left lower sternal border and increases with handgrip.
• C. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy: Murmur is best heard at the left sternal border and decreases with handgrip, but amyl nitrite also increases the murmur; the location here favors AS.
• D. Mitral regurgitation: Holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and increases with handgrip.
questions.learning: Aortic stenosis Aortic stenosis (AS) produces an ejection systolic murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space, often radiating to the carotids.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with bone pain for several months. A skull X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The skull X-ray demonstrates a thickened calvarium with a characteristic "cotton wool" appearance, where areas of sclerotic (dense) bone alternate with areas of lysis. This finding, combined with a history of chronic bone pain in an older adult, is classic for Paget's disease of bone (osteitis deformans). Paget's disease involves disordered bone remodeling with excessive resorption followed by the disorganized formation of new bone. Osteosarcoma (Option A) and Ewing's sarcoma (Option D) are highly malignant tumors that typically affect children and adolescents and show aggressive bone destruction. Osteochondroma (Option B) is a benign bony outgrowth usually found near joints, not as a diffuse skull condition. Biochemically, patients with Paget's disease often show a markedly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase level with normal calcium and phosphate. Treatment focuses on bisphosphonates to inhibit the abnormal bone remodeling
questions.learning: The skull X-ray demonstrates a thickened calvarium with a characteristic "cotton wool" appearance, where areas of sclerotic (dense) bone alternate with areas of lysis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man comes with complaints of fever and increasing fatigue for the past week. On examination, he is febrile, hypotensive and tachycardic. The findings of microscopic examination of his peripheral blood smear is given below. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmodium falciparum

The given clinical history and the blood smear shows multiple ring forms in RBCs are suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum.

Falciparum malaria shows a very high percentage of RBCs containing ring forms. This high-level parasitemia is more often seen in Plasmodium falciparum infection than in infection by the other plasmodia.

Binucleate rings (double chromatin) are common resembling stereo headphones in appearance.
