questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a feedforward mechanism?
options: Increase in heart rate on standing from supine position
Increase in cardiac output in response to anemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vasoconstriction after exposure to cold

Feedforward = anticipatory control

Body acts BEFORE a significant change occurs (like a smart thermostat that predicts winter, not waits for freezing). Feedforward control anticipates a disturbance and activates a response before core variables change. Cold exposure directly triggers cutaneous vasoconstriction via hypothalamic thermoregulatory pathways to prevent heat loss.

examples:

• Salivation before food (cephalic phase)
• ↑ HR before exercise (anticipatory response)
• Insulin release on sight of food

1. Feedback Mechanism (Reactive)

• Responds after change occurs
• Maintains homeostasis

Example: ↑ ADH in dehydration, Blood glucose regulation, Calcium homeostasis, Blood pressure control

2. Feedforward Mechanism (Anticipatory)

• Activated before actual disturbance
• Based on prediction / external cues

Example: Cold exposure → vasoconstriction BEFORE core temp drops

The other options are feedback responses correcting an already altered physiologic state. Thus cold-induced vasoconstriction is a classic feedforward mechanism.

B) Increase in heart rate on standing

• Due to baroreceptor reflex
• Trigger: ↓ BP after standing

This is negative feedback

C) Increase in cardiac output in anemia

• Trigger: ↓ O₂ delivery
• Body responds after deficit occurs

Feedback mechanism

D) Increased vasopressin (ADH) in dehydration

• Trigger: ↑ plasma osmolality

Negative feedback
questions.learning: Vasoconstriction after exposure to cold Feedforward = anticipatory control Body acts BEFORE a significant change occurs (like a smart thermostat that predicts winter, not waits for freezing).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following minerals help with stabilization of insulin secretion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zinc

Among the options provided, Zinc is best known for its role in the stabilization of insulin secretion.

Zinc is an essential trace element that plays a crucial role in various physiological processes, including insulin metabolism and secretion.

It is involved in the synthesis, storage, and secretion of insulin by pancreatic beta cells. Zinc acts as a cofactor for enzymes involved in insulin processing and storage within the beta cells.

Deficiency of zinc can lead to impaired insulin synthesis and secretion, which may contribute to metabolic disturbances seen in conditions like diabetes.

Other options:

* Copper is involved in the formation of enzymes called cuproenzymes, including ceruloplasmin, which plays a role in iron metabolism and antioxidant defense.

* Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal and is not known to have any beneficial role in the body, including insulin regulation.

* Iron is crucial for the formation of hemoglobin, which is responsible for transporting oxygen in the blood. It plays a role in overall metabolic processes and energy production within the body. Excess iron levels in the body can be harmful and are associated with various health conditions, including insulin resistance.
questions.learning: Zinc Among the options provided, Zinc is best known for its role in the stabilization of insulin secretion. Zinc is an essential trace element that plays a crucial role in various physiological processes, including insulin metabolism and secretion.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient is brought to the hospital, with complaints of seizures and the MRI image of the brain is given below. The disease is most probably caused by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cysticercosis cellulosae

The given clinical scenario and MRI brain showing scolex within multiple cystic lesions are suggestive of neurocysticercosis caused by the larval form of T. solium called Cysticercosis cellulosae.

Neurocysticercosis is the most common central nervous system parasitic infection.

The clinical features of neurocysticercosis include epilepsy, features of raised intracranial tension, and evident hydrocephalus. Patients can also have psychiatric disturbances, transient paresis, and visual disturbances.

The CT and MRI findings seen in neurocysticercosis are:

• Scolex within a cyst
• Cystic lesions with or without ring enhancement
• Nodular calcifications
• Focal enhancing lesions
• Multilobulated cystic lesions in the subarachnoid space.

Note: About 70% of adult-onset epilepsy is due to neurocysticercosis.

Albendazole is the drug of choice for neurocysticercosis. Glucocorticoid therapy is usually begun before initiating albendazole (an antiparasitic drug). This is continued for several days after the institution of therapy to reduce the incidence of side effects from inflammatory reactions to dead and dying cysticerci of Taenia solium.
questions.learning: Cysticercosis cellulosae — The given clinical scenario and MRI brain showing scolex within multiple cystic lesions are suggestive of neurocysticercosis caused by the larval form of T. solium called Cysticercosis cellulosae.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Rhinolalia clausa (closed nasality) is not seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Rhinolalia clausa (closed nasality) occurs when there is an obstruction in the nose or nasopharynx that prevents the normal nasal resonance of certain consonants (m, n, ng). Conditions that physically block the nasopharynx, such as a nasopharyngeal polyp (Option A), nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Option B), or nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (Option D), will all cause this "closed" speech sound. In contrast, a cleft palate (Option C) causes rhinolalia aperta (open nasality). In this condition, the failure of the soft palate to close the nasopharynx during speech allows excessive air to escape through the nose, leading to a "hypernasal" voice. Therefore, while obstructive lesions lead to "m" sounding like "b," a cleft palate leads to the inability to build up intraoral pressure for consonants. Consequently, cleft palate is the correct answer as it is associated with open rather than closed nasality
questions.learning: Rhinolalia clausa (closed nasality) occurs when there is an obstruction in the nose or nasopharynx that prevents the normal nasal resonance of certain consonants (m, n, ng).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old student presents with ocular redness, foreign body sensation, and excessive tearing following the use of a contact lens. An interface contrast microscopy from his corneal scraping is shown below. What would be the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acanthamoeba

The given clinical history and the demonstration of polygonal cysts in interface contrast microscopy are suggestive of amoebic keratitis caused by acanthamoeba.

Acanthamoeba culbertsoni is an opportunistic protozoan pathogen. It exists as trophozoite form and resistant cystic form. Both these forms are infective. The trophozoite is large and characterized by spine-like pseudopodia (acanthopodia).

Human beings acquire the infection by inhalation of cysts or trophozoites, directly through traumatized skin or eyes, or ingestion of cysts.

It chiefly presents as two chronic conditions:

* Acanthamoeba keratitis

* Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis

Acanthamoeba keratitis is an infection of the eyes that typically develops from the entry of the amebic cyst through abrasions on the cornea. Most of the cases are associated with the use of contact lenses.

Patients usually present with photophobia, excessive tearing, redness, and foreign body sensation and it can be bilateral in contact lens users.

Diagnosis of amoebic keratitis is made by the demonstration of the cyst in corneal scrapings by wet mount, histology, and culture. The cysts are smaller (12-25 μm) and polygonal or star-shaped.

Topical administration of biguanides or chlorhexidine with or without diamidine agents can be used for the management of acanthamoeba keratitis. In severe cases penetrating keratoplasty can be done.

The below image shows the ring lesion seen in acanthamoeba keratitis.

The below image shows cysts of acanthamoeba in lactophenol cotton blue staining.

Other options:

Option B- Naegleria fowleri causes a brain infection, primary amebic meningoencephalitis that leads to brain tissue destruction. Their cysts are spherical and have a smooth double wall.

Option C- Entamoeba histolytica causes intestinal and extraintestinal amebiasis. Their cysts are spherical in shape. A mature quadrinucleate cyst is the infective form.  An amebic ulcer is a typical lesion seen in intestinal amebiasis which is a flask-shaped ulcer in cross-section. Amebic liver abscess is extraintestinal amebiasis which has a center of abscess that contains thick colored brown pus termed anchovy sauce pus.

Option D- Balamuthia mandrillaris is a free-living ameba that causes granulomatous amebic encephalitis. Their cyst is usually spherical and surrounded by a three-layered cyst wall.
questions.learning: Acanthamoeba — The given clinical history and the demonstration of polygonal cysts in interface contrast microscopy are suggestive of amoebic keratitis caused by acanthamoeba.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presents with nasal obstruction. On examination, an irregular mass was visualized in the nasal cavity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Antrochoanal polyp

Most likely diagnosis is antrochoanal polyp.

Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. It arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium, comes out of it, and grows in the choana and nasal cavity. It is usually single and unilateral which are more commonly seen in children and young adults.

It has 3 parts namely

* Thin antral stalk,

* Round and globular choanal part, and

* Flat nasal part.

The clinical features include unilateral nasal obstruction, mucoid nasal discharge, and a hyponasal voice.

A large polyp may protrude from the nasal cavity and may appear pink and congested. It is soft and can be moved with a probe.Anterior rhinoscopy may miss it when it starts to grow posteriorly. Posterior rhinoscopy may reveal a globular mass filling the choana and hanging down behind the soft palate.

Diagnosis is made by radiograph of the paranasal sinuses reveals opacity of the involved antrum. Non-contrast CT scan reveals the extent of the polyp. Endoscopic examination reveals the antrochoanal polyp hidden posteriorly in the nasal cavity.

Endoscopic sinus surgery is the treatment of choice. Recurrence is uncommon after the complete removal of the polyp.

Option A thornwaldt cyst is the persistence of pouch of lushka and is located at the midline on the posterior nasopharyngeal wall. It rarely presents as a mass protruding in the nasal cavity

Option B hypertrophic rhinitis is the inflammation and thickening of nasal mucose, submucosa, glands and periosteum. It doesn't present as a mass lesion

Option C deviated nasal septum presents with nasal obstruction, but no mass lesion

Pearl PF1084: Antrochoanal Polyp

* Main etiological factors: Infection and allergy

* Usually affects children

* Site of origin: Mucosa of the maxillary antrum

* Clinical features:

* Usually single and unilateral

* Unilateral nasal obstruction which becomes bilateral when it grows posteriorly and obstructs opposite choana

* Mucoid nasal discharge

* Hyponasal voice

* Findings:

* Grows posteriorly and usually missed on anterior rhinoscopy

* Posterior rhinoscopy: Globular mass filling the choana or nasopharynx

* Investigation of choice: Nasal endoscopy. Shows nasal polyps that are pale, gelatinous and pedunculated

* Treatment of choice: FESS
questions.learning: Antrochoanal polyp Most likely diagnosis is antrochoanal polyp. Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of muscles used in ejaculation?
options: Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus contraction
Ischiocavernosus relaxation-External urethral sphincter contraction-Bulbospongiosus contraction
Ischiocavernosus relaxation-External urethral sphincter contraction-Bulbospongiosus relaxation
Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus relaxation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus contraction

The correct sequence of muscles used are Ischiocavernosus contraction-External urethral sphincter relaxation- Bulbospongiosus contraction.

There are 2 stages involved in this process - emission of the sperms into the prostatic urethra and ejaculation.

1.Emission:

* The sperm produced in the testes is brought into the urethra with contraction of the vas deferens and the ampulla and reach the seminal vesicles.

* Then contractions of the muscular coat of the prostate gland followed by contraction of the seminal vesicles expel prostatic and seminal fluid also into the urethra, forcing the sperm forward.

* All these fluids mix in the internal urethra with mucus already secreted by thebulbourethral glands to form the semen.

2.Ejaculation:

* The filling of the internal urethra with semen elicits sensory signals that are transmitted through the pudendal nerves to the sacral regions of the cord, giving
the feeling of sudden fullness in the internal genital organs.

* These sensory signals further exciter rhythmic contraction of the internal genital organs and cause contraction of the ischiocavernosus to further move the semen into the prostatic urethra.

* Retrograde ejaculation is prevented by the contraction of the internal urethral sphincter and relaxation of external urethral sphincter to help push the semen into the spongy urethra.

* The bulbocavernosus muscles contracts and compress the bases of the penile erectile tissue and cause rhythmic wave like increases in pressure in the erectile tissue of the penis and the genital ducts and urethra, which move the semen from the urethra to the exterior which is called ejaculation.

An image showing the muscles involved is shown below:

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: cMYC gene mutation is seen in which of the following neoplasms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Burkitt's lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by the translocation of the c-Myc gene on chromosome 8. This leads to increased MYC protein levels.

It can occur in 3 forms that have distinct clinical characteristics:

* African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma presents as a mass involving the mandible. It may also involve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands.

* Sporadic (non-endemic) is often seen as a mass involving the ileocecum and peritoneum.

* Aggressive lymphoma or acute leukaemia is seen in immunocompromised individuals

Histopathology shows tumour cells with round or oval nuclei, coarse chromatin, small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm, and a high mitotic index. The phagocytes have abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic “starry sky” pattern. Bone marrow aspiration shows tumour cells with royal blue cytoplasm containing clear cytoplasmic vacuoles.

The tumour cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, a phenotype consistent with a germinal centre B-cell origin.

Other options:

Option A: In Hodgkin's lymphoma, the most significant mutation is associated with the BCL6 gene on chromosome 3q27. The BCL6 gene mutation results in aberrant transcriptional regulation and contributes to the characteristic Reed-Sternberg cells seen in Hodgkin's lymphoma, which are large, abnormal lymphoid cells that are diagnostic of this type of lymphoma.

Option B: Pleomorphic adenoma is associated with chromosomal rearrangements that induce overexpression of PLAG1.  It is the most common salivary gland and lacrimal gland neoplasm. Microscopically, it contains a mixture of ductal (epithelial), myoepithelial, and mesenchymal cells.

Option D: Neuroblastoma is a tumour derived from primordial neural crest cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumour in childhood. They are associated with the n-MYC gene translocation. On histopathology, small round blue cells and Homer-Wright pseudorosettes are seen.
questions.learning: Burkitt's lymphoma Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by the translocation of the c-Myc gene on chromosome 8.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Once the diagnosis of gout is confirmed, which of the following medications—being a purine analog—is most appropriate for its management?
questions.explanation: Gout is a disease of hyperuricemia resulting in the deposition of monosodium urate crystals. For long-term management (urate-lowering therapy), the goal is to inhibit the enzyme xanthine oxidase. Allopurinol is the classic xanthine oxidase inhibitor and is chemically a purine analog (specifically an isomer of hypoxanthine). Because of its structure, it competitively inhibits the enzyme, reducing the production of uric acid. Febuxostat (Option D) is also a xanthine oxidase inhibitor but is a non-purine analog. Cytarabine (Option C) and Capecitabine (Option B) are pyrimidine analogs used in cancer chemotherapy and have no role in the management of gout. While Allopurinol is the most widely used agent, clinicians must be aware of its rare but serious hypersensitivity syndrome, particularly in patients with specific genetic markers like HLA-B5801. It is the standard-of-care purine analog for chronic gout prophylaxis
questions.learning: Gout is a disease of hyperuricemia resulting in the deposition of monosodium urate crystals. For long-term management (urate-lowering therapy), the goal is to inhibit the enzyme xanthine oxidase.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The investigation of choice for early follow-up in patients treated for anti-H. pylori drugs is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urea breath test

The urea breath test (UBT) is the investigation of choice for confirming eradication of Helicobacter pylori after completion of therapy. It is non-invasive, has high sensitivity and specificity, and detects active infection, making it ideal for early follow-up.

Why not the other options?

• B. Rapid urease test: Requires endoscopy and is not routinely used for follow-up.
• C. Stool H. pylori antigen test: Also detects active infection and is an acceptable alternative, but UBT is considered the preferred test.
• D. Serology for H. pylori: Not useful for follow-up, as antibodies may remain positive for months to years after successful eradication.
questions.learning: Urea breath test — The urea breath test (UBT) is the investigation of choice for confirming eradication of Helicobacter pylori after completion of therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A comatose patient after sustaining severe head injury has been admitted in neurosurgical ICU. Which of the following parameters should ideally be maintained in this patient? 1. pCO₂ = 4.5–5.0 kPa (33–38 mmHg) 2. MAP = 80–90 mmHg 3. pO₂ > 11 kPa (>80 mmHg) 4. Na⁺ <130 mEq/L Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

In severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), the goal is to prevent secondary brain injury by maintaining adequate oxygenation, cerebral perfusion, and normocapnia.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. pCO₂ = 4.5–5.0 kPa (33–38 mmHg): Correct. Normocapnia is maintained; prolonged hyperventilation is avoided.
• 2. MAP = 80–90 mmHg: Correct. Adequate MAP is required to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP).
• 3. pO₂ >11 kPa (>80 mmHg): Correct. Hypoxia must be avoided.
• 4. Na⁺ <130 mEq/L: Incorrect. Hyponatremia worsens cerebral edema. Serum sodium should be maintained in the normal or slightly high range.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 In severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), the goal is to prevent secondary brain injury by maintaining adequate oxygenation, cerebral perfusion, and normocapnia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent a laparoscopic cholecystectomy and had a drain in place until postoperative day 7, as there was bilious output of 300 mL/day. A CECT scan was normal, and an MRCP showed a leakage from the cystic duct stump. What is the next best step in management?
options: Re-laparoscopy and suture ligation of the cystic duct
ERCP with sphincterotomy and peripapillary stent placement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ERCP with sphincterotomy and peripapillary stent placement

B. ERCP with sphincterotomy and biliary stent placement

Post-cholecystectomy bile leak most commonly arises from the cystic duct stump, often due to clip slippage.

First-line management is ERCP with sphincterotomy and biliary stent placement, which lowers biliary pressure and diverts bile into the duodenum, allowing the leak to heal spontaneously.

Surgery is reserved for major bile duct injuries or large persistent leaks.
questions.learning: ERCP with sphincterotomy and peripapillary stent placement B. ERCP with sphincterotomy and biliary stent placement Post-cholecystectomy bile leak most commonly arises from the cystic duct stump, often due to clip slippage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with fatigue, anemia, and hepatomegaly, and hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrates the presence of HbS. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: The presence of Hemoglobin S (HbS) on electrophoresis confirms a diagnosis of Sickle Cell Anemia. Under low oxygen conditions, HbS polymerizes, causing red blood cells to sickle, leading to vaso-occlusion and chronic hemolysis. Hydroxyurea is the primary chronic therapy because it increases the production of fetal hemoglobin (HbF). Higher levels of HbF inhibit the polymerization of HbS, thereby reducing the frequency of painful crises and systemic complications. Blood transfusions (Option B) are reserved for acute severe anemia or emergencies rather than first-line long-term management. Iron supplementation (Option C) is contraindicated unless a concurrent iron deficiency is proven, as these patients are at risk for iron overload from hemolysis and transfusions. Vitamin B12 (Option D) treats macrocytic anemia and is not specific to sickle cell disease. Therefore, hydroxyurea remains the definitive treatment to modify the disease course
questions.learning: The presence of Hemoglobin S (HbS) on electrophoresis confirms a diagnosis of Sickle Cell Anemia. Under low oxygen conditions, HbS polymerizes, causing red blood cells to sickle, leading to vaso-occlusion and chronic hemolysis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: After how many days is the polymorphic rash of Varicella not contagious?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. After crust formation over lesions

Chicken pox or Varicella caused by Varicella zoster virus becomes non-contagious after the lesions have crusted.

* Varicella zoster virus is an α Herpes virus (Human Herpes Virus 3).

* Over half of primary infections occur before the age of 5 and 85% before puberty.

* The lesions are polymorphic - present at different stages in each site.

* In 2–4 days, a dry crust forms and soon separates, to leave a shallow pink depression which, in the absence of secondary infection, heals without scarring.

* Most common complication is secondary bacterial infection.

* Varicella confers lasting immunity and second attacks are uncommon.

* In histopathology, keratinocytes show ballooning degeneration creating multinucleated giant cells called Tzanck cells.

Characteristics of rash of chicken pox

* Superficial

* Pleomorphic

* Centripetal

* Unilocular

* Symmetrical

* Spares palms and soles, affects flexor surfaces and axilla

* Rapid evolution

* Dew drop on Rose-petal appearance

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman, G4P3 presents at 34 weeks gestation for an antenatal visit. She has a history of previous cesarean deliveries. During her routine ultrasound examination, the radiologist reports findings suggestive of placenta accreta. The patient has no symptoms at present. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option for this patient?
options: Expectant management with close monitoring and regular ultrasounds
Initiation of antenatal corticosteroids and scheduled cesarean section at 37 weeks gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preoperative planning for cesarean hysterectomy

Placenta accreta spectrum occurs when the placenta abnormally adheres to or invades the myometrium due to defective decidua basalis. It commonly occurs in women with previous cesarean deliveries. Major Risk Factors:

• Previous cesarean section (most important)
• Placenta previa
• Multiparity
• Previous uterine surgery or curettage

Normally the placenta separates after delivery.

In placenta accreta, the placenta is firmly attached to the myometrium, so attempted placental removal can cause massive postpartum hemorrhage.

When placenta accreta is diagnosed antenatally, the recommended management is Planned cesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ.

Usually planned at 34–36 weeks before onset of labor.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Immediate cesarean section: unnecessary if the patient is stable and asymptomatic.
• Expectant management alone: dangerous due to risk of sudden hemorrhage.
• Cesarean at 37 weeks: may allow labor or bleeding to occur, increasing maternal risk.
questions.learning: Preoperative planning for cesarean hysterectomy Placenta accreta spectrum occurs when the placenta abnormally adheres to or invades the myometrium due to defective decidua basalis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The commonest surgical approach to a retrosternal goiter is via:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neck

The commonest surgical approach to a retrosternal goiter is via the neck and the most common type of goitre approached is the secondary retrosternal goiter.

A goiter is considered to be retrosternal if at least 50% of the thyroid tissue is located intrathoracically. They can be primary or secondary.

Primary retrosternal goiter
Secondary retrosternal goiter

Occurrence
1%
Majority of retrosternal goiters

Origin

Arise from ectopic thyroid tissue in the chest

No connection with the thyroid tissue in the neck

Arise from the downward extension of cervical thyroid tissue along the fascial planes of the neck

Blood supply
Intrathoracic blood vessels
Superior and inferior thyroid arteries

Retrosternal goiter presents with dyspnoea, stridor, and dilated neck veins. Pemberton’s sign (venous congestion of the neck on the raising of hands above the head) is seen.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the neck is performed to assess the location of the thyroid. The definitive treatment is surgical excision of the ectopic thyroid.

Other options:

Option B & C: Median sternotomy (via chest) is indicated in:

• Primary mediastinal goiter
• Malignant retrosternal goiter
• Very large retrosternal goiter
• Recurrence in the mediastinum
questions.learning: Neck — The commonest surgical approach to a retrosternal goiter is via the neck and the most common type of goitre approached is the secondary retrosternal goiter.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Adrenaline acting via beta 2 receptors cause bronchodilation whereas histamine acts through H1 receptors to cause bronchoconstriction. Which type of antagonism it is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Physiological antagonism

It is a type of physiological antagonism.

Two drugs acting on different receptors and resulting in opposite responses means having pharmacological effects in the opposite direction and is termed as physiological antagonism.

E.g. Histamine and adrenaline on bronchial muscles.
questions.learning: Physiological antagonism — It is a type of physiological antagonism. Two drugs acting on different receptors and resulting in opposite responses means having pharmacological effects in the opposite direction and is termed as physiological antagonism.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the characteristic feature seen in ectopic pregnancy? hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
options: Ovarian mass with thin layer of endometrium
Empty uterus with adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis
Empty uterus and adnexal mass with ground glass appearance
Trilayer endometrium without an adnexal mass
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Empty uterus with adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis

An empty uterus with an adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis is the sign most suggestive of an ectopic pregnancy.

A pregnancy is considered ectopic if implantation occurs at a site outside the uterine cavity. The majority of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube, the ampulla being the most common site.

The most appropriate management for an unruptured ectopic pregnancy is single-dose methotrexate.

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

Expectant management: Ectopic pregnancies measuring <3 cm and with declining beta hCG levels initially <1500 mIU/mL may resolve without intervention and can be managed expectantly.

Medical management with single or multiple-dose methotrexate is preferred if:

* Hemodynamic stability

* Serum beta-hCG ≥1500 mIU/ml and ≤5000 mIU/mL

* Mean sac diameter <3.5cm with no fetal cardiac activity detected on transvaginal ultrasound.

* Patients are willing and able to comply with post-treatment follow-up and have access to emergency medical services within a reasonable time frame in case of a deterioration in the clinical status.

Methotrexate(MTX) can be given as a single IM dose of 50 mg/m2 or as a multiple-dose regimen of 1mg/kg on days 1, 3, 5, and 7.

Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

* Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met

* Gestational sac >3.5 cm

* Fetal cardiac activity present

* Beta hCG > 5000 mIU/mL

* Significant pain and hemoperitoneum

* Failure of expectant or medical management

* Clinical status of patient warrants urgent intervention

* Doubtful compliance with medical management

Milking of the tube through the fimbriae carries a high risk of bleeding, damage to the tube, the persistence of trophoblastic tissue, and recurrence of ectopic pregnancy.

Other Options:

Option A: Ovarian mass with thin layer of endometrium  is suggestive of an ovarian cyst.

Option C: Empty uterus and adnexal mass with ground glass appearance is suggestive of a chocolate cyst/ ovarian endometrioma.

Option D: Trilayer endometrium without an adnexal mass is the physiological state of the uterus.
questions.learning: Empty uterus with adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis — An empty uterus with an adnexal mass and fluid in pelvis is the sign most suggestive of an ectopic pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A patient presented with pain on the left side of the chest. On examination, there was dullness on percussion on left infra-axillary area. X-ray Chest showed left opaque hemithorax. Which one of the following is an indication for tube thoracentesis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pleural fluid glucose < 60 mg/dL

• The patient has a left-sided pleural effusion causing dullness to percussion and an opaque hemithorax. Tube thoracostomy (intercostal chest tube drainage) is indicated when the pleural fluid suggests a complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema, particularly when the pleural fluid glucose is <60 mg/dL.
• A low pleural fluid glucose indicates high metabolic activity of bacteria and inflammatory cells and impaired glucose transport across the inflamed pleura.

Why not the other options?

• A. Straw-coloured fluid: Common in uncomplicated pleural effusions and does not itself indicate chest-tube drainage.
• B. Pleural fluid pH >7.2: A pH >7.20 generally argues against a complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage. pH <7.20 is the important threshold.
• D. Pleural fluid LDH <600 IU/L: A low LDH does not indicate complicated infection. Markedly elevated LDH supports an inflammatory/exudative process.
questions.learning: Pleural fluid glucose 7.2: A pH >7.20 generally argues against a complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage. pH <7.20 is the important threshold. • D.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An 8-year-old child who previously underwent tonsillectomy now presents with snoring, palpitations, mouth breathing, mild hearing impairment, a high-arched palate, and poor academic performance, which has worried the mother. What should be the next step in management for this child?
questions.explanation: The child is displaying the classic "adenoid facies" (mouth breathing, high arched palate) and symptoms of adenoid hypertrophy, including snoring and declining school performance likely due to obstructive sleep apnea. The "slight hearing loss" and post-tonsillectomy status suggest that the adenoids are now the primary obstruction, also causing Eustachian tube dysfunction and subsequent Otitis Media with Effusion (glue ear). The most comprehensive next step is an Adenoidectomy to clear the airway and a Grommet insertion (myringotomy with tubes) to drain the middle ear fluid and restore hearing. Adenoidectomy alone (Option A) might not immediately resolve the established ear effusion. Myringoplasty (Option B) is for drum repair and is not indicated. Conservative management (Option D) is inappropriate given the significant impact on the child's sleep and academic performance. Thus, the combined surgical approach is the standard of care
questions.learning: The child is displaying the classic "adenoid facies" (mouth breathing, high arched palate) and symptoms of adenoid hypertrophy, including snoring and declining school performance likely due to obstructive sleep apnea.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following denotes an "infant at risk"?
options: Infant of mother who has not taken folic acid during pregnancy
Infant with history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Infant with history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation

An infant with a history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation will be considered a high-risk infant according to AIIMS protocols on Neonatology.

The inclusion criteria for high-risk neonates according to AIIMS protocol are:

1. Birth weight <1500 grams
2. Gestation age <32 weeks
3. Infants with a birth weight of ≥ 1500gm or gestation age ≥ 32 weeks with any of the following risk factors:

• Intrauterine growth centile <3rd centile
• Meningitis
• Received mechanical ventilation for 48 hours or more
• Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy stage 2 or higher
• Major malformation
• Inborn error of metabolism/ chromosomal or genetic disorders/ intrauterine infections
• Symptomatic hypoglycemia
• Symptomatic polycythemia
• Retrovirus positive mother
• Hyperbilirubinemia requiring exchange transfusion OR Rh isoimmunization/cholestasis
• Abnormal neurological examination at discharge/ seizures
• Major morbidities such as chronic lung diseases, IVH grade III or more and periventricular leukomalacia

Note: Although Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine mentions infants of working mothers (Option A) as high-risk infants, premature infant with < 32 weeks gestation is chosen over it, as AIIMS protocols are used as the preferred reference for AIIMS exams.
questions.learning: Infant with history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation An infant with a history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation will be considered a high-risk infant according to AIIMS protocols on Neonatology.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young man presented with hearing loss and tinnitus. Histology image is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Schwannoma

The history of hearing loss and tinnitus and the histology showing Verocay bodies are suggestive of Schwannoma.

Vestibular Schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), is a benign tumor that predominantly originates from the Schwann cells in the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve, but it rarely arises from the cochlear division. It commonly affects individuals aged 40-60, with no gender preference. Bilateral schwannomas occur in neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2).

The most common presenting manifestations are progressive, unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, often accompanied by tinnitus.

It can involve all cranial nerves except the first and second. Apart from the 8th cranial nerve, the earliest cranial nerve to be involved is the 5th cranial nerve leading to reduced corneal sensitivity and paraesthesia of the face. This indicates that the tumor is roughly 2.5 cm in diameter and occupies the cerebellopontine angle.

Facial nerve involvement causes hypoaesthesia of the posterior meatal wall (Hitzelberger sign), taste loss, and delayed blink reflex. The earliest sign is a delayed blink reflex.

Glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerve involvement result in dysphagia and hoarseness. Brainstem involvement manifests as ataxia, limb weakness, numbness, and increased tendon reflexes. Cerebellar involvement leads to an unsteady gait and dysdiadochokinesia.

Histopathologically, the tumor comprises dense Antoni A areas with spindle cells in a palisading pattern and Antoni B areas with loosely arranged spindle cells in a myxoid matrix. Verocay bodies are formed in the Antoni A region, characterized by nuclear-free zones surrounded by palisaded nuclei.

Pure tone audiometry reveals sensorineural hearing loss, particularly in high frequencies. Speech audiometry shows the roll-over phenomenon. The absence of the recruitment phenomenon is noted. Short Increment Sensitivity Index (SISI) ranges from 0-20%.

Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA) demonstrates a significant delay of >0.2 ms in wave V between the two ears. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) with gadolinium contrast is considered the gold standard for diagnosis.

The primary management is the surgical removal of the tumor via the middle cranial fossa approach, the trans-labyrinthine approach, the suboccipital (retro sigmoid) approach, or a combined trans-labyrinthine-suboccipital approach.

Conventional radiotherapy using external beam radiation is not effective. In cases where surgery is contraindicated, refused by the patient, or when a residual tumor remains, alternative treatments such as the x-knife or gamma knife can be considered.

Other options:

Option A: Neurofibromas are also benign nerve sheath tumours and the histological picture shows the presence of bland Schwann cells admixed with stromal cells such as mast cells, perineural cells, and fibroblasts. The stroma of the tumour contains loose collagen arranged in wavy bundles resembling carrot shavings.

Option C: Leiomyomas are benign smooth muscle neoplasms that may occur single or multiple. Microscopically, leiomyomas are comprised of well-differentiated, regular, spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells associated with hyalinization. Very less mitotic figures are seen.

Option D: Rhabdomyomas are the most frequent primary tumours of the heart in children. Microscopically, they are composed of bizarre, markedly enlarged myocytes with abundant glycogen. But due to routine histological processing, the glycogen content is reduced and looks like thin strands that stretch from the nuclei to the surface membrane, which appears like spider cells.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following physiological changes occurs in muscles during contraction while exercising?
options: M length increase and I decrease
questions.explanation: During muscle contraction, the sarcomere shortens according to the sliding filament theory. The I-band, which consists only of thin (actin) filaments, decreases in length as these filaments are pulled toward the center of the sarcomere, increasing their overlap with the thick (myosin) filaments. The H-zone, the region containing only thick filaments, also shortens or disappears. The A-band (Option B) corresponds to the full length of the thick filaments; since the filaments themselves do not change in length, the A-band remains constant during contraction. The M-line marks the central point where thick filaments are anchored and does not increase in length (Option A); it simply becomes more prominent. Option D is incorrect because the M-line length remains stable. Therefore, the only correct observation among the choices is the shortening of the I-band as the muscle fibers actively contract

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A patient presents with a 2-day history of watery diarrhea (5–6 episodes per day). Arterial blood gas analysis shows decreased PCO₂. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ↓ pH, ↓ HCO₃⁻, ↑ Cl⁻

Diarrhea causes a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis due to excessive loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid. The fall in serum HCO₃⁻ leads to metabolic acidosis (↓ pH), while compensatory hyperventilation (Kussmaul respiration) lowers PCO₂. To maintain electroneutrality, chloride is retained by the kidneys, resulting in hyperchloremia.

Why not the other options?

• A. ↑ pH, ↑ HCO₃⁻, ↑ Cl⁻: Suggests metabolic alkalosis, which is inconsistent with bicarbonate loss in diarrhea.
• C. ↑ pH, ↑ HCO₃⁻, ↓ Cl⁻: Typical of vomiting-induced hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
• D. ↓ pH, ↑ HCO₃⁻, ↑ Cl⁻: Elevated bicarbonate would not be seen in metabolic acidosis.
questions.learning: ↓ pH, ↓ HCO₃⁻, ↑ Cl⁻ Diarrhea causes a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis due to excessive loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Apoptotic bodies comprise of?
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is "programmed cell death," a tidy process designed to remove unwanted cells without triggering inflammation. During apoptosis, the cell shrinks and the DNA fragments. The cell then breaks apart into several membrane-bound fragments called apoptotic bodies. These bodies comprise cytoplasm, tightly packed organelles, and fragments of the nucleus (intranuclear material). Because they are enclosed in an intact plasma membrane, the toxic cellular contents do not leak out. Options B, C, and D are incomplete descriptions of these bodies. These fragments are rapidly recognized by phagocytes (like macrophages) through "eat-me" signals such as the flip of phosphatidylserine to the outer membrane leaflet. This efficient clearance prevents the inflammatory response that typically follows necrosis. Apoptosis is a vital physiological process during embryogenesis, immune system regulation, and the removal of DNA-damaged cells. Its dysregulation can lead to autoimmune diseases or cancer, making it a central theme in cell pathology
questions.learning: Apoptosis is "programmed cell death," a tidy process designed to remove unwanted cells without triggering inflammation. During apoptosis, the cell shrinks and the DNA fragments.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The relative risks associated with Vaccine 1 and Vaccine 2 are 0.5 and 2.0, respectively. Which of the following graphs correctly represents these relative risks?
questions.explanation: Relative Risk (RR) is a measure of the association between an exposure (vaccination) and an outcome. An RR of 1.0 indicates no difference in risk. If RR < 1, the exposure is protective; if RR > 1, the exposure increases risk. Vaccine 1 has an RR of 0.5, meaning it is protective. On a standard forest plot or relative risk graph, this would be represented by a bar or point below the null line (1.0), as seen in Graph 1. Vaccine 2 has an RR of 2.0, meaning it is associated with a doubling of risk (perhaps an adverse event study). This would be represented by a bar or point above the null line (1.0), as seen in Graph 2. Graph 3 (Option A and B) typically represents a different statistical distribution or an incorrect scale. Therefore, the pairing of Graph 1 for Vaccine 1 and Graph 2 for Vaccine 2 accurately visualizes these relative risk values
questions.learning: Relative Risk (RR) is a measure of the association between an exposure (vaccination) and an outcome. An RR of 1.0 indicates no difference in risk.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the image given below.
questions.explanation: The provided image is a horizontal (axial) section of the human brain at the level of the basal ganglia. The marked structure is a V-shaped band of white matter situated between the thalamus and caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. This is the internal capsule, a major highway for motor and sensory fibers connecting the cerebral cortex with the brainstem and spinal cord. The external capsule (Option A) is a thinner band of white matter located lateral to the putamen. The putamen (Option C) is the large, lateral portion of the lentiform nucleus. The caudate nucleus (Option D) is the C-shaped gray matter structure located in the wall of the lateral ventricle, medial to the internal capsule's anterior limb. Strokes involving the posterior limb of the internal capsule are common and result in significant contralateral hemiparesis. Precise identification of these deep brain structures is fundamental for neurologists to localize lesions based on a patient's clinical deficits
questions.learning: The provided image is a horizontal (axial) section of the human brain at the level of the basal ganglia. The marked structure is a V-shaped band of white matter situated between the thalamus and caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the staffing pattern of an Urban Primary Health Centre (UPHC) is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Under the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) guidelines, the staffing pattern for an Urban Primary Health Center (U-PHC) is specifically defined. A standard U-PHC is staffed by 4 to 5 staff nurses in total. Statement B is often considered "false" in examinations because the specific core staffing recommendation for a U-PHC typically lists 2 staff nurses as the essential baseline requirement for a facility serving a 50,000 population, with additional staff depending on the workload. The center does include 2 doctors (Option A—usually 1 full-time and 1 part-time/regular), 1 lab technician (Option C), and 1 pharmacist (Option D). The U-PHC serves as the primary urban healthcare delivery point, focusing on outpatient services and outreach. Therefore, according to fixed standard staffing charts, the figure of 5 multi-skilled nurses is an overstatement of the essential baseline staff
questions.learning: Under the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) guidelines, the staffing pattern for an Urban Primary Health Center (U-PHC) is specifically defined. A standard U-PHC is staffed by 4 to 5 staff nurses in total.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of spontaneous, unilateral, blood-stained discharge from a single duct of the right nipple. There is no palpable breast lump. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intraductal papilloma

Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of spontaneous, unilateral, blood-stained nipple discharge from a single duct in women aged 35–55 years. It is a benign papillary tumor arising within a major lactiferous duct, usually located beneath the areola.

Why not the other options?

• B. Fibroadenoma: Presents as a painless, mobile breast lump; nipple discharge is uncommon.
• C. Duct ectasia: Usually occurs in perimenopausal women and causes multiduct, thick green/brown, sticky discharge with nipple retraction.
• D. Breast carcinoma: May cause bloody nipple discharge, but is usually associated with a palpable hard irregular lump, skin changes, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
questions.learning: Intraductal papilloma Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of spontaneous, unilateral, blood-stained nipple discharge from a single duct in women aged 35–55 years.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are correct regarding pelvic cellular tissue? 1. It supports the pelvic organs. 2. It forms protective sheath for blood vessels and terminal part of ureter. 3. It prevents infection to be spread out of pelvis. 4. Marked hypertrophy of pelvic cellular tissue occurs in pregnancy. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Pelvic cellular tissue (endopelvic connective tissue) is a loose fibro-fatty connective tissue located between the pelvic fascia.

• 1. It supports the pelvic organs. ✓

• Pelvic cellular tissue helps support the uterus, cervix, vagina, bladder, and rectum, maintaining normal pelvic anatomy.

• 2. It forms a protective sheath for blood vessels and the terminal part of the ureter. ✓

• It encloses the uterine vessels, pelvic vessels, lymphatics, nerves, and terminal ureter, providing support and protection.

• 3. It prevents infection from spreading out of the pelvis. ✗

• Incorrect. Pelvic cellular tissue actually contains potential spaces through which infection (pelvic cellulitis/parametritis), hemorrhage, and malignant cells can spread.

• 4. Marked hypertrophy of pelvic cellular tissue occurs in pregnancy. ✓

• Under the influence of estrogen and progesterone, pelvic connective tissue becomes hypertrophied, edematous, and more vascular, facilitating uterine enlargement and childbirth.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Pelvic cellular tissue (endopelvic connective tissue) is a loose fibro-fatty connective tissue located between the pelvic fascia. • 1. It supports the pelvic organs. ✓ • Pelvic cellular tissue helps support the uterus, cervix, vagina, bladder,…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs belongs to the class of selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs)?
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen is the prototype of the Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators (SERMs). SERMs are unique compounds that exhibit tissue-specific activity; they act as estrogen receptor antagonists in some tissues while acting as agonists in others. Tamoxifen acts as an antagonist in breast tissue, making it a vital treatment for ER-positive breast cancer. Conversely, it acts as an agonist in the bone (preventing bone loss) and in the uterus, which unfortunately increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma. Estrogen (Option A) is a pure hormone agonist. Metformin (Option B) is a biguanide used for diabetes. Adriamycin (Option D), also known as Doxorubicin, is an anthracycline cytotoxic antibiotic used in cancer chemotherapy but is not a hormone modulator. Other SERMs include Raloxifene, which is an antagonist in both breast and uterus but an agonist in bone. Therefore, Tamoxifen is the correct classification for a SERM used in the management of hormone-sensitive malignancies
questions.learning: Tamoxifen is the prototype of the Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators (SERMs). SERMs are unique compounds that exhibit tissue-specific activity; they act as estrogen receptor antagonists in some tissues while acting as agonists in others.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male trekker ascending to an altitude of about 5,000 meters suddenly develops severe headache, dizziness, breathlessness, and blurred vision, forcing him to stop climbing. Based on this presentation, which high-altitude–related condition is most likely?
questions.explanation: At a high altitude of 5000 meters, both barometric pressure and the partial pressure of oxygen (PaO₂) are markedly reduced, leading to hypoxia. In response, peripheral chemoreceptors stimulate immediate hyperventilation to increase oxygen uptake. This increased ventilation causes excessive elimination of carbon dioxide (PaCO₂), resulting in hypocapnia. According to the Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship, a fall in PaCO₂ raises blood pH, producing respiratory alkalosis. Metabolic alkalosis (Option A) and metabolic acidosis (Option D) arise from primary disturbances in bicarbonate or fixed acids and are not directly caused by altitude exposure. Respiratory acidosis (Option C) results from hypoventilation with CO₂ retention, which is opposite to the physiological response at high altitude. Thus, the most likely initial acid–base disturbance at high altitude is acute respiratory alkalosis, a hallmark of early high-altitude illness. Over time, the kidneys compensate by increasing bicarbonate excretion
questions.learning: At a high altitude of 5000 meters, both barometric pressure and the partial pressure of oxygen (PaO₂) are markedly reduced, leading to hypoxia. In response, peripheral chemoreceptors stimulate immediate hyperventilation to increase oxygen uptake.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitric oxide is synthesized from which of the following amino acids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arginine

Nitric oxide is synthesized from arginine by a calcium-dependent reaction catalyzed by NO synthase.

Arginine, O2, and NADPH are substrates for cytosolic NO synthase. The co-enzymes of NO synthase include flavin mononucleotide (FMN), flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), heme, and tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).

Functions of NO:

* It is a potent vasodilator.

* It acts as a neurotransmitter in CNS.

* Antimicrobial and cytotoxic activity of various inflammatory cells.

* Inhibitor of platelet aggregation.

* In GIT, it relaxes smooth muscle.

Pearl PF1957: Amino Acid Derivatives

Pearl PF0102: Classification of Hormones According to their Chemical Structure

Proteins and polypeptide hormones

* Pituitary hormones - GH, ACTH, FSH, LH, Prolactin, Oxytocin and ADH

* Insulin and glucagon

* Parathormone

Steroid hormones

* Cortisol, aldosterone

* Estrogen, progesterone

* Testosterone

Derivatives of a specific amino acid

* Tyrosine

* Thyroid hormones, catecholamines

* Tryptophan

* Serotonin (5-HT), melatonin

* Arginine

* Nitric oxide

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is set up for health planning at the village level?
options: Village Health Planning and Management Committee
Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committee
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committee

Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) has been formed to take collective actions on issues related to health and its social determinants at the village level (local level community action).

The committee is formed at the revenue village level and it should act as a sub-committee of the gram panchayat. It should have a minimum of 15 members and ASHA residing in the village shall be the member secretary and convener of the committee.
questions.learning: Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committee Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) has been formed to take collective actions on issues related to health and its social determinants at the village level (local level community action).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
An 18-year-old male presents to the emergency department with epistaxis and a nasal mass. What is the investigation of choice to evaluate his condition?

Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography - (CECT)

Paranasal Sinuses - (PNS)

Magnetic Resonance Imaging - (MRI)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CECT PNS and nose

History of nasal mass and associated epistaxis in an 18-year-old raises the suspicion of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. CECT of the PNS and nose can be done to evaluate the patient.

CECT of the PNS and nose is particularly useful for revealing characteristic findings such as the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, known as the Antral sign or Holman-Miller sign (shown in the image below), which is indicative of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor that predominantly affects adolescent males aged 10-20 years. It typically originates from the posterior part of the nasal cavity near the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen and is thought to be testosterone-dependent. Clinically, this condition presents with profuse, recurrent spontaneous epistaxis, progressive nasal obstruction, conductive hearing loss, and otitis media with effusion. It may also cause additional features such as proptosis, cheek swelling, and broadening of the nasal bridge.

Diagnosis is primarily based on clinical presentation, with CECT serving as the preferred imaging technique to confirm the diagnosis and assess the extent of the tumor. Carotid angiography may be performed to evaluate the vascularity of the tumor and its feeding vessels, typically arising from the external carotid artery, and potentially from the internal carotid system in cases of larger tumors with intracranial extension. Biopsy of the mass is generally avoided due to the risk of severe bleeding.

Staging of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

Stage
Spread

IA
Limited to the nose and/or nasopharynx

IB
Extension into ≥ one paranasal sinus

IIA
Minimal extension into the sphenopalatine foramen with minimal part of pterygopalatine fossa

IIB
Full occupation of pterygopalatine fossa with Holman-Miller sign, may with erosion of orbital bones

IIC
Extension into the cheek, temporal fossa, or posterior to pterygoids through the pterygomaxillary fossa

IIIA
Erosion of skull base with minimal intracranial

IIIB
Erosion of skull base with extensive intracranial with or without cavernous sinus

Surgery is the treatment of choice. Embolization of the vessels can be done prior to surgery to reduce the risk of bleeding during the surgery. Radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and hormonal therapy can also be considered.
questions.learning: CECT PNS and nose History of nasal mass and associated epistaxis in an 18-year-old raises the suspicion of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. CECT of the PNS and nose can be done to evaluate the patient.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious following a fall from a ladder. On examination, he does not open his eyes even to painful stimuli, produces incomprehensible sounds, and shows abnormal flexion in response to pain. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) evaluates the level of consciousness using three components: Eye opening (E), Verbal response (V), and Motor response (M). In this patient: 1. Eye opening: No eye opening even to painful stimulus → E1 2. Verbal response: Incomprehensible sounds → V2 3. Motor response: Abnormal flexion to pain (decorticate posturing) → M3 The total GCS score is calculated as: A GCS score of 6 falls within the range of 3–8, which indicates a severe head injury. Patients with this level of consciousness are at high risk of airway compromise and secondary brain injury and often require urgent airway protection and intensive monitoring. The other options (5, 7, and 8) do not correctly match the neurological findings described. Accurate calculation of the GCS is essential in trauma care to guide immediate management decisions and prognosis assessment
questions.learning: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) evaluates the level of consciousness using three components: Eye opening (E), Verbal response (V), and Motor response (M).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In patients with indications for warfarin usage, what is the recommended range of INR in a patient with mechanical heart valves ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2.5 – 3.5

The INR ratio recommended for the administration of warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves is around 2.5-3.5.

Warfarin therapy is usually monitored by measuring prothrombin time. Prothrombin time is sensitive to the reduction in levels of prothrombin, factor VII, and factor X.  International normalized ratio (INR) was developed to standardize the reporting of prothrombin time.

Other options:

Option B: In most of the patients on regular warfarin therapy,  the INR target is around 2.0-3.0

Option A: The range of 1.0-1.5 is too low for beneficial effects.

Option D: INR >3.5 can result in increased adverse effects and is not recommended for any condition.
questions.learning: 2.5 – 3.5 The INR ratio recommended for the administration of warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves is around 2.5-3.5. Warfarin therapy is usually monitored by measuring prothrombin time.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presented with a tuft of hair over the lumbosacral region. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Any of the above

A tuft of hair over the lumbosacral region in a newborn is suggestive of occult spinal dysraphism or neural tube defect. It comprises a range of conditions, including spina bifida occulta, intradural lipoma, and dorsal dermal sinus.

Spinal dysraphism is due to the defective fusion of the midline embryonic neural, vertebral, and mesenchymal structures. Associated clinical features are high-arched feet, muscle size and strength differences between legs, and abnormal walking patterns. In newborns and young infants, the neurological examination is usually normal, but older children may experience a lack of sensation in the perineal area and back pain.

Most of the patients will have a cutaneous abnormality overlying the lower spine, including a small dimple, a tuft of hair, or a subcutaneous lipoma.

The image shows a tuft of hair in a case of spinal dysraphism:

Spinal dysraphism also includes meningocele, myelomeningocele, lipomeningocele, diastematomyelia (split spinal cord), thickened filum terminale, and cauda equina tumour.

The initial investigation is usually ultrasound in the neonate and the best investigation is MRI.

Spina bifida is the most common type of spinal dysraphism, in which the spinal column does not close completely, leaving the spinal cord and its protective covering exposed.

Myelomeningocele is the most severe form of spina bifida, where the spinal cord and nerve roots are exposed and may be damaged. A sac-like protrusion, containing spinal cord tissue, meninges, and cerebrospinal fluid, is visible outside the body, often leading to significant neurological impairments and disabilities.
questions.learning: Any of the above — A tuft of hair over the lumbosacral region in a newborn is suggestive of occult spinal dysraphism or neural tube defect. It comprises a range of conditions, including spina bifida occulta, intradural lipoma, and dorsal dermal sinus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents with elevated PSA levels and abnormal findings on digital rectal examination, raising suspicion for prostate cancer. Which lymph node group is most commonly involved in the metastatic spread of prostate cancer?
questions.explanation: Prostate cancer metastasis typically follows a predictable lymphatic drainage pattern. The prostate is a pelvic organ, and its primary lymphatic drainage is to the regional pelvic lymph nodes. The internal iliac (Option D) and obturator lymph nodes are the most common and earliest sites of nodal metastasis for prostate cancer. These are often followed by involvement of the external iliac and common iliac chains (collectively referred to as Pelvic nodes, Option B, though "Internal iliac" is the more specific primary site). Superficial inguinal nodes (Option C) and deep inguinal nodes (Option A) primarily drain the skin of the lower limbs, scrotum, and penis; they are not the primary drainage site for the prostate gland. Clinically, identification of internal iliac or obturator node involvement through imaging or biopsy is critical for staging and deciding between curative local therapy and systemic management for prostate cancer
questions.learning: Prostate cancer metastasis typically follows a predictable lymphatic drainage pattern. The prostate is a pelvic organ, and its primary lymphatic drainage is to the regional pelvic lymph nodes.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which one of the following conditions is a complication of bacterial pharyngitis involving extension of infection into the internal jugular veins leading to thrombosis and metastatic dispersal of the organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lemierre syndrome

Lemierre syndrome is a rare but life-threatening complication of bacterial pharyngitis or tonsillitis, most commonly caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic Gram-negative bacillus.

The syndrome is characterized by:

• Recent pharyngitis/tonsillitis
• Internal jugular vein thrombosis
• Septic emboli, especially to the lungs, causing multiple cavitating pulmonary nodules or abscesses
• Isolation of Fusobacterium necrophorum

Why not the other options?

• A. Cystic fibrosis: An inherited autosomal recessive disorder causing chronic sinopulmonary infections and pancreatic insufficiency; unrelated to jugular vein thrombosis.
• B. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis: Chronic fungal infection of the lungs, usually in patients with pre-existing lung cavities; not a complication of pharyngitis.
• D. Wegener’s granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with polyangiitis): ANCA-associated vasculitis involving the upper airway, lungs, and kidneys; not associated with internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis.
questions.learning: Lemierre syndrome Lemierre syndrome is a rare but life-threatening complication of bacterial pharyngitis or tonsillitis, most commonly caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum, an anaerobic Gram-negative bacillus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which diagnostic tool is preferred for metabolic disease screening in children?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tandem mass spectrometry

Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) is the preferred screening tool for inborn errors of metabolism in newborns and children. It can simultaneously detect multiple metabolic disorders by measuring amino acids, organic acids, and acylcarnitines from a single dried blood spot.

This method is widely used in newborn screening programs to identify disorders such as phenylketonuria, maple syrup urine disease, fatty acid oxidation defects, and organic acidemias, allowing early diagnosis and treatment to prevent severe complications.

Why not other options:

• CBC: Evaluates blood cells (RBCs, WBCs, platelets); not useful for detecting metabolic enzyme defects.
• Urinalysis: May detect some metabolites but is not sensitive or comprehensive for screening multiple metabolic disorders.
• Genetic testing: Confirms specific mutations but is not practical for large-scale initial screening of many metabolic diseases.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 9-year-old boy who presents with progressively worsening hip pain and limping, associated with muscle wasting, reduced abduction, and painful restriction of internal rotation of the hip?
questions.explanation: Perthes Disease (Legg-Calvé-Perthes) is an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head, classically affecting boys between the ages of 4 and 10. The clinical features described—progressive limping, hip pain, muscle wasting, and the specific loss of abduction and internal rotation—are diagnostic hallmarks of this condition in a 9-year-old. DDH (Option A) is typically diagnosed at birth or infancy and presents with leg length discrepancy or abnormal gait in toddlers. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) (Option B) usually occurs in obese adolescents (ages 12–15) and presents with the leg held in external rotation. Congenital Coxa Vara (Option D) involves a decreased femoral neck-shaft angle and is usually painless. Perthes disease requires long-term orthopedic follow-up to prevent permanent joint deformity. Given the specific age range and characteristic restriction of internal rotation, Perthes Disease is the most appropriate diagnosis
questions.learning: Perthes Disease (Legg-Calvé-Perthes) is an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head, classically affecting boys between the ages of 4 and 10.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the fluid of choice for shock in a child with severe acute malnutrition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose

The fluid of choice for shock in a child with severe acute malnutrition(SAM) is Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose.

If a child with SAM is lethargic or unconscious with cold extremities plus decreased capillary refill (>3 sec) or weak fast pulse, it is said to be in shock. Intravenous fluid resuscitation in SAM is only recommended in those with shock. IV fluids that can be used in these children are

* Ringer lactate with 5% dextrose

* Half-normal saline with 5% dextrose

* Half-strength Darrow solution with 5% dextrose.

If any of the above mixtures is not available, only then ringer lactate can be used.

10% glucose is given orally or IV in SAM to treat hypoglycemia and is not used to replenish intravascular volume.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following is not associated with Sprengel deformity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dextrocardia

Dextrocardia is not associated with Sprengel deformity.

Sprengel deformity is the congenital elevation of the scapula. It is characterized by an elevated shoulder on the affected side, with an abnormally high, smaller, and prominent scapula. The neck appears shorter, and there may be kyphosis or scoliosis of the upper thoracic spine. While shoulder movements are painless, abduction and elevation may be limited due to scapular fixation.

Abnormalities associated with Sprengel deformity include:

• Klippel-Feil Syndrome
• Kyphosis or Scoliosis
• Cervical rib
• Omovertebral bar (a bony bridge between the scapula and the cervical spine)
• Spina bifida
• Diastematomyelia (congenitally split spinal cord)
• Torticollis
• Renal abnormalities

questions.learning: Dextrocardia Dextrocardia is not associated with Sprengel deformity. Sprengel deformity is the congenital elevation of the scapula.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most common symptom of cannabis intake?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dream like state

The most common symptom of cannabis intake is a dream-like state.

After cannabis intake users have feelings of mild euphoria, relaxation, and perceptual alterations. Cognitive changes include impaired short-term memory and attention. The user feels lost in a pleasant dreamy state and has difficulty sustaining goal-directed mental activity.

Anxiety, decreased appetite, and depressed mood are the symptoms seen in cannabis withdrawal symptoms. Other withdrawal symptoms include irritability, insomnia, nervousness, and weight loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Heberden’s nodes are present mainly in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteoarthritis

Heberden’s nodes are bony enlargements of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints and are a classical feature of osteoarthritis (OA). They result from osteophyte (bony spur) formation due to degeneration of the articular cartilage and are commonly seen in elderly women.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Rheumatoid arthritis: Typically involves the MCP and PIP joints, while the DIP joints are usually spared. Rheumatoid nodules are found over pressure points, not at the DIP joints.
• C. Psoriatic arthritis: Can involve the DIP joints, but is associated with dactylitis, nail pitting, and pencil-in-cup deformity, not Heberden’s nodes.
• D. Gouty arthritis: Characterized by tophi and recurrent episodes of acute monoarthritis, most commonly involving the first MTP joint (podagra).
