questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A farmer adds a chemical to a water pool that acts by inhibiting cellular respiration. The substance specifically targets Complex III of the electron transport chain, disrupting electron transfer and proton gradient formation required for ATP synthesis. Which chemical produces this effect by inhibiting Complex III?
questions.explanation: Antimycin A is a well-known antibiotic and piscicide (fish poison) that specifically inhibits Complex III (ubiquinone-cytochrome c oxidoreductase) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. By binding to the Qi site, it blocks the transfer of electrons from cytochrome b to cytochrome c1, effectively halting the generation of the proton gradient necessary for ATP synthesis. Rotenone (Option A) is an insecticide that inhibits Complex I. TTFA (Option B, thenoyltrifluoroacetone) is a specific inhibitor of Complex II. Cyanide (Option D) is a lethal poison that inhibits Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) by binding to the heme iron. Understanding these specific inhibitors is fundamental for biochemistry and toxicology. Antimycin is often used in laboratory research to isolate the functions of different segments of the respiratory chain. For the farmer's use in a "water pool" as a piscicide, Antimycin's mechanism of action is the defining characteristic
questions.learning: Antimycin — A is a well-known antibiotic and piscicide (fish poison) that specifically inhibits Complex III (ubiquinone-cytochrome c oxidoreductase) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following about Minimal Access Surgery are correct? I. Decreased intraoperative heat loss II. Improved visualization III. Increased chances of herniation IV. Improved mobility Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and IV

Minimal Access Surgery (MAS), also known as laparoscopic surgery, is performed through small incisions using a camera and specialized instruments. Compared with open surgery, MAS is associated with reduced surgical trauma, faster recovery, less postoperative pain, and shorter hospital stay.

The following statements are true:

• I. Decreased intraoperative heat loss: Smaller incisions and reduced exposure of abdominal viscera result in less evaporative heat loss, thereby reducing intraoperative hypothermia.
• II. Improved visualization: The laparoscope provides magnified, high-definition visualization, allowing better identification of anatomical structures and meticulous dissection.
• IV. Improved mobility: Patients experience less postoperative pain, allowing earlier ambulation, reduced pulmonary complications, and faster recovery.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. Increased chances of herniation: Laparoscopic surgery is associated with a lower incidence of incisional hernias because of the small port-site incisions. Although port-site hernias can occur, they are uncommon and mainly seen with ports ≥10 mm if fascial closure is inadequate.
questions.learning: I, II and IV Minimal Access Surgery (MAS), also known as laparoscopic surgery, is performed through small incisions using a camera and specialized instruments.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient develops endophthalmitis following cataract surgery. On examination, visual acuity is limited to hand movements. Based on this level of vision, what is the appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Postoperative endophthalmitis is a devastating intraocular infection and an ophthalmic emergency. The management strategy is largely determined by the patient's initial visual acuity, based on the landmark Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS). If the vision is "hand movements" (HM) or better, the recommended first-line treatment is immediate Intravitreal antibiotic injections (typically vancomycin and ceftazidime) and a diagnostic vitreous tap. Pars plana vitrectomy (Option B) is only indicated as the initial treatment if the vision is "Light Perception" (LP) or worse, although it may be performed later if the condition fails to improve with injections. Redo surgery (Option C) is not a treatment for infection. Topical antibiotics (Option D) are used as an adjunct but are insufficient for treating the deep intraocular infection. Early intervention with intravitreal drugs is vital to sterilize the eye and prevent total vision loss. Patients must also be started on intensive topical fortified antibiotics and sometimes systemic steroids
questions.learning: Postoperative endophthalmitis is a devastating intraocular infection and an ophthalmic emergency. The management strategy is largely determined by the patient's initial visual acuity, based on the landmark Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: For a 52-year-old woman receiving radiotherapy for stage IIB carcinoma of the cervix, which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Point B is 3 cm lateral to point A
Point A is 2 cm above the external os and 5 cm lateral to the internal uterine canal
Point A receives a dose of 7000 cGy
Point B received a dose of 6000 cGy
questions.explanation: In cervical cancer brachytherapy, Point A and Point B are critical reference points for dose calculation. Point A is defined as being 2 cm superior to the vaginal lateral fornix (external os) and 2 cm lateral (NOT 5 cm) to the uterine canal. This point represents the intersection of the ureter and the uterine artery, making its dose critical for both tumor control and safety. Statement B is therefore incorrect. Point B is indeed 3 cm lateral to Point A (total 5 cm from the midline) and represents the dose delivered to the pelvic side wall and lymph nodes (Option A). In standard protocols, Point A typically receives a cumulative curative dose of approximately 7000–8500 cGy (Option C), while Point B receives significantly less, usually around 4500–6000 cGy (Option D). Therefore, the 5 cm lateral definition for Point A is the definitively inaccurate statement
questions.learning: In cervical cancer brachytherapy, Point — A and Point B are critical reference points for dose calculation. Point A is defined as being 2 cm superior to the vaginal lateral fornix (external os) and 2 cm lateral (NOT 5 cm) to the uterine canal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An 18 month old child is brought with no history of vaccination. From the following, which vaccines would be appropriate to give this child according to the National Immunization Schedule (NIS), India?
options: BCG, DPT-1, OPV-1, Measles – 1, Vit. A -1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. DPT-1, OPV-1, Measles – 1, Vit. A – 1

• An 18 month old, completely un-immunized child should receive first doses of DPT, OPV, measles vaccine and vitamin A, according to the National Immunization Schedule (NIS), India.
• BCG can be given only up to one year of age.
questions.learning: A – 1 • — An 18 month old, completely un-immunized child should receive first doses of DPT, OPV, measles vaccine and vitamin A, according to the National Immunization Schedule (NIS), India. • BCG can be given only up to one year of age.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A hypertensive pregnant woman with abdominal pain, bleeding per vaginum, and loss of fetal movements. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abruptio placenta

The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vaginum, and loss of fetal movements in a hypertensive pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

Placenta previa (option B) refers to when the placenta is implanted partially or completely over the internal os and it usually presents with painless vaginal bleeding.

Hydramnios (option C) refers to a state where the volume of amniotic fluid exceeds 2000mL and it does not present with bleeding per vaginum.

In preterm labor (option D) fetal movements are not compromised.

Abruptio placenta is the partial/total placental separation from its implantation site before delivery. The bleeding may be:

• Revealed (blood dissects downwards between membranes and uterine wall to escape through the cervix)
• Concealed (blood accumulates between the detached placenta and uterus)

Hypertension in pregnancy is the most important risk factor for abruptio placenta. Patients often present with sudden onset abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness, and frequent contractions.

The hemorrhage into decidua basalis causes separation and compression of the placenta. This leads to a compromise of circulation to the fetus, leading to fetal distress.

Clinical classification of placental abruption:

Grade 1
Grade 2
Grade 3

Vaginal bleeding is slight
Vaginal bleeding mild to moderate
Bleeding is moderate to severe or concealed.

Uterus irritable, minimal tenderness

Uterine tenderness is always present
Uterine tenderness is marked.

Maternal BP and fibrinogen unaffected
Maternal pulse increased, BP maintained
Shock is pronounced

FHS good
Fetal distress present
Fetal death is the rule

Maternal shock absent
Maternal shock absent
Associated coagulation defect or anuria may complicate
questions.learning: Abruptio placenta — The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vaginum, and loss of fetal movements in a hypertensive pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most appropriate immediate management for a 25-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident who has a respiratory rate of 25/min, blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg, and hyper-resonance on the left side of the chest?
options: Wide bore needle insertion in the right 5th ICS
Wide bore needle insertion in the left 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits the life-threatening triad of a Tension Pneumothorax: respiratory distress (RR 25), obstructive shock (BP 80/45 mmHg), and hyper-resonance on the affected side . Tension pneumothorax occurs when a one-way valve allows air into the pleural space but not out, causing mediastinal shift and compromising venous return to the heart. Immediate decompression is mandatory. Modern ATLS guidelines recommend needle decompression at the 5th intercostal space (ICS) at the anterior axillary line, which must be immediately followed by the insertion of an intercostal chest tube. Option A is incorrect as the clinical findings are on the left side. Option C is inappropriate as the pathology involves air, not fluid. Option D is incorrect as the condition is fatal if not treated immediately. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; treatment must never be delayed for radiographic confirmation
questions.learning: The patient exhibits the life-threatening triad of a Tension Pneumothorax: respiratory distress (RR 25), obstructive shock (BP 80/45 mmHg), and hyper-resonance on the affected side .

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A group of experts each delivers an individual speech on a common topic without any discussion among them, and one person provides a summary at the end. What is this type of academic session called?
options: Workshop (B) Symposium A Symposium is an academic session where multiple experts present prepared individual speeches or papers on different aspects of a single common topic. A defining characteristic of a symposium is the lack of interaction or discussion between the experts themselves during the presentations; instead, a chairperson or moderator provides a summary of the key points at the conclusion. In a Panel Discussion (Option A), the experts interact with each other and often engage in a Q&A session with the audience. A Seminar (Option C) is usually a more interactive study session for a smaller group led by an expert. A Workshop (Option D) emphasizes hands-on, practical training and active participation by all attendees to learn a specific skill. Therefore, the "serial speech" format without inter-panel discussion is specific to a symposium.
questions.explanation: A Symposium is an academic session where multiple experts present prepared individual speeches or papers on different aspects of a single common topic. A defining characteristic of a symposium is the lack of interaction or discussion between the experts themselves during the presentations; instead, a chairperson or moderator provides a summary of the key points at the conclusion. In a Panel Discussion (Option A), the experts interact with each other and often engage in a Q&A session with the audience. A Seminar (Option C) is usually a more interactive study session for a smaller group led by an expert. A Workshop (Option D) emphasizes hands-on, practical training and active participation by all attendees to learn a specific skill. Therefore, the "serial speech" format without inter-panel discussion is specific to a symposium. A chronic smoker with a 20-year occupational history of working in a cement factory develops mesothelioma. This association is most likely attributable to which exposure? (A) Bagassosis (B) Silicosis (C) Asbestosis (D) Coal worker pneumoconiosis
questions.learning: A Symposium is an academic session where multiple experts present prepared individual speeches or papers on different aspects of a single common topic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old female patient came with complaints of chest pain, palpitation, and shortness of breath. On examination, a mid-diastolic murmur was heard, and a prominent 'a' wave was found on JVP. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tricuspid stenosis

The presence of a mid-diastolic murmur and a prominent a-wave in JVP is suggestive of tricuspid stenosis.

Mid-diastolic murmurs result from obstruction and/or augmented flow at the level of the mitral or tricuspid valve. Thus, both mitral stenosis (MS) and tricuspid stenosis (TS) present with a mid-diastolic murmur. However, the presence of a prominent a-wave in JVP points toward tricuspid stenosis.

Causes for mid-diastolic murmur:

1. Mitral stenosis
2. Tricuspid stenosis
3. Atrial myxomas
4. Austin Flint murmur in severe aortic regurgitation
5. Carey-Coombs murmur in acute rheumatic fever

Tricuspid stenosis:

It always occurs in association with MS and is rheumatic in origin. Mid-diastolic murmur in TS is best heard along the left sternal border and over the xiphoid process. Murmur is augmented during inspiration and reduced during expiration. The jugular veins are distended, and a giant a-wave is seen in JVP. There is a slow y descent due to impedance of right atrial emptying during diastole. ECG shows features of right atrial enlargement, which includes tall, peaked P wave in lead II and a prominent, upright P wave in lead V1.

Other options:

Option A: Mid-diastolic murmur is seen in mitral stenosis (MS). It occurs most commonly in rheumatic fever. Loud S1 (first heart sound) with an opening snap and a following S2 (second heart sound) is heard. S2 is followed by a low-pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur, which is best heard at the apex with the patient in a lateral recumbent position.

Option C: Holosystolic murmur is seen in mitral regurgitation (MR). The major causes of MR are infective endocarditis, myocardial infarction, rheumatic fever, and cardiomyopathies. Soft S1 with a widely split S2 and a low-pitched S3 (third heart sound) is heard in MR. In addition, a holosystolic murmur is prominent at the apex and radiates to the axilla.

Option D: Holosystolic murmur is seen in tricuspid regurgitation (TR). TR is most commonly due to functional defects such as tricuspid annular dilatation and leaflet tethering caused by rheumatic heart disease, myocardial infarction, etc. The jugular vein is distended. Prominent c-v waves and rapid y descents are seen in severe TR. A blowing holosystolic murmur along the lower left sternal margin, which is augmented during inspiration (Carvallo's sign) and reduced during expiration is seen in TR.
questions.learning: Tricuspid stenosis — The presence of a mid-diastolic murmur and a prominent a-wave in JVP is suggestive of tricuspid stenosis. Mid-diastolic murmurs result from obstruction and/or augmented flow at the level of the mitral or tricuspid valve.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Oligohydramnios is associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Renal agenesis

Oligohydramnios is associated with renal agenesis.

Oligohydramnios is a condition where the liquor amnii is deficient in an amount to the extent of less than 200mL at term.

Sonographically, it is defined when the maximum vertical pocket of liquor is less than <2 cm or when amniotic fluid index (AFI) is less than 5 cm (less than 5 percentile).

Fetal urine production begins between 8-11 weeks but it does not become a major component of amniotic fluid until the 2nd trimester and is the major part of amniotic fluid after 20 weeks. In a case of renal agenesis, there is decreased or no urine output leading to oligohydramnios, which does not manifest till after 18 weeks.

Etiology of oligohydramnios:

* Placental condition:

* Amnion nodosum (failure of secretion by the cells of the amnion covering the placenta).

* Fetal conditions:

* Fetal chromosomal or structural anomalies

* Renal agenesis

* Obstructed uropathy

* Spontaneous rupture of membrane

* Intrauterine infection

* Drugs (PG inhibitors, ACE inhibitors)

* Post maturity

* IUGR

* Maternal conditions:

* Hypertensive disorders

* Uteroplacental insufficiency

* Dehydration

* Idiopathic

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient came with a history of dyspnea. His CT scan is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
options: Mediastinal mass with fat and calcification
This is characteristic of mediastinal Hydatid cyst
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mediastinal mass with fat and calcification

In a patient with dyspnea, a CT scan shows a mediastinal mass with an attenuation of -62 HU, indicative of fat content, along with areas of calcification. This suggests the presence of a mediastinal mass comprised of fat and calcified tissue.

Thymic neoplasms usually are detected in the anterior mediastinum. Fewer than 4% of thymic tumors occur in the middle mediastinum, defined as mediastinal space surrounded by the left brachiocephalic vein, superior vena cava, esophagus, trachea, and main bronchus up to the cross-section of the left brachiocephalic vein and the center of the trachea. Thymic carcinoma is a rare thymic neoplasm. Moreover, few reports of middle mediastinal thymic carcinomas are histopathologically diagnosed as having immunohistochemical features.

Other options:

Option A: The CT shows a mediastinal mass but no clear evidence of vascular invasion.

Option B: It shows a picture of a mediastinal mass rather than aorta.

Option D: A mediastinal hydatid cyst on a chest CT can confirm the diagnosis by objectifying a mass of fluid density, often very limited, unmodified by the injection of contrast, however, contrast uptake by a pericyst can be observed. The presence of peripheral calcifications supports the diagnosis. A predilection for the posterior compartment of the mediastinum has been reported in the literature.
questions.learning: Mediastinal mass with fat and calcification — In a patient with dyspnea, a CT scan shows a mediastinal mass with an attenuation of -62 HU, indicative of fat content, along with areas of calcification.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents to you with left-sided flank pain. A CT scan was done which is shown below. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the condition?
options: Cyst contents can produce anaphylactic reaction
A segmented dog tapeworm is the causative agent
FNAC or biopsy to be done before nephrectomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. FNAC or biopsy to be done before nephrectomy

FNAC or biopsy to be done before nephrectomy is the incorrect statement regarding cystic echinococcosis. The given CT image shows left-sided renal hydatid cyst.

Echinococcosis (hydatidosis) is caused by Echinococcus granulosus (larval stage). It is a segmented tapeworm. Dogs are the definitive hosts and pass the eggs in their feces. Intermediate hosts include humans, sheep, and cattle. Patients present with abdominal pain, palpable mass, jaundice, cough, and dyspnea. Rupture of a hydatic cyst can result in fever, pruritus, or anaphylaxis.

Daughter cysts within the larger cyst seen on CT imaging is diagnostic. A biopsy is not recommended because of the risk of fluid leakage which can result in anaphylaxis or dissemination of the infection.

Percutaneous aspiration, infusion of scolicidal agents, and reaspiration (PAIR) is the primary treatment. It is contraindicated in superficial loculated cysts and in cysts that communicate with the biliary tree.

Isolated involvement of the kidneys is rare. Patients can present with nonspecific symptoms, renal colic, and hydatiduria. Due to the lack of an effective systemic scolicidal agent, surgical treatment is necessary when kidneys are involved. Simple excision of the cyst is preferred. If there is extensive involvement, partial or total nephrectomy is warranted. It is recommended to start albendazole one week to one month before the surgery to decrease the risk of spillage.
questions.learning: FNAC or biopsy to be done before nephrectomy FNAC or biopsy to be done before nephrectomy is the incorrect statement regarding cystic echinococcosis. The given CT image shows left-sided renal hydatid cyst.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for an overactive bladder in a patient with dementia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tolterodine

Overactive bladder is treated with antimuscarinic agents that reduce detrusor overactivity. Tolterodine has relative bladder selectivity and less CNS penetration, making it safer in dementia. Tiotropium is for COPD, tropicamide is ophthalmic, and telenzepine is gastric selective. Tolterodine provides urinary control with fewer cognitive effects.

B) Tiotropium

No urinary role

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with a lump in the upper outer quadrant of her breast. Histopathological examination of the mass showed cells in mucin pools and faint nuclei. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Colloid carcinoma

The given scenario is suggestive of colloid or mucinous carcinoma of the breast.

Colloid carcinoma is an invasive breast carcinoma, which shows intracellular and extracellular mucin deposition.

On histopathological examination, extracellular type shows tumor cells with faint nuclei, arranged in clusters, floating in lakes or pools of mucin. In intracellular type, nuclei are pushed to the periphery to form a signet ring appearance.

Option B: Microscopic image of papillary carcinoma of the breast showing true papillae with a leaf-like arrangement of fibrovascular tissue lined by the tumor cells is shown below.

Option C: Microscopic image of medullary carcinoma of the breast consisting of sheets of highly pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures (anaplastic cells), lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate is shown below.

Option D: Microscopic image of lobular carcinoma of the breast shows infiltrating small monomorphic discohesive tumor cells arranged in an Indian-file or single-file pattern is shown below.
questions.learning: Colloid carcinoma — The given scenario is suggestive of colloid or mucinous carcinoma of the breast. Colloid carcinoma is an invasive breast carcinoma, which shows intracellular and extracellular mucin deposition.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Identify the correct statement regarding gastric carcinoma.

1. It is mostly hereditary.
2. E-cadherin adhesion defect is seen in diffuse-type of gastric CA.
3. Wnt signaling pathway defect is seen in intestinal-type gastric CA.
4. Depth of cancer has no role in prognosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3

The correct statements regarding gastric carcinoma are 2 and 3.

Most cases of gastric cancer are sporadic (statement 1).

Lauren's system classifies gastric cancer into Type I - intestinal and Type II - diffuse.

At the molecular level,

• the diffuse-type is characterized by decreased E-cadherin mainly due to loss-of-function mutations in the CDH1 gene (statement 2).
• the intestinal type of cancer is characterized by mutations in the APC gene or β-catenin  causes increased signaling via the Wnt pathway (statement 3).

Symptoms of both types include nausea, dyspepsia, dysphagia, weight loss, anorexia, early satiety, and anemia.

The image below shows the histopathological appearances of intestinal and diffuse types of gastric carcinoma:

Endoscopy and biopsy of the lesion (gold standard) are performed to diagnose gastric carcinoma.

When possible, surgery remains the preferred treatment approach. Local invasion into the duodenum, pancreas, and retroperitoneum is common, where chemo or radiation therapy with palliative care is the treatment.

The TNM staging is most widely used. It uses depth of invasion along with nodal and distant metastases as prognostic indicators (statement 4).
questions.learning: 2, 3 The correct statements regarding gastric carcinoma are 2 and 3. Most cases of gastric cancer are sporadic (statement 1).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: FAST stands for __________________
options: First assessment with sonography in trauma
Focussed assessment with sonography in trauma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Focussed assessment with sonography in trauma

FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography in Trauma.

It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries. It can be performed within 2-4 minutes.

Technique:

• The patient is placed in a supine position and the following regions are scanned:

• Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries
• Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch
• Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury
• Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Limitations of eFAST are:

1. Operator-dependent
2. Bowel gas and subcutaneous air distort images.
3. Can miss diaphragm, bowel, and pancreatic injuries
4. Unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum
5. Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma
6. May need repeating or supplementing with other investigations
questions.learning: Focussed assessment with sonography in trauma FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography in Trauma. It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A particular community population has been consuming Maize as a staple diet for years. The vitamin deficiency most likely to be seen in this population is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Niacin

A maize-based staple diet is classically associated with niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, leading to pellagra.

Maize is deficient in tryptophan and contains niacin in a bound, poorly absorbable form, especially when not processed by alkali treatment.

This results in the characteristic triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia, making niacin deficiency the most likely outcome.
questions.learning: Niacin — A maize-based staple diet is classically associated with niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, leading to pellagra. Maize is deficient in tryptophan and contains niacin in a bound, poorly absorbable form, especially when not processed by alkali treatment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following options is not a physiological function of glucagon?
questions.explanation: Glucagon is a catabolic hormone secreted by the pancreatic alpha cells in response to low blood glucose levels. Its primary goal is to increase blood sugar by acting on the liver. Glucagon stimulates gluconeogenesis (synthesis of new glucose) (Option B) and glycogenolysis (breakdown of stored glycogen) (Option C). It also promotes ketogenesis (production of ketone bodies) (Option D) as an alternative energy source. Critically, glucagon inhibits glycolysis (Option A) in the liver to prevent the immediate consumption of the glucose it is trying to produce. By inhibiting key glycolytic enzymes like phosphofructokinase-1, glucagon ensures that glucose is exported to the systemic circulation rather than broken down into pyruvate. Therefore, while the other processes mentioned are stimulated by glucagon to maintain energy balance during fasting, glycolysis is the only pathway listed that it actively suppresses
questions.learning: Glucagon is a catabolic hormone secreted by the pancreatic alpha cells in response to low blood glucose levels. Its primary goal is to increase blood sugar by acting on the liver.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman with no other comorbid conditions develops preeclampsia. She enquires about the cause. The doctor explains that it is due to the failure of the invasion of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spiral artery by extravillous trophoblasts

During early pregnancy, Extravillous Trophoblast invade the maternal uterine vessels. Their role is to remodel the maternal spiral arteries.

Extravillous trophoblast invasion

↓

Remodeling of spiral arteries

↓

Low resistance vessels

↓

Adequate placental blood flow

This transformation converts narrow spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance vessels.

In Preeclampsia:

Failure of trophoblastic invasion

↓

Spiral arteries remain narrow

↓

High resistance blood flow

↓

Placental ischemia

↓

Release of antiangiogenic factors

↓

Maternal endothelial dysfunction

↓

Hypertension and proteinuria

Preeclampsia results from abnormal spiral artery remodeling.

Spiral arteries supply the placenta and intervillous space. Their remodeling is crucial for:

• Adequate uteroplacental circulation
• Proper fetal growth

Failure leads to:

• Preeclampsia
• Fetal growth restriction

A) Spiral artery by villous trophoblasts

Villous Trophoblast

• Responsible for maternal–fetal exchange, not arterial invasion.

B) Radial artery by cytotrophoblasts

• Radial arteries are not the primary vessels remodeled in pregnancy.

D) Arcuate artery by extravillous trophoblasts

• Arcuate arteries lie deeper in the uterus and do not undergo trophoblastic remodeling.
questions.learning: Spiral artery by extravillous trophoblasts During early pregnancy, Extravillous Trophoblast invade the maternal uterine vessels. Their role is to remodel the maternal spiral arteries.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the image shown?
options: Only the roots of this plant are poisonous
Drug of choice for poisoning is Atropine
Mitha zaher is one of the variety of this plant
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Only the roots of this plant are poisonous

The image is of aconite. All parts of this plant (especially the roots and seeds) are poisonous.

Varieties of this plant are monkhood, mitha zaher, bish, and bikh.

It is a cardiac poison and causes AV block, bradycardia. Atropine is used in the treatment of its toxicity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A middle aged cement factory worker has developed mesothelioma. This is likely to be associated with
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asbestosis

Mesothelioma is classically associated with asbestos exposure, leading to asbestosis. Asbestos fibers cause chronic pleural inflammation and malignant transformation of mesothelial cells.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is part of trotter's triad, seen in nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
options: Conductive hearing loss, Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis
Sensorineural hearing loss, Contralateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis
Sensorineural hearing loss, Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis
Conductive hearing loss, Contralateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Conductive hearing loss, Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis

Trotter’s triad seen in nasopharyngeal carcinoma consists of conductive hearing loss, ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia, and palatal paralysis.

Trotter’s triad consists of the following:

* Conductive hearing loss due to Eustachian tube obstruction.

* Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia due to involvement of the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) which presents as facial pain.

* Palatal paralysis, due to involvement of the vagus nerve(CN X) which presents as palatal asymmetry.
questions.learning: Conductive hearing loss, Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia,Palatal paralysis Trotter’s triad seen in nasopharyngeal carcinoma consists of conductive hearing loss, ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia, and palatal paralysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A full-term newborn is noted on routine screening to have elevated TSH and low thyroxine (T4) levels. The infant appears clinically well. Imaging reveals a small ectopic thyroid gland located near the base of the tongue. Early initiation of thyroid hormone replacement therapy is most important to prevent which of the following complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Impaired neurocognitive development

This newborn has congenital hypothyroidism, most commonly due to thyroid dysgenesis (ectopic or absent thyroid gland).

Thyroid hormone is essential for:

• Neuronal migration
• Myelination
• Synapse formation

Deficiency during early life leads to:

• Irreversible intellectual disability (cretinism)
• Developmental delay
• Growth retardation

Early treatment with levothyroxine (within the first 2 weeks of life) prevents these complications and allows normal neurodevelopment.
questions.learning: Impaired neurocognitive development — This newborn has congenital hypothyroidism, most commonly due to thyroid dysgenesis (ectopic or absent thyroid gland).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A person who met with an accident, and suffered from a skull fracture presents with the following finding. Identify this clinical finding.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Battle sign

The given image shows ecchymosis over the retro auricular and mastoid area suggestive of Battle's sign. It is typically seen in fractures of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma. Battle sign is prominent when there is a fracture of the petrous temporal bone.

Other options:

Option B: Bezold abscess is a complication of acute otomastoiditis where the infection/pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck.

Option C: Acute mastoiditis is used to refer to an acute infection that spreads from the mucosa lining the mastoid air cells to involve the bony walls of the mastoid air cell system. Mastoiditis presents as retro-auricular redness and swelling which is painful.

The image below shows a smooth ironed-out mastoid with erythema seen in acute mastoiditis.

Option D: The Griesinger sign refers to edema of the postauricular soft tissues overlying the mastoid process as a result of thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein seen in sagittal sinus thrombosis. It is a complication of acute otomastoiditis.
questions.learning: Battle sign — The given image shows ecchymosis over the retro auricular and mastoid area suggestive of Battle's sign. It is typically seen in fractures of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
A study is conducted to identify the association between vaccination and the development of a disease in a community. Based on the data, 6 vaccinated individuals and 12 unvaccinated individuals developed severe disease. Calculate the relative risk for this community.

Developed disease
Didn't develop disease
Total

Vaccinated
6

100

Non vaccinated

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 0.5

The relative risk in this case will be 0.5.

Relative risk is the ratio of the incidence of disease (or death) among exposed and the incidence among non-exposed. It is a direct measure of the strength of the association between suspected cause and effect in a cohort study.

Here,

Incidence of disease among exposed (Vaccinated) = 6

Incidence of disease among non-exposed (Unvaccinated) = 12

Relative risk (RR) = Incidence exposed/incidence unexposed = 6/12 = 0.5

Relative Risk

* The ratio of incidence of disease or death among exposed to that among the non-exposed is called relative risk (RR).

* It is also called the risk ratio.

* It is the direct measure of the strength of association between suspected cause and effect in cohort studies.

* RR = 1 indicates no association.

* RR of 2 or higher indicates a 100% increase in risk.

Pearl PF2127: Relative and Attributable Risk

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the function of the biceps brachii muscle during flexion of the forearm?
questions.explanation: When a muscle provides the majority of the force required to perform a specific movement, it is classified as the primary mover, or agonist. In the act of elbow flexion (lifting the forearm), the biceps brachii serves as the primary mover. It contracts concentrically to pull the radius toward the humerus, effectively bending the elbow joint. A synergistic muscle (Option A), such as the brachialis, assists the primary mover in its action. A fixator muscle (Option B) stabilizes the origin of the primary mover, such as the rotator cuff muscles stabilizing the shoulder during arm movement. An antagonist muscle (Option C), in this case the triceps brachii, must relax and yield to the movement of the primary mover. Because the biceps brachii is the dominant muscle responsible for the deliberate lifting of the forearm, its role is definitively defined as the primary mover
questions.learning: When a muscle provides the majority of the force required to perform a specific movement, it is classified as the primary mover, or agonist. In the act of elbow flexion (lifting the forearm), the biceps brachii serves as the primary mover.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following features differentiates the exocrine pancreas from the parotid gland?
options: Basal lamina lining the serous acini
Presence of serous acini with acidophilic tip
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absence of striated duct

Absence of striated duct in exocrine pancreas differentiates it from the parotid gland.

The exocrine pancreas is comprised entirely of serous acini. Hence, its general structure is similar to that of the parotid gland, but the two are easily distinguished by:

• The parotid gland has striated and intercalated intralobular ducts, whereas the pancreas has only the intercalated type.
• The excretory ducts of the parotid gland are striated columnar, whereas the excretory duct of the pancreas is a simple columnar.
questions.learning: Absence of striated duct Absence of striated duct in exocrine pancreas differentiates it from the parotid gland. The exocrine pancreas is comprised entirely of serous acini.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A nulligravida woman presents to the outpatient department with uterine prolapse. There is no evidence of associated cystocele or rectocele on examination. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abdominal sling surgery

For a nulligravid woman with uterine prolapse and no cystocele or rectocele, we will perform an abdominal sling surgery.

Abdominal sling operations are designed for women with type II or III degree prolapse and who are desirous of retaining childbearing function and menstrual function.

The descent of one or more of the genital organs below their normal anatomical position is called pelvic organ prolapse (POP). It occurs when the muscles and tissues that support the pelvic organs become weakened or damaged, leading to one or more organs bulging into the vaginal canal.

Clinical types are:

1. Vaginal prolapse

a) Anterior vaginal wall

*

*

* Upper two-thirds – Cystocele

* Lower one-third – Urethrocele

b) Posterior vaginal wall

*

*

* Upper one-third – Enterocele

* Lower two-thirds – Rectocele

2. Uterine descent

Treatment options may include pessary, pelvic floor exercises or surgery depending on the severity of prolapse.

Abdominal sling surgeries: Young women desirous of retaining menstrual and reproductive functions are ideal candidates. These surgeries use tapes as slings to prevent organ descent. These include:

* Abdominal wall cervicopexy (modified by Purandare and Mathre): sling attached to cervix posteriorly near uterosacral ligaments.

* Shirodkar's sling surgery: the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia.

* Khanna's sling surgery: - sling fixed to the anterior superior iliac spine, strengthening the Mackenrodt's ligament.

Other options :

Option A: Le fort's repair - is done in patients who satisfy the following criteria:

* Very elderly menopausal patient with an advanced prolapse

* Do not wish to retain sexual function

* Medically unfit for major surgeries

Option B: Fothergill surgery - Also known as Manchester's operation is suitable for women under 40 years who are desirous of retaining their menstrual and reproductive functions. It involves anterior colporrhaphy with amputation of the cervix. The mackenrodt ligaments are sutured in the front of the cervix and colpoperineorrhaphy is done. It increases the risk of cervical incompetence leading to recurrent abortions and preterm deliveries. Shirodkar's modification of Fothergill's repair avoids cervical amputation, hence subsequent pregnancy complications are avoided.

Option D: Shirodkar sling surgery - the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient under general anesthesia is identified to be in a “cannot intubate, cannot ventilate” (CICV) situation. What is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?
questions.explanation: A "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" (CICV) scenario is a critical anesthesia emergency that requires an immediate surgical airway to prevent hypoxic brain injury. An emergency cricothyroidotomy is the fastest and most reliable method because the cricothyroid membrane is superficial and easy to access quickly. Nasopharyngeal airways (Option A) and laryngeal mask airways (Option C) are non-invasive measures that by definition have already failed in a CICV state. A tracheostomy (Option D) is a complex surgical procedure that takes significantly more time to perform than a cricothyroidotomy and is not suitable for a rapid hypoxic emergency. Therefore, cricothyroidotomy is the mandated life-saving intervention
questions.learning: A "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" (CICV) scenario is a critical anesthesia emergency that requires an immediate surgical airway to prevent hypoxic brain injury.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 2-week-old girl is brought to her primary care provider for a routine visit. Newborn screening results from hemoglobin electrophoresis are as follows: Hemoglobin F: 70% Hemoglobin A: 20% Hemoglobin S: 10% Examination shows a well-appearing infant with no pallor or splenomegaly. Which of the following is most likely true about this patient?
options: Life expectancy will be shorter than average
Mean corpuscular volume will be decreased
She has relative protection from Plasmodium falciparum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. She has relative protection from Plasmodium falciparum

A 2-week-old infant with Hemoglobin F = 70% is completely normal.

At birth, HbF makes up about 60–80% of total hemoglobin. It gradually declines over the first 6 months as HbA increases.

So this electrophoresis result is physiologic, not pathologic.

Now let’s evaluate the options:

• Life expectancy shorter than average → ❌ No disease indicated.
• Mean corpuscular volume decreased → ❌ Not suggested here.
• Reticulocyte count elevated → ❌ No hemolysis present.
• Relative protection from Plasmodium falciparum → ✅ Correct.

Because:

HbF interferes with the growth of P. falciparum inside red blood cells.

That’s why newborns (and people with persistent HbF like in sickle cell disease treated with hydroxyurea) have some protection against severe malaria.

Why does HbF not let P. Falciparum survive inside rbcs?

Ans: Parasite-infected RBCs normally stick to vascular endothelium (via PfEMP1).

HbF-containing RBCs show reduced expression of these adhesive proteins, meaning:

Less sequestration → milder disease.
questions.learning: She has relative protection from Plasmodium falciparum A 2-week-old infant with Hemoglobin F = 70% is completely normal. At birth, HbF makes up about 60–80% of total hemoglobin.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is related to Navjat Shishu Suraksha karyakram?
questions.explanation: The Navjat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (NSSK) is a national program in India specifically designed to improve the survival rates of the Newborn population. The program focuses on providing essential newborn care and basic resuscitation training to healthcare providers who attend births at all levels of the healthcare system. The primary interventions include the prevention of hypothermia, prevention of infection, initiation of early breastfeeding, and basic newborn resuscitation using a bag and mask. While the health of the Mother (Option A) and Pregnant woman (Option D) is closely linked to neonatal outcomes, they are the focus of separate programs like Janani Suraksha Yojana. The term Children (Option B) usually refers to an older age group handled under programs like the IMNCI. NSSK specifically targets the first few minutes and hours of life, which are the most critical for reducing the high neonatal mortality rate. Ensuring that every birth is attended by a trained provider who can deliver these essential services is the program's ultimate goal
questions.learning: The Navjat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (NSSK) is a national program in India specifically designed to improve the survival rates of the Newborn population.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The given picture shows lesions found on the glans penis and pigmentation in the chin and oral cavity. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lichen sclerosis

White atrophic patches on the glans penis along with extragenital manifestations like hyperpigmentation of the face and oral mucosa are suggestive of lichen sclerosis.

Lichen sclerosis is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects the anogenital area. On the glans penis, it presents as white, atrophic patches that can become porcelain-white in appearance. The condition often shows extragenital manifestations, particularly hyperpigmentation in areas like the face and oral cavity. The disease process involves dermal sclerosis and atrophy of the epidermis, leading to characteristic whitish patches.

Treatment typically involves potent topical corticosteroids, and regular monitoring is necessary as there's a small risk of malignant transformation in longstanding cases.

Other options:

Option B: Condyloma acuminata is a genital infection caused by the human papillomavirus(HPV) commonly HPV‐6 and HPV‐11. HPV‐1 and HPV‐2 may also occur in genital warts. The lesions present as soft, pink, fleshy, anogenital warts. These growths may be pedunculated discrete or verrucous that coalesce to form large cauliflower-like growths. It commonly occurs on the glans, corona, and frenulum in men and the posterior fourchette in women.

Option C: Peyronie's disease is characterized by penile deformity, palpable penile plaques within the penis, erectile dysfunction, and pain on erection. It causes the penis to bend, usually towards the side of the plaque. It can be associated with Dupuytren's contracture.

Option D: Syphilis is primarily a sexually transmitted disease caused by Treponema palladium but vertical transmission is also possible. It commonly presents as a hard, painless genital ulcer with induration, followed by the development of rubbery enlargement of inguinal lymph nodes.
questions.learning: Lichen sclerosis White atrophic patches on the glans penis along with extragenital manifestations like hyperpigmentation of the face and oral mucosa are suggestive of lichen sclerosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitric oxide is synthesized from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. L - arginine

Nitric oxide is synthesized from arginine by a calcium-dependent reaction catalyzed by NO synthase.

The co-enzymes of NO synthase include FMN, FAD, Heme, and Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).

Pearl PF0661: Amino Acid Derivatives

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 16-month-old boy is found to weigh 8kg. A WHO growth chart(weight-for-age) is provided below. Plot the growth chart for this child. What is the most appropriate advice based on the plotted graph?
options: Severe malnutrition - refer to nutrition rehabilitation center
Moderate malnutrition - teach the mother on how to feed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Moderate malnutrition - teach the mother on how to feed

The weight for age of the child falls in between -2SD and -3SD as shown in the growth chart below, which is suggestive of moderate malnutrition and the mother should be taught to feed the baby properly.

The primary treatment in mild and moderate malnutrition involves providing sufficient protein and energy intake, with a recommended minimum of 150 kcal/kg/day. Nutritious home food is advised, and frequent feeding (up to 7 times a day) may be required to achieve the necessary energy intake. High-fat foods are often used to increase energy in therapeutic diets.

Animal-source foods, such as milk and eggs, are recommended by WHO as they provide necessary amino acids and nutrients. Plant-source foods like legumes and cereals can also be good protein sources. A slight increase in protein intake (3g/kg/day) is sufficient for catch-up growth with high energy intake. Milk and vegetable protein mixtures can be used as a protein source and adequate minerals and vitamins are also added.

Weight gain is the best measure of treatment efficacy for mild and moderate malnutrition.

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) should be referred to a hospital for proper management. Uncomplicated SAM can be managed at home under supervision. Complicated SAM should be treated as an inpatient.

Management of SAM is summarized in the image below.

The World Health Organization(WHO) has established international standards for normal child growth from birth to 5 years of age. The normalization of the anthropometric measures is done in terms of z-scores (standard deviation scores). The anthropometric indicators are marked in a growth chart which is compared with a reference curve.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

• Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition.
• High weight-for-height indicates overweight.
• Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.
• Low weight for the age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is used for the screening of wasting in children between 6 months to 5 years. In children aged 6 months to 5 years, MUAC <11.5cm is considered as severe malnutrition.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which among the following drugs is the new FDA approved immune check point inhibitor for carcinoma endometrium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pembrolizumab

The new FDA-approved immune checkpoint inhibitor for carcinoma endometrium is pembrolizumab.

Pembrolizumab acts by inhibiting programmed death receptor - 1 (PD-1) and was used for the treatment of advanced melanoma. Now, the FDA has approved the use of pembrolizumab for any cancer with mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency or high microsatellite instability (MSI-H).

On March 21, 2022, the food and drug administration approved pembrolizumab, as a single agent, for patients with advanced endometrial carcinoma that is microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) or mismatch repair deficient (dMMR), as determined by an FDA-approved test.

Other options:

Option A: Nivolumab is an immune checkpoint inhibitor that acts by inhibiting programmed death receptor - 1 (PD-1) and is used for the treatment of advanced melanoma and relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

Option C:  Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits the HER2 receptor. It is used in the treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer.

Option D: Ipilimumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to cytotoxic T lymphocyte–associated Protein 4 (CTLA-4) and is approved for the treatment of late-stage melanoma.
questions.learning: Pembrolizumab — The new FDA-approved immune checkpoint inhibitor for carcinoma endometrium is pembrolizumab. Pembrolizumab acts by inhibiting programmed death receptor - 1 (PD-1) and was used for the treatment of advanced melanoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked structure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medial pectoral nerve

The marked structure in the image is the medial pectoral nerve.

The given image shows the medial pectoral nerve arising from the medial cord of the brachial plexus. It also shows the axillary artery traversing inferior to the median pectoral nerve and the thoracoacromial artery. The medial pectoral nerve and the thoracoacromial artery both contribute to the neurovascular supply of the pectoral muscles.

After originating from the medial cord, the medial pectoral nerve passes anterior to the axillary artery. This nerve is specifically known for its anatomical path of piercing the pectoralis minor muscle before branching out to supply both the pectoralis minor and the pectoralis major muscles.
questions.learning: Medial pectoral nerve — The marked structure in the image is the medial pectoral nerve. The given image shows the medial pectoral nerve arising from the medial cord of the brachial plexus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the National Deworming Day?
questions.explanation: In India, National Deworming Day (NDD) is a nationwide initiative observed every year on 10th February. The program aims to deworm all children and adolescents aged 1–19 years to prevent Soil-Transmitted Helminths (STH) infections. A "mop-up" round is typically conducted on 15th February for those who missed the initial dose. While a second biannual round often occurs in August (Option B), 10th February is the officially designated primary National Deworming Day. Options C (10th March) and D (11th January) are not associated with this public health campaign. During NDD, single doses of Albendazole (400 mg) are administered in schools and Anganwadi centers. This initiative is crucial for reducing childhood anemia and improving overall nutritional status and educational outcomes. Therefore, 10th February is the specific date for this high-priority health intervention
questions.learning: In India, National Deworming Day (NDD) is a nationwide initiative observed every year on 10th February. The program aims to deworm all children and adolescents aged 1–19 years to prevent Soil-Transmitted Helminths (STH) infections.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman with a history of chronic cholecystitis recently underwent cholecystectomy and now presents with worsening digestive symptoms. What is the most common post-cholecystectomy complication that could explain her complaints?
questions.explanation: Following a cholecystectomy, the body no longer has a reservoir to store and concentrate bile. Bile now flows continuously and less efficiently into the small intestine. For some patients, this leads to malabsorption of fats, resulting in the most common long-term postoperative digestive complication: Steatorrhea (Option C). Steatorrhea is characterized by oily, foul-smelling stools and bloating. Acute kidney injury (Option A) and Osteoporosis (Option B) are unrelated to the removal of the gallbladder. While some epidemiological studies have suggested a very slight potential increase in the long-term risk of colorectal cancer (Option D), it is not a "common complication" that would explain immediate worsening of digestive issues after surgery. Therefore, the physiological loss of bile storage and its impact on fat digestion identifies steatorrhea as the definitive clinical consequence described. Management typically involves dietary modifications, such as consuming smaller, lower-fat meals to improve digestion
questions.learning: Following a cholecystectomy, the body no longer has a reservoir to store and concentrate bile. Bile now flows continuously and less efficiently into the small intestine.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 56-year-old female patient presented with progressive dysphagia for solids, loss of weight, and loss of appetite. A barium swallow done is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carcinoma esophagus

A patient with the given history and barium swallow findings of irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction, and shouldered margins of esophagus, are suggestive of carcinoma esophagus.

Esophageal carcinoma is more common in men, with tobacco use and alcohol being the strongest risk factors. The squamous cell carcinoma variant usually affects the upper 2/3rd, and the adenocarcinoma variant usually affects the lower 1/3rd of the esophagus. Clinical features include progressive dysphagia (most common), regurgitation of food, vomiting, odynophagia and weight loss.

On barium swallow, carcinoma esophagus presents with irregular narrowing and ulceration of esophagus. Flexible endoscopy with biopsy is preferred for confirmation of diagnosis. Contrast-enhanced CT and PET can be used to assess distant metastasis. Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) is the investigation of choice to assess tumor invasion and lymph node metastasis.

Other options:

Option B:  Diffuse esophageal spasm results in the corkscrew appearance of the esophagus on barium study.

Option C: Esophageal leiomyoma appears as a smooth, semilunar filling defect on barium swallow. it is seen as a discrete ovoid mass that is well outlined by barium.

Option D: Esophageal webs occur in the upper and middle esophagus as a thin membrane that can be identified by the translucent part on contrast radiology.
questions.learning: Carcinoma esophagus — A patient with the given history and barium swallow findings of irregular narrowing, mucosal destruction, and shouldered margins of esophagus, are suggestive of carcinoma esophagus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Marked structure is derived from the______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endocardial cushions

The structure marked is the membranous part of the interventricular septum. It is derived from endocardial cushions.

Endocardial cushions are soft tissue masses that protrude in the atrioventricular and conotruncal regions.

• Atrioventricular cushions are derived from overlying endocardial cells.
• The conotruncal cushions are derived from the neural crest cells.

Endocardial cushions contribute to the formation of:

• Atrial septa
• Ventricular septa (membranous portion)
• Atrioventricular canals
• Atrioventricular valves
• Aortic and pulmonary channels

Defects in endocardial cushion formation can result in cardiac malformations, including ASDs, VSDs, and defects involving the great vessels (transposition of the great vessels, common truncus arteriosus, and tetralogy of Fallot).
questions.learning: Endocardial cushions — The structure marked is the membranous part of the interventricular septum. It is derived from endocardial cushions.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which statement is false regarding late decelerations?
options: Starts after peak of uterine contraction and ends after uterine contraction ends
At least 10 beats, 2 times in a 20 min period above baseline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. At least 10 beats, 2 times in a 20 min period above baseline

The false statement about late decelerations among the given options, is option C- at least 10 beats, 2 times in a 20 min period above baseline.

Typically, a late deceleration causes a fall in the fetal heart rate (FHR) by a depth of <10 to 20 bpm below the baseline. It is usually not accompanied by accelerations (Option D).

Late decelerations are smooth, gradual, (Option B) symmetrical decline in the FHR that begins at or after the peak of uterine contraction and ends only after the contraction has ended (Option A).

It is usually indicative of uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia. Other causes of late decelerations include hypotension from epidural anesthesia, excessive use of oxytocin, maternal hypertension, diabetes, and placental abruption.

A late deceleration plus decreased variability in FHR is predictive of fetal acidemia and neonatal morbidity.

The given CTG shows late decelerations and it's relation with the uterine contraction.

The below CTG shows early decelerations. In early decelerations, the onset, it's nadir and the recovery of deceleration coincide with the beginning, peak, and ending of uterine contraction respectively.

Early decelerations are seen in fetal head compression. They typically cause a fall of ≤ 20 to 30 bpm below the baseline. These early decelerations are common during active labour and are benign in nature.

A variable deceleraton is a drop in the FHR that begins with the uterine contactions onset and reaches a nadir in <30 seconds.Its depth is ≥15 bpm in and the deceleration lasts between 15 seconds to 2 minutes.

The slope of FHR change is erratic, giving the wave form its jagged shape. A variable deceleration is indicative of umbilical cord occlusion.

The below CTG depicts variable deceleration.
questions.learning: At least 10 beats, 2 times in a 20 min period above baseline The false statement about late decelerations among the given options, is option C- at least 10 beats, 2 times in a 20 min period above baseline.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding an increase in Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)?
options: Increase in the resistance of the afferent arteriole
Decrease in the resistance of the efferent arteriole
Increase in Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure
questions.explanation: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is determined by the balance of Starling forces across the glomerular capillaries. An increase in renal perfusion (blood flow to the kidney) increases the hydrostatic pressure within the glomerular capillaries, which directly leads to an increase in GFR. Increasing the resistance of the afferent arteriole (Option A) would decrease flow and pressure, thus decreasing GFR. Decreasing the resistance of the efferent arteriole (Option B) allows blood to exit the glomerulus more easily, lowering the filtration pressure and decreasing GFR. Increasing Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure (Option C)—which might happen in a urinary tract obstruction—opposes filtration and decreases GFR. In essence, GFR is increased by anything that "pushes" more fluid out of the blood and into the capsule, primarily high glomerular capillary pressure. This pressure is regulated by the relative constriction or dilation of the afferent and efferent arterioles, a process known as renal autoregulation

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: “Objectives are set forth for different units and subunits, each of which prepares its own plan of action, usually on a short-term basis.” The definition best sums up which one among the following terms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Management by objectives

Management by Objectives (MBO) is a participative management approach developed by Peter F. Drucker in which organizational goals are translated into specific objectives for departments, units, and individual employees. Each unit develops its own action plan to achieve these predefined objectives, usually over a short-term period, with periodic review of performance.

Why not the other options?

• A. Input-Output analysis: An economic and planning tool used to study relationships between inputs and outputs in production systems.
• B. Personnel management: Deals with recruitment, training, appraisal, and welfare of employees; it is not based on objective-setting.
• D. Work sampling: A work measurement technique used to estimate how workers spend their time through random observations.
questions.learning: Management by objectives Management by Objectives (MBO) is a participative management approach developed by Peter F. Drucker in which organizational goals are translated into specific objectives for departments, units, and individual employees.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An anti-diabetic drug causes a decrease in HbA1C by causing an increase in GIP and GLP-1 levels and a decrease in glucagon levels. It is an oral drug causing a reduction in both pre and post-prandial glucose. The drug is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alogliptin

Alogliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP) inhibitor. Glucagon-like peptide (GLP) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) are both incretins that promote the exocytosis of insulin into circulation. Both these incretins are rapidly inactivated by dipeptidyl peptidase. So, inhibition of dipeptidyl peptidase enhances the action of incretins and facilitates insulin release. Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors enhance the release of insulin postprandially, decrease glucagon, and thereby lower mealtime as well as fasting glucose.

Other DPP-4 inhibitors include saxagliptin, linagliptin, alogliptin, and vildagliptin. They are weight neutral.

DPP-4 inhibitors are associated with severe joint pain which reduces on discontinuation of the drug. Linagliptin is cleared primarily by hepatobiliary system, with little renal clearance. Only saxagliptin is metabolized by the liver and must be used in lower doses if used along with a cytochrome p450 enzyme inhibitor drug. Other drugs are renally excreted and hence must be used with caution in renal insufficiency.

Other options:

Option A - Pramlintide is an amylin agonist. It reduces postprandial glycemia and leads to weight loss.

Option C - Liraglutide is also a GLP-1 receptor agonist and is given only in the subcutaneous injectable form. It was recently approved for the treatment of obesity.

Option D - Metformin belongs to the biguanides class of oral hypoglycemic agents. It acts by activation of AMP-dependent protein kinase (AMPK). This results in reduced hepatic glucose production. Side effects of metformin are lactic acidosis, gastrointestinal disturbance, and vitamin B12 deficiency.
questions.learning: Alogliptin Alogliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP) inhibitor. Glucagon-like peptide (GLP) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) are both incretins that promote the exocytosis of insulin into circulation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man sustains a perineal injury after falling into a manhole and subsequently develops difficulty in passing urine with blood seen at the urethral meatus. He is diagnosed with a bulbar urethral injury. In this condition, at which anatomical site would urine extravasation be least likely to occur?
questions.explanation: A fall-astride injury commonly causes a rupture of the bulbar urethra. When the urethra ruptures below the urogenital diaphragm, extravasated urine and blood are contained by Colles’ fascia. Colles’ fascia is continuous with Scrotal (Dartos) fascia and Scarpa’s fascia of the "anterior abdominal wall" (Option B), but it is firmly attached to the fascia lata of the thigh. Therefore, while urine can freely track into the "perineum" (Option A), "root of the scrotum" (Option D), and up the abdominal wall, it cannot track into the "medial portion of the thigh" (Option C). This creates a characteristic "butterfly" or "scrotal" swelling pattern. Diagnosis is confirmed via Retrograde Urethrography (RGU). Management usually involves the placement of a suprapubic catheter to divert urine, followed by delayed surgical repair of the urethra to avoid aggravating the injury or causing infection
questions.learning: A fall-astride injury commonly causes a rupture of the bulbar urethra. When the urethra ruptures below the urogenital diaphragm, extravasated urine and blood are contained by Colles’ fascia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a case of drowning, the following finding is seen at autopsy. What is it called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cadaveric spasm

The image shown above represents a firm hand grip on weeds and mud, found in a victim of drowning. It is indicative of the last action performed by the victim. This is an example of a cadaveric spasm.

Cadaveric spasm/Instantaneous rigor/cataleptic rigidity/death clutch:

* It is a phenomenon where a group of muscles that are in a state of contraction at the time of death remains contracted after death till molecular death occurs.

* It occurs immediately after death. There is no stage of primary relaxation.

* It is seen in cases of deaths coupled with emotional disturbances like in case of excitement, fear, severe pain, exhaustion at the time of death, cerebral hemorrhage, injury to the nervous system, drowning, strychnine poisoning.

* It is an ante mortem phenomenon and it indicates the manner of death and not the time since death.

Other options:

Option B: Cutis anserina (goose-skin or goose-flesh), in which the skin has a granular and puckered appearance can be seen on the anterior surfaces of the body, especially on the thighs.  It is produced by the spasm of the erector pilae muscles, attached to each hair follicle, and can occur in the living when the skin comes in contact with cold water. It can occur on submersion of the body in cold water immediately after death, while the muscles were still warm and irritable. It can also be produced by rigor mortis of the erector muscles.

Option C: Rigor mortis is a postmortem phenomenon indicative of molecular death. It is useful in estimating the time since death. The mechanism of rigor mortis is due to muscle ATP breakdown below the critical level.  It appears 2-3 hours after death and is usually preceded by postmortem flaccidity. It involves both the voluntary and involuntary muscles of the body and persists for about 12-24 hours.

Option D: Washerwoman’s hands is a specific change that is seen in the skin of the palm and sole, which comprises of wrinkled, swollen, whitish sodden appearance of hands or feet. It can also be considered as water maceration of skin of the hand, due to absorption of water into the outer layers of skin. Though the washerwomen’s hand and feet changes are usually seen in dead bodies recovered from water, this cannot be considered as a sign of antemortem drowning.

Pearl PF0229: Differentiating features between Antemortem amd Postmortem drowning

Antemortem drowning
Postmortem drowning

Foam/froth at nostrils or mouth
Not present

Cadaveric spasm
Not present

Lungs usually are voluminous, bulky, water-logged and over-inflated ,called as emphysema aquosum.
Passive collection of water  in the lungs without any formation of columns of froth,has been called as oedema aquosum.

Presence of foam, fluid, debris, weeds, vegetation, etc. in the bronchi and bronchioles.
Foreign matter may passively find access only to the upper respiratory passage.

Demonstration of diatoms in the lungs, liver, brain, bone marrow, etc.
Diatoms may reach the lungs but not to the distant organs because of absence of circulation.

Stomach may contain water and foreign material like sand, weed, dirt etc which may be swallowed while struggling for life.
Water could enter the stomach. However, quantity of foreign matter may become the decisive issue.
