questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following operative procedures is/are confirmatory for the diagnosis of bicornuate uterus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hysteroscopy and laparoscopy

A bicornuate uterus is a Class IV Müllerian duct anomaly resulting from partial failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts, leading to a uterus with two uterine horns and a deep external fundal cleft (>1 cm). The definitive diagnosis requires assessment of both the uterine cavity and the external uterine contour, making combined hysteroscopy and laparoscopy the operative gold standard.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Dilatation with curettage (D&C): D&C has no role in diagnosing congenital uterine anomalies.
• B. Hysteroscopy: Hysteroscopy alone visualizes only the uterine cavity and cannot assess the external fundal contour, making it difficult to distinguish a bicornuate uterus from a septate uterus.
• D. Hysterectomy: Hysterectomy is not a diagnostic procedure and is unnecessary for confirming a bicornuate uterus.
questions.learning: Hysteroscopy and laparoscopy — A bicornuate uterus is a Class IV Müllerian duct anomaly resulting from partial failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts, leading to a uterus with two uterine horns and a deep external fundal cleft (>1 cm).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following local anaesthetic causes hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cocaine

The local anesthetic that causes hypertension is cocaine. This is due to the inhibition of norepinephrine at the adrenergic terminals leading to increased sympathetic stimulation. This effect occurs at all concentrations of cocaine and causes hypertension and ventricular ectopies.

Treatment is with the help of benzodiazepines, α-adrenergic antagonists and amiodarone.

All local anesthetics are mainly cardiodepressants causing reduced contractility and vasodilation. However, at low concentrations, all local anesthetics cause vasoconstriction due to the inhibition of nitric oxide. Only cocaine produces vasoconstriction and hypertension at all concentrations.

Accidental intravascular injection of local anesthetic like bupivacaine results in bupivacaine-induced cardiotoxicity. Management is by resuscitation followed by intralipid therapy. A rapid bolus of intralipid 20% IV is administered without delay.

Other adverse effects of local anesthetics include neurologic toxicity, respiratory depression, and hypersensitivity reactions. Nervous system manifestations are circumoral numbness, tongue paresthesia, dizziness, tinnitus, and disorientation. Finally, respiratory depression can lead to respiratory arrest.
questions.learning: Cocaine — The local anesthetic that causes hypertension is cocaine. This is due to the inhibition of norepinephrine at the adrenergic terminals leading to increased sympathetic stimulation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: When radiotherapy is administered in combination with chemotherapy for bladder cancer, which drug usually requires a dose reduction because of an increased risk of toxicity?
questions.explanation: In the concurrent chemoradiotherapy (trimodality therapy) used for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, Cisplatin is the primary radiosensitizing agent of choice. When used in combination with radiation, cisplatin carries a significantly increased risk of synergistic toxicity, most notably nephrotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy. To minimize these risks, the dosage must be carefully adjusted, often being delivered in lower, frequent weekly doses rather than high-dose pulses used in standard systemic therapy. Gemcitabine (Option B) is also used but is a more potent radiosensitizer with a higher risk of local bowel and bladder inflammation (toxicity). Paclitaxel (Option C) and Ifosfamide (Option D) are typically reserved for salvage therapy or metastatic disease rather than primary concurrent radiosensitization protocols. Therefore, because of its gold-standard status and dose-limiting renal and neurological side effects during radiation, Cisplatin is the medication most critical for dosage adjustment
questions.learning: In the concurrent chemoradiotherapy (trimodality therapy) used for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, Cisplatin is the primary radiosensitizing agent of choice.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: LIFT procedure in fistula surgery stands for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ligation of intersphincteric fistula tract

LIFT (Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract) is a sphincter-preserving procedure used for the treatment of fistula-in-ano.

Principle

• The fistulous tract is identified in the intersphincteric plane.
• The tract is ligated close to the internal opening.
• The tract is divided, thereby disconnecting the internal opening from the external tract.
• This eradicates the fistula while preserving the anal sphincters.

Advantages

• Preserves continence (minimal risk of fecal incontinence).
• Suitable for complex transsphincteric fistulas.
• Less sphincter damage compared with fistulotomy.
• Good healing rates with low morbidity.

High-Yield MCQ Points

• LIFT = Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract.
• Indicated mainly for transsphincteric fistula-in-ano.
• A sphincter-saving procedure.
• Preferred when preservation of continence is important.
questions.learning: Ligation of intersphincteric fistula tract LIFT (Ligation of Intersphincteric Fistula Tract) is a sphincter-preserving procedure used for the treatment of fistula-in-ano.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which cellular process does Bedaquiline primarily target to exert its therapeutic effect?
questions.explanation: Bedaquiline is a novel, breakthrough diarylquinoline antibiotic used specifically for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Its unique mechanism of action involves the inhibition of ATP synthesis within the Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacterium. It specifically binds to the C-subunit of the mycobacterial ATP synthase enzyme, which is the rotary engine that generates ATP through the proton gradient. By cutting off the energy supply, bedaquiline effectively kills both active and dormant bacilli, as even non-replicating bacteria require ATP for survival. Mycolic acid synthesis inhibition (Option B) is the mechanism of isoniazid and ethionamide. Protein synthesis inhibition (Option C) is how aminoglycosides or linezolid work. Inhibiting reverse transcriptase (Option D) is the mechanism for antiretroviral drugs used in HIV. Clinically, bedaquiline is reserved for complex cases due to its risk of QT interval prolongation, but its targeted action on bioenergetics makes it a cornerstone of modern MDR-TB regimens
questions.learning: Bedaquiline is a novel, breakthrough diarylquinoline antibiotic used specifically for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Its unique mechanism of action involves the inhibition of ATP synthesis within the Mycobacterium tuberculosis…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Maple syrup urine disease is due to a defect in which enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase

Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is due to deficiency of branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH).

Leucine, isoleucine, and valine are the 3 essential amino acids, which are branched-chain amino acids. Their decarboxylation is accomplished by BCKDH using thiamine (vitamin B1) pyrophosphate as a coenzyme.

Leucine is metabolized by BCAA aminotransferase to α-ketoisocaproic acid, which leads to the disrupted metabolism of neurotransmitters and amino acids (glutamate, GABA, glutamine, alanine, and aspartate). α-Ketoisocaproic acid can reversibly inhibit oxidative phosphorylation and result in cerebral lactic acidosis. Collectively, these processes are detrimental to the normal function of neurons and glia, clinically manifesting as encephalopathy and brain edema and referred to as leucinosis.

Treatment options include hemodialysis, restricting dietary substances, thiamine for milder forms, and orthotopic liver transplant.

Other options:

B. Isovaleryl CoA dehydrogenase: Isovaleryl CoA dehydrogenase is involved in the breakdown of isovaleryl-CoA, a compound derived from the metabolism of the amino acid leucine. Deficiency of isovaleryl CoA dehydrogenase is associated with a different metabolic disorder called isovaleric acidemia, but not maple syrup urine disease.

C. Pyruvate carboxylase: Pyruvate carboxylase is an enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis, a process by which glucose is synthesized from non-carbohydrate sources. Deficiency of pyruvate carboxylase results in a different metabolic disorder known as pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, but it is not associated with maple syrup urine disease.

D. Acetyl CoA carboxylase: Acetyl CoA carboxylase is an enzyme involved in fatty acid synthesis. Deficiency of acetyl CoA carboxylase can lead to a different condition called malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, but it is not related to maple syrup urine disease.

Pearl PF0080: Maple syrup urine disease(MSUD)
questions.learning: Branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is due to deficiency of branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDH). Leucine, isoleucine, and valine are the 3 essential amino acids, which are branched-chain amino acids.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with chronic productive cough and progressive breathlessness is diagnosed with COPD. He develops type II respiratory failure. Which of the following statements regarding his condition is not true?
options: Bronchial wall inflammation is a characteristic finding
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lung compliance is decreased

COPD is a spectrum:

• Chronic bronchitis → airway disease
• Emphysema → parenchymal destruction

Both lead to airflow obstruction, but their mechanics differ beautifully (and examiners love this contrast).

Chronic smoking / irritants

Airway inflammation + mucus hypersecretion

Airflow obstruction (↓ FEV1)

Air trapping + hyperinflation

↑ CO2 retention (hypercapnia)

Type II respiratory failure

| Feature | Emphysema (“Pink puffer”) | Chronic Bronchitis (“Blue bloater”)

| ------- | ------------------------- | -----------------------------------

| Main issue | Alveolar destruction | Airway obstruction

| Compliance | ↑ | Normal/slightly ↑

| CO₂ retention | Late | Early

| Cyanosis | Minimal | Prominent

| Body type | Thin | Obese

| Feature | COPD (Emphysema) | Restrictive Lung Disease (ILD)

| ------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------

| Lung compliance |  Increased |  Decreased

| Elastic recoil | Decreased | Increased

| Lung volumes | Increased (hyperinflation) | Decreased

| FEV₁/FVC | ↓ (<70%) | Normal/↑

| TLC | Increased | Decreased
questions.learning: Lung compliance is decreased COPD is a spectrum: • Chronic bronchitis → airway disease • Emphysema → parenchymal destruction Both lead to airflow obstruction, but their mechanics differ beautifully (and examiners love this contrast).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: At what pressure does the marked structure open?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30-40 cm H2O

In the image, the marked structure is the adjustable pressure-limiting (APL) valve of Mapelson-C anaesthetic breathing system and it will open at the pressure of 30-40 cm H2O. This valve is designed to release gas when a certain pressure is exceeded to prevent excessive pressure from building up in the patient's airway.

The APL valve typically opens at pressures of 30-40 cm H₂O to allow for safe ventilation without causing barotrauma to the lungs. This range is appropriate for manual ventilation to prevent high airway pressures that could lead to lung injury.
questions.learning: 30-40 cm H2O In the image, the marked structure is the adjustable pressure-limiting (APL) valve of Mapelson-C anaesthetic breathing system and it will open at the pressure of 30-40 cm H2O.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presented with complaints of bone pain and abdominal cramps. Her family says she has a history of abnormal behavior. The consultant doctor arrived at a provisional diagnosis based on the clinical features. Which of the following would be the best investigation to arrive at a definitive diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sestamibi scan

The given clinical features are suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. Parathyroid adenoma is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism and the Tc99m sestamibi scan is used for diagnosis of parathyroid adenoma.

Clinical features of hyperparathyroidism:

* Bones:

* Pathological fractures

* Subperiosteal bone resorption - 2nd and 3rd digits, most common in radial aspect

* Salt and pepper skull

* Osteitis fibrosa cystica or VonReckling Hausen’s disease

* Stones

* Multiple and recurrent renal stones - most common

* Nephrocalcinosis

* Abdominal groans - colicky due to pancreatitis

* Psychiatric overtones - raised PTH causing CNS depression and psychiatric symptoms

* Band keratopathy

* Features of hypercalcemia -

* Vomiting

* Confusion

* ECG changes: increased PR interval, shortened QT interval

Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabeled Sestamibi is a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue. It is now regarded as the most accurate and reliable method for imaging the parathyroid glands.

Other options:

Option A: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is not commonly used to image the parathyroid glands

Option B: Ultrasonography of the neck is a safe and widely used technique for the localization of abnormal parathyroid glands.

Option D: Multiphase CT imaging has become widely utilized to localize the disease. It gives both anatomical as well as functional information about the parathyroid glands. The disadvantage is the higher radiation dose when compared to others.
questions.learning: Sestamibi scan — The given clinical features are suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. Parathyroid adenoma is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism and the Tc99m sestamibi scan is used for diagnosis of parathyroid adenoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A neonate shows hypoplasia of the mandible and zygomatic bones, malformed external ears, and downward-slanting palpebral fissures. Abnormal development of which pharyngeal arch most likely accounts for these anomalies?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation described is characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome, which results from the abnormal development of the first pharyngeal arch. The first pharyngeal arch, also known as the mandibular arch, is responsible for forming the mandible, maxilla, zygomatic bones, and certain structures of the external and middle ear. Specifically, the maxillary process forms the zygomatic bone and maxilla, while the mandibular process forms the mandible through Meckel’s cartilage. Defects in the second pharyngeal arch (Option B) would primarily affect the stapes, styloid process, and muscles of facial expression. The third arch (Option C) contributes to the greater horn of the hyoid and stylopharyngeus muscle. The fourth arch (Option D) is involved in forming laryngeal cartilages and pharyngeal constrictors. Therefore, because the zygomatic and mandibular bones are the primary structures affected, the first pharyngeal arch is the definitive site of abnormal embryological development
questions.learning: The clinical presentation described is characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome, which results from the abnormal development of the first pharyngeal arch.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A middle-aged man complains of very early ejaculation during intercourse. What is the non-pharmacological management that can be advised to the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Squeeze technique

The clinical scenario of ejaculation very early on vaginal penetration is suggestive of premature ejaculation (PE), and the squeeze technique is a non-pharmacological management (behavioral method) used to prevent it.

PE is a disorder of the orgasm phase of the normal sexual cycle.

In premature ejaculation, there is a persistent or recurrent achievement of orgasm and ejaculation before the patient actually wishes to. According to DSM-5, it is classified as follows:

• Mild if ejaculation occurs within approximately 30 seconds to 1 minute of vaginal penetration
• Moderate if ejaculation occurs within approximately 15 to 30 seconds of vaginal penetration
• Severe if ejaculation occurs at the start of sexual activity or within approximately 15 seconds of vaginal penetration.

Pharmacologic therapy when combined with behavioral treatment appears to be more effective in treating premature ejaculation.

The squeeze technique is a behavioral method used on the penis to prevent premature ejaculation. Here, the penis is stimulated until just before orgasm after which it is gently squeezed.

Other options:

Option A: Although Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can be beneficial for some patients with sexual dysfunction. It is not a specific technique for managing PE. Instead, CBT is more useful in addressing underlying psychological issues or relationship problems that may contribute to the condition. CBT is used in the treatment of depression, phobia, anxiety and panic disorders, OCD, personality disorders, and somatoform disorders.

Option B: Exposure and response prevention therapy is a strategy within CBT that is effective in the management of OCD. It is also useful in other conditions like tics but is not a suitable method for managing premature ejaculation.

Option D: Sensate focus therapy is a couple-oriented sex therapy that involves the exchange of sensual touch between partners to alleviate anxiety and negativity associated with sex and to build better sexual intimacy and communication. It does not specifically address the issue of premature ejaculation like the squeeze technique does and is hence not useful.
questions.learning: Squeeze technique — The clinical scenario of ejaculation very early on vaginal penetration is suggestive of premature ejaculation (PE), and the squeeze technique is a non-pharmacological management (behavioral method) used to prevent it.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man, newly diagnosed with HIV infection, presents with low-grade fever, productive cough, and weight loss. A chest X-ray reveals nodules suggestive of TB. Sputum GeneXpert reveals Mycobacterium tuberculosis with rifampicin resistance. He is not yet started on ART. His CD4 count is 110 cells/mm³. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start BPaLM regimen for 6 months and follow up for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)
Start HEZ plus levofloxacin for 9 months and monitor for optic neuritis
Start HEZ plus linezolid for 9 months and monitor for hepatotoxicity
Start kanamycin-based MDR regimen for 20 months and continue ART without interruption
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Start BPaLM regimen for 6 months and follow up for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)

In HIV patients with rifampicin-resistant (RR/MDR) tuberculosis, the recommended management is an all-oral, shorter regimen such as BPaLM (Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid + Moxifloxacin) for \~6 months.

• GeneXpert showing rifampicin resistance = treat as MDR-TB
• BPaLM regimen is now preferred:

o    Shorter duration (≈6 months)

o    Fully oral (no injectables)

o    Higher success rates

HIV considerations:

• Start ATT immediately
• Initiate ART early (within 2 weeks for CD4 <200)
• Monitor for IRIS after ART initiation

Why not other options:

• HEZ regimens → ineffective in rifampicin-resistant TB
• Kanamycin-based regimens → outdated, toxic (ototoxicity), longer duration
• Injectable regimens are no longer preferred

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old man presents with bleeding per rectum for 4 months. On examination, there is a 5 cm ulceroproliferative growth arising from the anal canal above the dentate line. Biopsy reveals squamous cell carcinoma. Contrast-enhanced CT shows no distant metastasis. What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the anal canal is treated primarily with definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT), which is the standard of care for localized disease without distant metastasis. This approach preserves the anal sphincter and achieves high rates of local control, avoiding the need for radical surgery in most patients.

Nigro Protocol

• 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) or Capecitabine
• Mitomycin C
• External beam radiotherapy

This is the gold standard treatment for anal canal SCC.

Why not the other options?

• A. Wide local excision: Reserved only for small, well-differentiated perianal (anal margin) tumors, not anal canal SCC.
• B. Surgery followed by radiotherapy: Surgery is not first-line because it requires abdominoperineal resection (APR) with permanent colostomy.
• C. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery: Routine surgery after CRT is not recommended. Surgery is reserved for persistent or recurrent disease.
questions.learning: Definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the anal canal is treated primarily with definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT), which is the standard of care for localized disease without distant metastasis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text:
Match the following

a. Patch test
1. Leprosy

b. KOH mount
2. Lupus vulgaris

c. Biopsy
3. Contact dermatitis

d. Slit skin smear
4. Tinea corporis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. a-3, b-4, c-2, d-1

The correctly matched option is a-3, b-4, c-2, d-1.

a. Patch test
3. Contact dermatitis

b. KOH mount
4. Tinea corporis

c. Biopsy
2. Lupus vulgaris

d. Slit skin smear
1. Leprosy

Lupus vulgaris is one of the prevalent forms of cutaneous tuberculosis that occurs in previously sensitized individuals with high immunity. It is characterized by reddish-brown papules and slow-growing plaques with elevated borders and central atrophy. Diagnosis is made by biopsy. Caseating granulomas are pathognomonic of tuberculosis.

Tinea corporis/ ringworm infection is caused by the dermatophyte Trichophyton rubrum. It results from invasion and proliferation of the causal fungi in the stratum corneum with lesions on the trunk and limbs. Characteristic lesions are circular, usually sharply marginated with a raised edge with central resolution.

KOH mount is used for the diagnosis. Branching hyphae are seen in Tinea corporis.

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes.

Cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy:

• Characteristic skin lesions- hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation.
• Peripheral nerve involvement- thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen.
• Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR.

Allergic contact dermatitis is an eczematous reaction that occurs as an immunological response that occurs due to exposure to a substance towards which the immune system has previously been sensitized.

The patch test is used to detect delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity to antigens that come in contact with the skin, by applying the suspected antigen under occlusive patches to the skin. Patches are removed after 48 hours (or sooner if there is itching and burning).

• 48 hours: Patch removal for initial reading to detect delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
• 72-96 hours: Final reading done for confirmation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following parameters is decreased in acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation triggers the liver to change its protein production, leading to increases in "positive" acute-phase reactants and decreases in "negative" acute-phase reactants. Albumin is a classic negative acute-phase reactant, meaning its serum levels decrease during significant inflammation. This occurs because the liver shifts its synthetic machinery toward producing protective proteins and because of increased capillary permeability. Conversely, C-reactive protein (CRP) (Option A), Ferritin (Option C), and Hepcidin (Option B) are all positive acute-phase reactants that increase significantly. CRP is used clinically as a sensitive marker for systemic inflammation. Increased Hepcidin levels lead to the sequestration of iron within macrophages, contributing to the "anemia of chronic disease" by limiting iron availability for erythropoiesis. Recognizing these patterns is essential for interpreting laboratory results; for instance, a low albumin level in an acutely ill patient may reflect the severity of the inflammatory response rather than poor nutritional status alone
questions.learning: Acute inflammation triggers the liver to change its protein production, leading to increases in "positive" acute-phase reactants and decreases in "negative" acute-phase reactants.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Purpose of the device shown in the picture?
options: Measure the length of the uterus
questions.explanation: Menstrual regulation/aspiration. The device shown in the image is a manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) tool, consisting of a specialized syringe and a Karman cannula. The primary clinical purpose of this instrument is menstrual regulation or the aspiration of the uterine cavity (Option D) . It is commonly used for early medical termination of pregnancy, management of incomplete abortions, or obtaining an endometrial biopsy. Hysterosalpingography (Option A) requires a different specialized cannula for injecting contrast under pressure. Measuring the uterine length (Option B) is performed using a uterine sound, which is a thin, graduated metal rod. Retraction (Option C) is a function of speculums or surgical retractors. Because the MVA provides a handheld, low-pressure suction mechanism specifically designed for intrauterine contents, it is the definitive tool for regulation and aspiration procedures. Recognizing this equipment is fundamental for practitioners providing reproductive health and outpatient gynecological services. .
questions.learning: The device shown in the image is a manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) tool, consisting of a specialized syringe and a Karman cannula. The primary clinical purpose of this instrument is menstrual regulation or the aspiration of the uterine cavity (Option D) .

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which segment of the nephron has the lowest osmolality under the influence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH)?
options: Descending limb of the loop of Henle
questions.explanation: The early distal tubule maintains the lowest osmolality in the nephron, regardless of the presence of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). This segment is functionally impermeable to water but actively reabsorbs sodium and chloride (NaCl), which further dilutes the tubular fluid, making it hypotonic. In contrast, the descending limb of the loop of Henle (Option B) is highly permeable to water, leading to a significant increase in osmolality as fluid moves into the hypertonic medulla. Under the influence of ADH, the collecting duct (Option C) and the late distal tubule (Option D) become highly permeable to water via aquaporins. This allows water to be reabsorbed along the osmotic gradient, which concentrates the urine and increases the osmolality of the fluid within these segments significantly. Therefore, the early distal tubule remains the most dilute segment because it removes solutes without allowing water to follow

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient has profuse bleeding after the removal of an IV cannula. He underwent a small bowel resection and was given broad-spectrum antibiotics during his hospital stay. The deficiency of which of the following vitamins is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin K

The deficiency of vitamin K is responsible for this condition.

Vitamin K deficiency in adults may be seen in patients with chronic small-intestinal diseases like celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, obstructed biliary tracts, and after small-bowel resection. Additionally, broad-spectrum antibiotics can precipitate Vitamin K deficiency by reducing the number of gut bacteria, which synthesize menaquinones.

It is a fat-soluble vitamin that has two natural forms: Vitamin K1, also known as phylloquinone, from vegetable sources, and vitamin K2, or menaquinones, which are synthesized by bacterial flora and found in hepatic tissue.

Vitamin K is required for the posttranslational carboxylation of glutamic acid, which is necessary for calcium binding to γ-carboxylated proteins such as

* prothrombin (factor II)

* factors VII, IX, and X

* protein C, protein S

Patients with vitamin K deficiency usually present with a history of bleeding either at venipuncture sites or minor trauma.

It is diagnosed on the basis of an elevated prothrombin time or reduced clotting factors. It is treated with supplementation by oral or IV route.

Other options:

Option A: Riboflavin or Vitamin B2 deficiency manifests as angular stomatitis, magenta tongue, seborrhea, corneal vascularization. It is seen in alcoholism, and individuals with a poor diet and decreased intake of dairy products.

Option B: Vitamin E deficiency manifests as peripheral neuropathy, spinocerebellar ataxia, skeletal muscle atrophy, and retinopathy. Usually seen with fat malabsorption or genetic abnormalities of vitamin E metabolism.

Option C: Niacin deficiency manifests as pellagra, which includes symptoms of diarrhea, a pigmented rash over sun-exposed areas, bright red tongue, memory loss, and altered sensorium. Alcoholism, vitamin B6 deficiency, riboflavin, and tryptophan deficiencies predispose to this condition.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which hormone levels increase during stress, starvation, and deep sleep?
questions.explanation: Growth Hormone (GH) secretion is pulsatile and is significantly stimulated by various physiological factors, including stress, starvation (hypoglycemia), and deep sleep (Stage 3 and 4). During starvation, GH helps mobilize fatty acids for energy while sparing glucose. Its secretion peaks during the early hours of deep sleep, which is vital for tissue repair and growth in children. Glucocorticoids/Cortisol (Options B and C) definitely increase during stress and starvation but typically decrease during sleep. Prolactin (Option D) levels do rise during sleep and stress, but its primary stimulus is not starvation; rather, it's related to lactation and reproductive triggers. Understanding these hormonal triggers is crucial for diagnosing endocrine disorders. For example, the "insulin tolerance test" uses insulin-induced hypoglycemia (a form of starvation stress) to test if the pituitary gland can normally secrete GH. If GH levels fail to rise during this test, it indicates a deficiency
questions.learning: Growth Hormone (GH) secretion is pulsatile and is significantly stimulated by various physiological factors, including stress, starvation (hypoglycemia), and deep sleep (Stage 3 and 4).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT typically associated with fibroids?
questions.explanation: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors. The most common symptoms include a palpable pelvic mass (Option A), menstrual irregularities (Option D)—specifically heavy bleeding (menorrhagia) and prolonged periods—and infertility (Option C) due to cavity distortion . Amenorrhea (the absence of periods) (Option B) is not a feature of fibroids. In fact, fibroids are far more likely to cause excessive bleeding rather than no bleeding at all. Amenorrhea should prompt a clinician to investigate for pregnancy, PCOS, or hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis disorders. Fibroids grow in response to estrogen, so they typically regress after menopause. If a woman with known fibroids develops amenorrhea, it is usually due to a concurrent condition or the natural onset of menopause rather than the fibroids themselves. Therefore, amenorrhea is the correct "not" answer for typical fibroid presentations

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not involved in meta-analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Randomization

All the above steps are involved in meta-analysis except for randomization.

Meta-analysis is a set of statistical techniques for combining quantitative results from multiple studies to produce a summary of empirical knowledge on a given topic. It refers to a method of a systematic review.

Four basic steps involved in a meta-analysis are:

• Identification: This is the first step in a meta-analysis and it includes finding all of the articles or studies related to the topic.
• Selection: After assembling all the related studies, it is important to select the right or necessary studies by using inclusion (also called eligibility) criteria. Examples are minimum sample size (as very small studies may be unrepresentative), study design (controlled trials only vs randomized controlled trials only), etc.
• Abstraction: Once an appropriate group of studies has been identified, the author has to abstract the relevant data from each study.
• Analysis: This is the last step of meta-analysis.

Objectives of meta-analysis include,

• Summarize results from individual studies.
• Analyze differences in results among studies.
• Overcome small sample sizes of individual studies to detect the effects of interest.
• Determine if new studies are needed to investigate an issue.
• Generate new hypotheses for future studies.

Note- Randomization involves randomly assigning patients to different groups, like experimental and control groups. Clinical trials usually involve randomization and are hence called randomized clinical trials (RCTs). It is done to prevent confounding.
questions.learning: Randomization All the above steps are involved in meta-analysis except for randomization. Meta-analysis is a set of statistical techniques for combining quantitative results from multiple studies to produce a summary of empirical knowledge on a given topic.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child presents with elevated liver enzyme levels, and ocular examination reveals a golden to greenish-brown ring at the periphery of the cornea. What is the underlying cause of this clinical finding?
questions.explanation: The clinical description points toward the Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring, a pathognomonic sign of Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration). This condition is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to defective copper transport and its subsequent accumulation in various tissues. In the eye, copper deposits in the Descemet's membrane at the periphery of the cornea, creating the characteristic golden-brown or greenish ring. The child's concurrent elevated liver enzymes reflect the primary hepatic involvement of Wilson's disease, where copper toxicity causes cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis. Glucose (Option B), galactose (Option C), and mannose (Option D) are sugars. While galactose is associated with early-onset "oil droplet" cataracts, it does not cause corneal rings. KF rings are best visualized using a slit-lamp examination and are present in nearly all patients with the neurological form of the disease and about 50-60% of those with primarily hepatic presentation. Early identification is crucial as the disease is treatable with copper-chelating agents like penicillamine

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which urinary substances are measured as a screening test for pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla chromaffin cells. Because these tumors release excessive epinephrine and norepinephrine, their metabolic breakdown products are excreted in high quantities. Measurement of 24-hour urinary metanephrines and Vanillylmandelic Acid (VMA) is the standard, highly sensitive screening tool used to diagnose this condition. Metanephrines are considered superior due to their longer half-life. Albumin (Option B) is a marker for kidney disease or pre-eclampsia. 5-HIAA (Option C) is the urinary metabolite of serotonin and is specifically used to screen for carcinoid syndrome. Glucose (Option D) in the urine is a screen for diabetes mellitus. Therefore, because metanephrines and VMA directly reflect the abnormal sympathetic activity of the tumor, they are the definitive markers for pheochromocytoma. A positive screening result is typically followed by CT or MRI imaging for localization
questions.learning: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla chromaffin cells. Because these tumors release excessive epinephrine and norepinephrine, their metabolic breakdown products are excreted in high quantities.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the given cystometrogram?
options: Segment Ia is due to residual urine
Segment Ib is due to Laplace law
Micturition fails to happen in segment II
The dotted line represents that micturition has occurred
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Segment Ib is due to Laplace law

The true statement regarding the given cystometrogram is that segment Ib is due to Laplace law.

Cystometrogram is a plot of intravesical pressure against the volume of fluid in the bladder. The curve shows three segments:

• Ia- initial slight rise in pressure when the first increments in the volume are produced
• Ib- long, nearly flat segment as further increments are produced
• II- sudden, sharp rise in pressure as the micturition reflex is triggered (not failure).
• The dotted line- pressure-volume relation if the micturition had not occurred.

The flatness of segment Ib is a demonstration of the law of Laplace. The law of Laplace states that the pressure (P) in a spherical viscus is equal to twice the wall tension (T) divided by the radius (R). This is expressed as P= 2T/R. In the bladder, the tension increases as the bladder get filled. Since the radius also increases there is only a slight increase in pressure until the bladder is relatively full.

The first urge to void is felt at a bladder volume of about 150 mL. A marked sense of fullness is felt at a bladder volume of 400ml.

Micturition reflex is the result of sensory signals from the stretch receptors in the bladder wall, which are conducted to the sacral segments of the cord through the pelvic nerves and then efferent signals conducts back again to the bladder through the parasympathetic nerve fibers.

The micturition reflex pathway is given below.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A newborn is seen to have an abnormal lump in the lower back. Identify the condition from the MRI given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meningocele

The MRI given represents meningocele.

Meningocele involves the midline protrusion of the meninges. A fluctuant midline mass, that may transilluminate is present in the lower back along the vertebral column. Meningomyelocele involves the protrusion of the spinal cord with the meningeal covering. Neurological dysfunction is more common in these open defects.

Spina bifida occulta refers to fusion defects of the posterior part of the vertebral body. There is no associated protrusion of the spinal cord or meninges. These neonates are usually asymptomatic, without any neurological signs. They present only with a tuft of hair over the lower back.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A tumor in the anterior pituitary pressing on the optic chiasma will present as a case of ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bitemporal hemianopia

A lesion in the optic chiasma will present as bitemporal hemianopia, due to the decussation of nasal fibres which are affected.

Other notable defects:

* Pie in the sky defects

* Superior quadrantic hemianopia

* Involvement of Meyer’s loop - inferior fibers of optic radiations

* Contralateral temporal lobe

* Pie in the floor defects

* Inferior quadrantic hemianopia

* Involvement of Baum’s loop - superior fibers of optic radiations

* Contralateral parietal lobe

* Homonymous hemianopia

* Involvement of retrochiasmal regions such as optic tract, geniculate body, optic radiations.

* Sparing of the macula and more congruous field defect (both sides have the same extent of field loss) when the occipital cortex is involved.

Pearl PF0246: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman, gravida 2 with one living child, presents at 18 weeks of gestation with vaginal bleeding for the past 4 hours. On examination, the membranes are ruptured and uterine contractions are present. Transvaginal ultrasonography reveals a cervical length of less than 25 mm with funneling of the internal os measuring more than 1 cm. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cervical incompetence (or cervical insufficiency) is the inability of the cervix to retain a pregnancy in the absence of signs and symptoms of clinical contractions, or in response to minimal pressure. However, it often leads to the presentation described: painless dilatation, funneling, and eventually premature rupture of membranes and contractions in the second trimester (16–24 weeks). The ultrasound findings of a short cervix (<25 mm) and "funneling" are highly characteristic markers of an incompetent cervix. Placenta previa (Option B) involves the placenta covering the os and typically presents with "painless" bleeding without ruptured membranes at 18 weeks. Abruptio placentae (Option C) involves premature separation of the placenta and usually presents with "painful" bleeding and a tense uterus later in pregnancy. Traumatic injury (Option D) requires a specific history of trauma. Management for cervical incompetence includes elective cerclage in subsequent pregnancies or emergency cerclage if detected before membranes rupture, though prognosis is poor once rupture has occurred
questions.learning: Cervical incompetence (or cervical insufficiency) is the inability of the cervix to retain a pregnancy in the absence of signs and symptoms of clinical contractions, or in response to minimal pressure.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with high-grade chills and violent shaking (rigors), along with sudden-onset severe pain in the right flank. This clinical picture raises concern for a serious infectious or inflammatory condition involving the abdomen or flank. Based on these symptoms and the expected findings from appropriate diagnostic investigations, including imaging studies, which of the following conditions should be considered in the differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of high-grade fever with rigors and acute right flank pain in a 55-year-old patient points strongly toward a severe renal infection. As established in the previous analysis, Emphysematous Pyelonephritis is the most likely diagnosis that accounts for such intense systemic symptoms and localized flank distress. This condition involves gas-forming bacteria invading the kidney tissue. Cholecystitis (Option A) would typically present with right upper quadrant pain radiating to the shoulder and positive Murphy's sign, rather than primary flank pain and rigors. Small Bowel Obstruction (Option C) and Volvulus (Option D) present with diffuse abdominal distension, vomiting, and constipation rather than localized flank pain and a high febrile response. Diagnosis of emphysematous pyelonephritis is confirmed via CT scan showing gas in the kidney. Immediate management focuses on broad-spectrum antibiotics and stabilization of any underlying diabetes, as this condition carries a high mortality rate without rapid intervention
questions.learning: The clinical combination of high-grade fever with rigors and acute right flank pain in a 55-year-old patient points strongly toward a severe renal infection.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl presents with Tanner stage II breast development along with a white, non-foul-smelling vaginal discharge. This physiological discharge is most likely caused by the action of which hormone?
questions.explanation: During the early stages of puberty, specifically Tanner stage II (breast budding), rising levels of estrogen from the developing ovaries stimulate the vaginal epithelium. This hormone causes the epithelium to proliferate and produce glycogen. The presence of glycogen supports the growth of lactobacilli, which create an acidic environment and result in physiological leukorrhea—a normal, odorless, white vaginal discharge that typically precedes menarche. GnRH (Option A) is the hypothalamic hormone that triggers the pituitary but does not directly act on the vaginal mucosa. Inhibin B (Option C) is involved in the feedback loop for FSH and does not produce discharge. B-Lynch suture (Option D) is a surgical technique used to control postpartum hemorrhage and is irrelevant to adolescent puberty. Thus, the discharge is a benign, estrogen-mediated developmental sign
questions.learning: During the early stages of puberty, specifically Tanner stage II (breast budding), rising levels of estrogen from the developing ovaries stimulate the vaginal epithelium.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about retrosternal goitre?
options: Operated in all patients regardless of symptoms
Sternal incision is always required to operate
It receives blood supply from the thoracodorsal artery
Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision

Most of the retrosternal goiters can be removed by neck incision (transcervical approach).

Retrosternal goitre is defined as having >50% of the goiter below the suprasternal notch. It can be either primary or secondary.

• Primary: rare and arises from ectopic thyroid tissue in the mediastinum; receives blood supply from intrathoracic blood vessels. It is not related to thyroid tissue in the neck.
• Secondary: they are the most common type; an extension of enlarged thyroid from the neck, usually arising from the lower pole of nodular goitre. It receives its blood supply from superior and inferior thyroid vessels.

The majority of patients are asymptomatic or have minimal symptoms. If the gland enlarges within the thoracic inlet, the pressure may lead to dysphagia, tracheal compression, and eventually airway symptoms. Pemberton sign can be positive (facial flushing and dilatation of cervical veins upon raising the arms above the head).

CECT neck and thorax is the investigation of choice.

Over 95% of retrosternal goiters can be removed via a transcervical incision since they are an extension from thyroid tissue in the neck.

Other options:

Option A: Surgical removal of the retrosternal goiter is indicated in patients with significant airway compression, and in young patients who have symptoms such as dyspnoea or dysphagia.

Option B: Median sternotomy approach is indicated in:

• Primary mediastinal goiter
• Malignant retrosternal goitre
• Very large retrosternal goiter
• Recurrence in the mediastinum

For a primary mediastinal goiter whose boundaries are completely within the chest, resection is often achieved through median sternotomy or thoracotomy to ensure that the vessels supplying the tumor are properly ligated. Removing the tumor through a cervical approach can result in uncontrolled bleeding and is generally avoided.

Option C: Blood supply to the retrosternal goiter is from the thyroid vessels (secondary retrosternal goiter).
questions.learning: Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision Most of the retrosternal goiters can be removed by neck incision (transcervical approach).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient underwent cystoscopy, which showed multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder. The histopathology image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malakoplakia

The cystoscopy findings of multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder and histopathology image showing Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are consistent with the diagnosis of malakoplakia.

Malakoplakia is a rare inflammatory reaction seen in chronic cystitis. It is caused due to acquired defects in phagocyte function, chronic bacterial infection by Escherichia coli or Proteus species, and immunosuppression (renal transplant patients).

The term malakoplakia means soft plaques. Grossly, malakoplakia appears as soft, yellow, slightly raised mucosal plaques.

Microscopically, they are composed of large, foamy macrophages mixed with occasional multinucleate giant cells and lymphocytes. The macrophages in malakoplakia have abundant granular cytoplasm due to phagosomes stuffed with undigested bacterial products and intracellular deposition of calcium and iron within enlarged lysosomes form laminated basophilic concretions. These are known as Michaelis–Gutmann bodies, pathognomonic of malakoplakia (shown below).

The image given below shows the Von Kossa stain demonstrating calcium and iron-containing Michaelis-Gutman bodies (MG bodies) in malakoplakia.

Note: Xanthogranulomatous cystitis is morphologically and probably pathogenetically similar to malakoplakia, but it lacks Michaelis–Gutmann bodies.

Other options:

Option A: Interstitial cystitis, also known as chronic pelvic pain syndrome, is a disorder of the urinary bladder that presents with urinary tract symptoms of more than six weeks duration of unknown etiology. Grossly, it is associated with chronic mucosal ulcers called Hunner's ulcers. Microscopically, there is a non-specific increase in mast cells in the submucosa. Biopsy should be done in all cases to rule out carcinoma in situ.

The cystoscopy image shows Hunner's ulcer, seen in interstitial cystitis.

Option C: Polypoid cystitis is an inflammatory lesion resulting from irritation of the bladder mucosa, most commonly due to indwelling catheters. The urothelium is thrown into broad bulbous polypoid projections due to marked submucosal edema. They must be differentiated from papillary urothelial carcinoma.

The given image below shows polypoid cystitis showing broad polypoid growth, prominent blood vessels, and metaplastic urothelium in H&E stain.

Option D: Acute cystitis is characterized by an inflammation of the urinary bladder following infection, most commonly by Escherichia coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter. It is more commonly seen in women due to the short urethra. Microscopically, there is hyperemia and neutrophilic infiltration of the mucosa.
questions.learning: Malakoplakia — The cystoscopy findings of multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder and histopathology image showing Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are consistent with the diagnosis of malakoplakia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A gross specimen of the colon obtained from a 14-year-old boy is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial adenomatous polyposis

The gross specimen in the image shows the presence of multiple polyps in the colon suggestive of familial adenomatous polyposis.

Familial adenomatous polyposis is an autosomal dominant disease that usually occurs in teenagers

* It is caused by mutations in the APC gene, which is a key negative regulator in the WNT signaling pathway

* 75% of the cases are inherited and a few are sporadic

* The polyps are morphologically indistinguishable from sporadic adenomas. The gross appearance will be a sessile or pedunculated mass between 0.3 to 10 cm in diameter. The texture will be velvet or raspberry. Histologically, the hallmark of epithelial dysplasia is nuclear hyperchromasia, elongation, and stratification. They can be classified as tubular, villous, or tubulovillous based on architecture

* Colorectal carcinoma occurs in 100% of cases before the age of 50.

* Prophylactic colectomy is recommended in patients with APC gene mutations.

* At least 100 polyps are required to make a diagnosis of familial adenomatous polyposis.

Pearl PF0293: Features of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis

Gastrointestinal manifestations:

* Colon and rectum: Multiple adenomatous polyp usually >100

* Gastric and duodenal polyps are present in 50% cases.

* Gastric polyp: fundal gland polyp, gastric adenoma.

* Duodenal polyp usually in the ampullary region: Adenomatous and premalignant

Extraintestinal manifestations

* Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) seen in 75% of cases; it is detected by indirect ophthalmoscopy.

* Epidermoid cysts

* Desmoid tumors in the abdomen

* Osteoma: In the skull, mandible, and tibia

* Brain tumors

* Tumors of the thyroid, adrenal, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, and bile duct
questions.learning: Familial adenomatous polyposis — The gross specimen in the image shows the presence of multiple polyps in the colon suggestive of familial adenomatous polyposis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents in a disoriented state with bradycardia (heart rate 50/min), hypotension (80/60 mmHg), marked respiratory depression (7 breaths/min), hypothermia (95°F), and pinpoint pupils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic "opioid toxidrome" triad: CNS depression (disorientation), respiratory depression (7 breaths/min), and pinpoint pupils (miosis). Other supporting clinical signs include bradycardia (50 bpm), hypotension (80/60 mmHg), and hypothermia (95 F). Benzodiazepine overdose (Option A) also causes CNS and respiratory depression but typically results in normal or dilated pupils. Cocaine intoxication (Option B) is a sympathomimetic syndrome characterized by tachycardia, hypertension, and dilated pupils (mydriasis). Opioid withdrawal (Option C) presents with symptoms opposite to intoxication, such as agitation, tachycardia, diarrhea, and dilated pupils. The presence of pinpoint pupils is a highly specific marker for opioid toxicity, necessitating immediate airway support and the administration of Naloxone. Therefore, opioid intoxication is the definitive diagnosis for this clinical presentation
questions.learning: The patient presents with the classic "opioid toxidrome" triad: CNS depression (disorientation), respiratory depression (7 breaths/min), and pinpoint pupils (miosis).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child is urgently brought to the emergency department after ingesting a large quantity of iron tablets, presenting with severe abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, and lethargy. What is the preferred treatment in this case?
questions.explanation: Acute iron poisoning is a pediatric medical emergency that classically progresses through five clinical stages, beginning with severe gastrointestinal irritation, vomiting, diarrhea, and bleeding, followed by systemic toxicity. The specific antidote and treatment of choice for significant systemic iron toxicity is Deferoxamine mesylate. Deferoxamine is a potent iron-chelating agent that binds ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to form ferrioxamine, a water-soluble complex that is readily excreted in the urine. Importantly, deferoxamine does not chelate iron bound to hemoglobin, myoglobin, or cytochromes, preserving essential physiological functions. Penicillamine (Option A) is used in Wilson disease (copper) and for lead poisoning, not iron. Dimercaprol (BAL) (Option B) is indicated for arsenic and mercury poisoning but is contraindicated in iron toxicity because the BAL–iron complex is toxic. Activated charcoal (Option C) is ineffective, as it does not bind iron. Indications for deferoxamine include serum iron levels >500 µg/dL or clinical evidence of severe toxicity such as metabolic acidosis or shock. A classic sign of effective chelation is “vin rose” (reddish-pink) urine due to ferrioxamine excretion
questions.learning: Acute iron poisoning is a pediatric medical emergency that classically progresses through five clinical stages, beginning with severe gastrointestinal irritation, vomiting, diarrhea, and bleeding, followed by systemic toxicity.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with nausea and severe abdominal pain after accidental ingestion of iron tablets. What is the recommended antidote for managing iron toxicity in this child?
questions.explanation: Deferoxamine is the specific chelating agent used as the antidote for acute iron poisoning. It works by binding to free ferric iron to form ferrioxamine, which is then safely excreted in the urine, often giving the urine a characteristic "vin rose" (reddish) color. This treatment is indicated in severe cases where the patient shows signs of shock, systemic toxicity, or has an extremely high serum iron level. EDTA (Option A) is used primarily for lead poisoning. British anti-Lewisite (BAL) (Option C) is a chelator for arsenic, gold, and mercury. Penicillamine (Option D) is used for copper toxicity (Wilson's disease) and some cases of lead poisoning. Acute iron ingestion in a toddler is life-threatening because iron is directly corrosive to the gastric mucosa, causing the described abdominal pain, and can lead to fulminant hepatic failure. Therefore, prompt administration of deferoxamine is the standard life-saving procedure

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 54-year-old woman presents with cervical cancer stage 2A. It is decided to give neoadjuvant chemotherapy. What does neoadjuvant chemotherapy mean?
options: Chemotherapy given before radical surgery to reduce bulk of tumor
Chemotherapy given after radical surgery for micrometastases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chemotherapy given before radical surgery to reduce bulk of tumor

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is defined as chemotherapy given before the definitive treatment (usually surgery) to reduce the bulk of the tumor.

Neoadjuvant therapy is a type of induction therapy that is given before the definitive surgery to downstage the tumor, reduce the morbidity of treatment, know the in vivo response of the tumor to therapy, and increase its chances of success. Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or hormonal therapy can be given as neoadjuvant therapy.

Option A: Treatment that involves the administration of chemotherapy along with radiation is called chemoradiation.

Option B: Hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) is used during surgery in which a hyperthermic solution of anticancer drugs is infused directly into the abdominal cavity after the definitive surgery to kill any residual tumor cells. It is often used to treat cancers that have spread to the peritoneum.

Option D: Treatment given after surgical resection of the tumor to reduce the risk of recurrence and micrometastasis is called adjuvant therapy. Adjuvant therapy can be chemotherapy, radiation therapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, or biological therapy.
questions.learning: Chemotherapy given before radical surgery to reduce bulk of tumor Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is defined as chemotherapy given before the definitive treatment (usually surgery) to reduce the bulk of the tumor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Glymphatics is the lymphatic like structure of which system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Central Nervous System

The glymphatic system is a lymphatic-like waste clearance pathway of the central nervous system (CNS). It facilitates the exchange of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with interstitial fluid (ISF) through perivascular spaces, allowing the removal of metabolic waste products from the brain.

The system is dependent on astrocytic aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels and is most active during sleep.

• The glymphatic system is unique to the CNS and functions as the brain’s waste clearance mechanism.
• It removes:

• β-amyloid
• Tau protein
• Other metabolic waste products

• Impaired glymphatic function has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease, traumatic brain injury, and other neurodegenerative disorders.

Why not the other options?

• B. Respiratory system: Does not possess a glymphatic system.
• C. Renal system: Has lymphatics but no glymphatic pathway.
• D. Gastrointestinal system: Has a conventional lymphatic system, not a glymphatic system.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old pregnant women came with a history of thyroid swelling. FNAC report was suggestive of papillary carcinoma thyroid and the nodule was “cold” on scan. Which of the following will not be a treatment option for her?
options: Total thyroidectomy plus lymph node dissection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radioiodine ablation of thyroid

Radioactive ablation of the thyroid is an absolute contraindication in pregnancy as it can cause fetal goiter and hypothyroidism.

Radioactive ablation of the thyroid is done using the radioactive isotope of iodine (I-131), which has a half-life of 8 days. I-131 emits gamma rays (useful in imaging) and beta particles (useful in therapy). I-131 is concentrated within the thyroid follicles and emits radiation from within the tissue. The beta particles penetrate only 0.5-2 mm of the tissue. The thyroid follicular cells are affected from within and undergo pyknosis and necrosis followed by fibrosis without damage to neighboring tissues.

Radioactive iodine is administered as the sodium salt of I-131 dissolved in water and taken orally.

Therapeutic uses of radioactive iodine:

• Distant metastasis at diagnosis (papillary or follicular carcinoma)
• Incomplete tumor resection
• Patients at high risk for mortality or recurrence
• Graves disease
• Toxic multinodular goitre

The average therapeutic dose is 3-6 m curie, calculated based on previous tracer studies and thyroid size.

Contraindications:

• Pregnancy
• Lactation
• Young age (<25 years)
• Moderate to severe Graves ophthalmopathy

Management of differentiated thyroid cancer in pregnancy:

• Thyroidectomy after delivery for patients with no evidence of advanced disease or no rapid progression and in the second trimester for patients with rapid progression or signs of advanced disease.
• Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation. If it is needed after delivery, breastfeeding shall be stopped at least 6 weeks before ablative therapy and mothers should be advised against nursing.
• Levothyroxine supplementation: as a suppressive treatment for those who decided to postpone surgery till the second trimester or after delivery, as a replacement therapy after thyroidectomy, and as a suppressive therapy for patients with residual disease.
• Differentiated thyroid cancer not responding to radioactive iodine can be treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

Diagnostic radioiodine scan:  25–100 µ curie of I-131 is given; counting or scanning is done at intervals.
questions.learning: Radioiodine ablation of thyroid Radioactive ablation of the thyroid is an absolute contraindication in pregnancy as it can cause fetal goiter and hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the options below best defines LD50?
options: 50% animal mortality in an experiment after exposure to the drug
50% reduction of infection in the given population of experimental animals
Dose of the drug that causes adverse effects in 50% of the population
Range of concentration at which the likelihood of efficacy is high and the probability of adverse effects is low
questions.explanation: 50% animal mortality is an experiment after exposure to the drug In toxicology and pharmacology, Median Lethal Dose (LD50) is a standardized measure used to evaluate the acute toxicity of a substance. It is specifically defined as the dose required to cause death in exactly 50% of the tested population of experimental animals within a specified time frame. Option B is incorrect as it describes the curative dose (ED50) or infection control. Option C refers to the Median Toxic Dose (TD50), which measures adverse side effects rather than lethality. Option D describes the Therapeutic Window or Index, which is a safety margin between effective and toxic concentrations. Determining the LD50 is a fundamental step in safety assessment, helping researchers understand the relative danger of chemicals and drugs. A lower LD50 value indicates higher toxicity, as a smaller dose is needed to reach the 50% mortality threshold in the study subjects.
questions.learning: 50% animal mortality is an experiment after exposure to the drug In toxicology and pharmacology, Median Lethal Dose (LD50) is a standardized measure used to evaluate the acute toxicity of a substance.

questions.text: Common precursor amino acid for urea, creatine and nitric oxide is____.

Arginine is the common precursor for urea, creatine and nitric oxide.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman presents with acute right lower abdominal pain for 4 hours, with tenderness at McBurney’s point. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm a diagnosis of appendicitis?
questions.explanation: While acute appendicitis is often a clinical diagnosis based on history and tenderness at McBurney's point, a CT Scan of the abdomen (ideally with contrast) is currently the most accurate and "best suited" investigation to confirm the diagnosis (Option A) . It has high sensitivity and specificity for identifying an inflamed appendix, periappendiceal fat stranding, or an appendicolith. A plain X-ray (Option B) is rarely useful and may only show non-specific signs. Serum ESR (Option C) is a non-specific marker of inflammation that does not provide localized diagnostic information. MRI (Option D) is highly accurate but is generally reserved as a second-line option for pregnant patients or children to avoid ionizing radiation. Therefore, for a 23-year-old non-pregnant female, the CT scan remains the definitive gold standard imaging modality. It allows for prompt surgical planning and helps rule out other pelvic pathologies like ovarian torsion
questions.learning: While acute appendicitis is often a clinical diagnosis based on history and tenderness at McBurney's point, a CT Scan of the abdomen (ideally with contrast) is currently the most accurate and "best suited" investigation to confirm the diagnosis (Option A) .

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient with longstanding hypertension and diabetes mellitus is evaluated for renal function. In explaining the role of glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which statement correctly describes how GFR is regulated?
options: An increase in sympathetic function increases GFR
An increase in RPF increases GFR
A decrease in RPF increases GFR
questions.explanation: The Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is heavily dependent on Renal Plasma Flow (RPF). Under physiological conditions, an increase in RPF increases the GFR because it maintains a high hydrostatic pressure across the glomerular capillaries and prevents the rapid rise of oncotic pressure that would otherwise oppose filtration. Afferent arteriolar constriction (Option B) or an increase in sympathetic activity (Option A) both cause a decrease in RPF and a subsequent decrease in GFR by reducing the blood entering the glomerulus. A decrease in RPF (Option D) would lead to a decrease in GFR. GFR is also regulated by autoregulatory mechanisms (tubuloglomerular feedback) and hormones like Angiotensin II. For a patient with diabetes and hypertension, maintaining an optimal GFR is vital to prevent the progression of chronic kidney disease. Understanding that RPF and GFR are generally directly proportional is a core principle of renal physiology, making Option C the only accurate statement

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient’s blood sample tests positive for infectious hepatitis B. Which serological marker best indicates this infectious state?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis of an active and highly infectious Hepatitis B infection requires specific serological markers. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is the first marker to appear and its presence indicates that the person is currently infected. The Hepatitis B "e" antigen (HBeAg) is a marker of high viral replication and signifies that the patient is highly infectious. Therefore, the combination of HBsAg and HBeAg (Option B) is the definitive indicator of an active, infectious state. Isolated HBeAg (Option A) is not used for primary diagnosis without HBsAg. Hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg) (Option C) is not typically detected in blood as it is sequestered within the viral envelope. The presence of anti-HBe (Option D) usually indicates a transition to a lower infectivity state. For these reasons, HBsAg + HBeAg remains the gold standard for identifying high-risk infectious cases
questions.learning: The diagnosis of an active and highly infectious Hepatitis B infection requires specific serological markers. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is the first marker to appear and its presence indicates that the person is currently infected.

questions.text: Which clinical examination is being done in the picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fluid thrill

The clinical examination elicited is Fluid thrill.

The fluid thrill is elicited to clinically diagnose ascites.

It is not a reliable sign and is only felt when there is a large amount of fluid under tension.

Method: The patient is placed supine and his abdomen is exposed after consent. Place one hand of the examiner flat over the lumbar region while an assistant's hand is kept firmly on the midline of the abdomen with the side of his hand kept longitudinally. This is done to dampen any impulse that can be transmitted via the fat of the abdominal wall. Now the examiner flicks or taps the opposite side of the abdomen where his palm is not resting and a fluid thrill or wave is felt on the resting hand.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A middle-aged woman with a history of renal calculi complaints of bone pain and abdominal cramps. X-ray shows subperiosteal resorption of 2nd and 3rd metacarpals and phalanges. On investigation, serum calcium and PTH were raised and phosphate levels were decreased. Which of the following investigations will help localise the primary pathology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 99Tc-Radiolabelled Sestamibi scan

The given clinical picture is highly suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a solitary parathyroid adenoma arising sporadically. It is best localised using a 99Tc- Radiolabelled sestamibi scan.

Hyperparathyroidism is caused by elevated parathyroid hormone and is classified into primary, secondary, and tertiary types.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism

an autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH)

compensatory hypersecretion of PTH in response to prolonged hypocalcemia
persistent hypersecretion of PTH even after the cause of prolonged hypocalcemia is corrected

Parathyroid  adenoma or hyperplasia
chronic renal failure
after renal transplant.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is one of the most common endocrine disorders, and it is an important cause of hypercalcemia. Tumours of the parathyroid glands usually come to attention because of excessive secretion of PTH rather than mass effects. It can also be associated with MEN1 and MEN 2A syndromes.

The clinical manifestations of hyperparathyroidism can be summarized as “painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans.” Skeletal manifestations of hyperparathyroidism include bone resorption, osteitis fibrosa cystica, and brown tumours. Renal changes include nephrolithiasis (stones) and nephrocalcinosis.

Localisation of parathyroid is difficult. Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabeled Sestamibi is a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue. It is now regarded as the most accurate and reliable method for imaging the parathyroid glands.

Other options:

Option B: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is not commonly used to image the parathyroid glands

Option C: Ultrasonography of the neck is a safe and widely used technique for the localization of abnormal parathyroid glands. However, ultrasonography is operator, lesion size and location dependent. Ectopic locations are difficult to locate.

Option D: Multiphase CT imaging has become widely utilized to localize the disease. It gives both anatomical as well as functional information about the parathyroid glands. The disadvantage is the higher radiation dose when compared to others.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids are necessary for purine ring formation?
questions.explanation: The purine ring (the core of adenine and guanine) is constructed atom-by-atom on a ribose-5-phosphate scaffold. Three specific amino acids contribute various nitrogen and carbon atoms to this structure: Glycine, Aspartate, and Glutamine. Glycine contributes the C4, C5, and N7 atoms. Glutamine provides the amide nitrogen for N3 and N9. Aspartate contributes the amino nitrogen for N1. Other contributors (not listed) include and N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate. Valine (Option A) and Glutamate (Option C) are not directly incorporated into the purine ring. Asparagine (Option D) is not a purine precursor. This pathway is clinically targeted by many drugs: methotrexate inhibits folate contribution, while 6-mercaptopurine and mycophenolate mofetil interfere with purine synthesis to treat cancers and autoimmune diseases. Understanding the raw materials required for nucleotide synthesis is a classic high-yield biochemistry topic, linking nutrition and metabolism directly to the body's ability to replicate DNA and produce energy-carrying molecules like ATP
questions.learning: The purine ring (the core of adenine and guanine) is constructed atom-by-atom on a ribose-5-phosphate scaffold. Three specific amino acids contribute various nitrogen and carbon atoms to this structure: Glycine, Aspartate, and Glutamine.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During general anesthesia, which peripheral nerve is most commonly stimulated with a nerve stimulator to monitor the depth of neuromuscular blockade?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is the standard site for peripheral nerve stimulation during anesthesia to monitor neuromuscular blockade (NMB). It is preferred because it is superficial at the wrist and provides a clear, measurable motor response in the adductor pollicis muscle. This response accurately reflects the depth of muscle relaxation and helps determine the timing for reversal or extubation. The radial nerve (Option A) is deeper and less reliable for this purpose. The median nerve (Option C) is typically used for somatosensory monitoring rather than NMB. While the tibial nerve (Option D) can be monitored, it is technically more difficult and less standardized than the ulnar approach. Thus, the ulnar nerve remains the gold standard
